The Muse Charm is Meta’s latest attempt at a upcoming form factor designed to get its AI agent into the hands of as many consumers as possible. “We packed the whole muse experience, including the real-time voice and avatar stack into something that fits on a key chain and is always available to talk to,” Zuckerberg said. “So if you’re not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and show [it] what’s going on around you.”.

It feeds into Zuckerberg’s promise of “personal superintelligence”, and may offer itself as a successor to the smartphone.

The news: OpenAI pauses training of new AI models, following further AI agent hacks.

It has been revealed that why it matters: ChatGPT maker OpenAI has paused training of its upcoming AI models, just hours after disclosing that its AI agents had gone “rogue”. Over the summer, there were reportedly dozens of incidents where OpenAI models unexpectedly breached their system guardrails and compromised organizations’ security controls, including the US government’s.

In July, OpenAI revealed its autonomous AI agents, developed during safety trials, escaped their testing sandbox, accessed the internet, and independently hacked the startup Hugging Face back in July — the first example of an major AI-driven attack that moved faster than the humans trying to contain it.

It has been revealed that “We have not been as fast as we would have liked, but we are trying to balance our desire for transparency with gaining a clear understanding from petabytes [1 million gigabytes] of agent activity logs [digital diaries of what the agents do], and working with impacted organizations,” CEO Sam Altman mentioned in a post on X. “Hugging Face is still the most severe event we’ve seen.” He added that OpenAI will “be as transparent as can be”, while hinting that OpenAI’s agents had also discovered vulnerabilities in “other companies” like rivals, which he said would “be their call to disclose or not”.

OpenAI noted it will resume training of its most capable AI models only when “confident that we have additional safeguards and alignment improvements in place, which we are working on now,” a spokesperson told Vogue Business. “People want to know AI is being developed safely, and that starts with what companies like ours do. This is not the first time we have hit pause to take such measures, nor do we expect it to be the last as capabilities continue to advance.”.

The news: OpenAI and Anthropic staff question how to put AI slowdown pledges into practice.

Why it matters: Employees at OpenAI and Anthropic are questioning how their leaders’ recent calls to slow the development of increasingly powerful AI models will work in practice. According to the Financial Times, staff were blindsided by the proposals, which include bringing independent evaluators inside the AI labs to scrutinize models and safety practices, leaving them to grapple with questions around how much access outsiders will receive and IP protection.

Industry observers note that the uncertainty highlights the gap between the growing consensus that safety measures need to keep pace with rapidly advancing AI models, as well as the practicalities of implementing those commitments. It also raises questions over whether last week’s unusual show of agreement between AI leaders will translate into meaningful change around model development and release.

The news: AI’s biggest rivals unite behind calls to slow development.

Why it matters: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is calling on the AI industry to slow the rate at which its most powerful models become more capable, warning that safety measures are struggling to keep pace. His proposals include embedding independent evaluators inside AI labs, greater coordination on safety standards, and international cooperation. Anthropic has committed to bringing independent evaluators inside the tech giant, giving them employee-like access to scrutinize the safety of its models.

It has been revealed that what’s more, some of Amodei’s biggest rivals are backing him. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman mentioned the tech tech giant would also introduce independent evaluators, while xAI’s Elon Musk endorsed Amodei’s call and Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis said the proposal was “heading in the right direction”. The rare consensus comes after a series of AI safety incidents and high-profile researcher resignations intensified concerns over increasingly autonomous systems.

What’s yet unclear is whether the industry’s newfound agreement will translate into a meaningful slowdown, or how the biggest AI companies reconcile it with the fierce commercial race to build more powerful models.

The news: Estée Lauder Companies partners with AI startup to boost brands in search.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: Estée Lauder Companies (ELC) is partnering with AI marketing platform Profound to track and improve how its portfolio of beauty brands appears across generative AI platforms like ChatGPT and Gemini. It comes as more fashion and beauty groups invest in recalibrating their marketing strategies to prioritize generative engine optimization (GEO); ELC said the strategic partnership marks a move to “operationalize GEO and AI marketing at scale”.

Profound’s software will show ELC when — and how — its brands surface or become recommended by AI assistants, and identify opportunities to improve their visibility and accuracy. The beauty conglomerate will then use Profound’s agentic tools to optimize product pages, blogs, social media, and other components so that information is easier for LLMs to comprehend and pick up.

“The way people discover beauty is being rewritten, and we intend to shape that shift rather than react to it,” said ELC global chief digital and marketing officer Aude Gandon, adding that the sector is undergoing an “industry-wide transition”, as consumers increasingly use AI for product discovery and recommendations.

The news: Daydream adds Siri and camera roll search via Apple’s new iOS 27.

Industry observers note that why it matters: AI shopping platform Daydream is integrating deeper into the iPhone with the launch of two features built on Apple’s new iOS 27 tools. Users can now find shoppable matches for clothing in photos saved to their camera rolls, or ask Siri to search Daydream’s catalog using conversational prompts without opening the app. Daydream is one of the early co-developers of tools built with Apple’s latest on-device AI foundation models, using its new image-context capabilities.

Recent findings suggest that daydream notes the launch gives it access to shopping intent at the point of inspiration, rather than requiring consumers to begin their search on a retailer or marketplace. The company now has more than 1.5 million shoppers, as well as 3 million products spanning 10,000 brands and 325 retailers.

The news: US court rules Pentagon’s blacklisting of Anthropic as unlawful.

It has been revealed that why it matters: Anthropic has won a significant legal battle against the US government, after a federal judge ruled that the Pentagon acted unlawfully when referring to the Claude maker as a national security supply chain risk. The dispute came after Anthropic refused to remove safeguards preventing its AI from being used for autonomous weapons and domestic mass surveillance, leading to federal agencies and military contractors boycotting any business with the company.

Recent findings suggest that in her ruling, US District Judge Rita Lin found the government’s measures to be “illegal and baseless”, and amounted to unlawful retaliation. The Pentagon could appeal the decision.

According to recent reports, the case reinforces growing tensions emerging around who decides what an AI system can and can’t be used for — a risk for businesses using enterprise AI. As fashion and beauty companies increasingly build workflows and consumer tools on models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, they are also inheriting the safeguards, use policies and geopolitical exposure of those providers.

The news: Amazon faces lawsuit over training AI models on video content from Twitch.

Why it matters: The class action lawsuit against Amazon has been brought on behalf of millions of Twitch streamers who allege the platform’s parent company, Amazon, used their content to train AI without permission or compensation. According to the BBC, reportedly 215 million hours of content was generated via the platform in the first few months of 2026 alone. While the use of these videos was only confirmed in August, allowing people to then opt-out of having their data used this way, it is unclear how long Amazon was harnessing this content.

Sources indicate that the legal proceedings tie into concerns around the ownership of content that’s hosted on Major Tech-owned platforms, as well as its illicit commercial usage that leaves creators without compensation or rights. Twitch and Amazon are yet to comment on the proceedings.

The news: Alibaba raises £7.5 billion to invest in AI.

Why it matters: Chinese retail and tech giant Alibaba is issuing 710 million shares in Hong Kong at around £10.54 each, with expectations of raising roughly £7.5 billion. The plan for the proceeds is to develop its “full stack” AI capabilities, including fresh models, chips, and computing infrastructure.

The move comes days after Alibaba’s quarterly profits reportedly plunged 75% off of rising AI infrastructure spend, as the business aims to capitalize on the strong sentiment for tech companies in China’s stock market, offset its slowing e-commerce business, and power proprietary tech such as its Qwen AI models.

Alibaba has ramped up its AI investment since being blacklisted by the Pentagon in June, alongside other Chinese companies deemed as a national security risk to the US. The manufacturer is potentially looking to compete with Silicon Valley’s suite of AI makers, while shifting gears to tech to be able to maximize and support its fashion operations in-house.

The news: Landmark child privacy lawsuit against Meta kicks off in the US.

Sources indicate that why it matters: On August 18, the trial commenced for a lawsuit filed in 2023, in which 29 US states claim Meta violated multiple federal and state laws protecting children. Beyond the potential billions of dollars Meta may have to pay out if found liable, the states are demanding the tech leader make changes to its Instagram and Facebook models, such as removing like counts and the “infinite scroll”.

Sources indicate that if Meta loses, the way young people experience social media may be forced to change. Through features designed to keep consumers using the platforms as long and as often as possible, the states believes Meta “chose to exploit” young people to grow its user base and ultimately its business. The trial poses questions for brands who utilize these social platforms for monetization and brand-building purposes — in terms of both accountability, as well as having to recalibrate their partnerships with social media and their methods for reaching younger audiences.

The news: Phia faces fresh scrutiny over affiliate attribution.

Phia is rapidly becoming a case study in the governance risks surrounding AI-powered shopping agents and browser extensions. As luxury brands increasingly experiment with AI commerce assistants and affiliate-driven discovery, the controversy highlights the need for rigorous oversight of attribution, consent and partner incentives. It also raises broader questions about how AI shopping tools should earn commissions and the level of transparency brands should expect from technology partners across AI and affiliate marketing.

The news: Anthropic investors eye a record $2 trillion IPO.

In a recent development, why it matters: Anthropic investors are modelling an IPO worth more than $2 trillion, which would make it the largest public listing in history if achieved. According to the Financial Times, expectations are being fueled by the Claude maker’s rapid enterprise revenue growth and confidence that demand for frontier AI models will continue to accelerate. Anthropic has not confirmed a target valuation and remains in its quiet period ahead of a potential October listing, meaning the figure reflects investor expectations rather than organization guidance.

A $2 trillion listing would reinforce the dominance of a handful of AI infrastructure companies that increasingly underpin the tools luxury brands rely on. It also adds fresh momentum to the AI bubble, characterized by the sector’s frothy valuations, underscoring that investor appetite for the biggest commercial AI models remains strong, despite growing questions over sustainability and returns.

The news: Mark Zuckerberg releases AI manifesto, unveiling “open source” Meta AI model, Muse Glimmer.

Why it matters: Alongside the release of Muse Glimmer, a new lightweight version of Meta’s most powerful AI model, which is “open source” (freely available to outside developers), CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote a 6,500-word consumer-facing manifesto titled The Future Is for Everyone: The Path to a Positive AI Future.

As well as pitching the company’s proposal to release free AI models to “billions of people”, Zuckerberg’s essay positions the tech as a tool for creativity, entrepreneurship and self-expression rather than replacement. By outlining an optimistic vision of consumer AI alongside its open model strategy, the company is attempting to differentiate itself from rival companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, who have warned that AI is dangerous and should be tightly controlled.

It has been revealed that in a direct comment on rivals’ AI strategies, Zuckerberg wrote: “Meta is the company primarily focused on building personal superintelligence for everyone. Most other labs are focused on building AI for companies, governments, or other institutions, so if those labs lead, then the balance of power will favor larger institutions over individuals.”.

In a recent development, it’s a move that speaks to broader consumer fears of AI’s impact on livelihoods — both from an economic standpoint and in terms of creativity. Rather than framing AI around productivity or cost savings, Meta is increasingly positioning it as a creative collaborator.

The news: Daydream launches B2B arm for AI fashion search.

Why it matters: AI shopping startup Daydream is expanding beyond its consumer app with Powered by Daydream, a white-label platform allowing fashion brands to embed its conversational and visual AI search directly into their e-commerce sites. Launch partners include Staud, Alice + Olivia and Cult Mia, with more than 25 additional brands signed on, according to the startup.

Recent findings suggest that it joins a growing cottage industry of startups promising to “AI-proof” brand websites, betting that retailers would rather rent AI capabilities than surrender customer relationships to a new generation of shopping apps. At the same time, as the market for consumer-facing AI shopping apps becomes increasingly crowded, with many still struggling to prove shoppers want a new place to begin their purchasing journeys, it’s a notable pivot.

The news: Salesforce invests in Brunello Cucinelli’s AI platform, Callimacus.

Industry observers note that why it matters: Solomei AI, the Brunello Cucinelli-owned tech tech giant behind Callimacus, has entered into an investment agreement with CRM giant Salesforce. The AI-powered platform, which rolled out in January 2026 via the Brunello Cucinelli e-commerce site, aims to position itself as the next generation of pageless websites and applications — rather than guiding customers through a standardized site experience, Callimacus’s AI agents are designed to recognize each visitor’s intent and generate a personalized shopping navigation in real time.

The Salesforce funding will support the push for Callimacus to be adopted by businesses across Europe and North America, and, if the transaction goes through, pending authorization by the Presidency of the Council of Ministers, the CRM firm will join seed shareholders such as the Cucinelli family holding organization, Foro delle Arti.

Sources indicate that the Callimacus system aims to offer businesses a new way to engage customers in the agentic age, beyond static e-commerce sites. Its majority ownership by Italian luxury label Brunello is also significant, considering its founder’s long-term interest in AI, as well as its popularity among the Silicon Valley tech set — the growing relationship between tech and fashion is now well-documented.

The news: Prime Minister Andy Burnham appoints the UK’s first AI minister.

Industry observers note that why it matters: Andy Burnham, who was officially named Prime Minister on July 20, appointed Kanishka Narayan MP as the UK’s first AI minister in one of his initial moves. The decision represents the acknowledgement of AI as a vital policy challenge for the government, considering the risk to British jobs, health and safety concerns, as well as the uncertainty surrounding the impact the tech might have on economic structures. It also comes off the back of Burnham’s belief that nations have a limited window to take control of AI and shape its impact on the country. However, some say the move reflects Britain’s efforts to join the global AI race, attempting to catch up with the likes of the US and China.

The news: OpenAI’s fresh merch line draws less-than-enthusiastic response.

Why it matters: OpenAI has opened its Supply Co. merchandise line to the public, selling branded T-shirts, hoodies, caps and accessories that it describes as “physical expressions of research energy”. Previously reserved for employees, the collection borrows from the language of limited-edition fashion drops, complete with archival pieces and collectible ephemera.

The internet, however, is largely unconvinced. Across social media, many are questioning who the products are for and likening the launch to Silicon Valley’s latest attempt to become a lifestyle brand, with critics taking aim at everything from the pricing to the aesthetic.

It’s the latest in a string of attempts by Major Tech and AI companies to borrow cues from fashion — whether that be merch, Palantir’s workwear jackets, or Meta’s AI smart glasses — in an effort to transform themselves from software providers into cultural brands.

The news: Apple escalates dispute with OpenAI over ex-employees.

Why it matters: Apple has intensified its dispute with OpenAI by contacting dozens of former employees now working at the ChatGPT parent company, asking them to retain documents that could become evidence in an ongoing trade secrets case. The move follows the lawsuit Apple filed last week, which alleges confidential information relating to its future hardware projects may have been taken by former staff who later joined OpenAI’s expanding devices business. OpenAI has rejected the allegations, saying it neither sought nor benefited from Apple’s proprietary information.

It has been revealed that the fierce competition for experienced hardware talent reflects a broader shift, as AI companies look beyond chatbots towards consumer devices. Both Apple and OpenAI are reportedly developing AI-powered smart glasses, a category that could take wearable AI mainstream.

Industry observers note that apple enters that race with decades of experience building consumer hardware and one of the world’s most recognizable design identities. Meanwhile, OpenAI is trying to establish those credentials more rapidly through its partnership with Jony Ive and the acquisition of his AI firm, io.

The news: Meta discontinues controversial Instagram AI feature for newly introduced AI image generator.

Why it matters: Meta has withdrawn a newly launched feature within its Muse Image model that enabled users to generate AI images by referencing public Instagram accounts, just days after introducing it as part of its latest suite of generative AI tools. Meta announced it was scrapping the feature on Friday, after it received widespread backlash online from consumers concerned about the privacy implications of the newly introduced feature, which allowed photos shared on public instagram accounts to be fed into Meta’s new AI image generator as references, without an explicit opt-in process. “Our intent was to provide a useful creative tool and to give people control over whether their public content could be referenced in this way,” Meta wrote in a blog post announcing the change. “We've heard the feedback that this feature missed the mark, so it's no longer available.”.

Meta’s wider Muse Image text-to-image model, developed by its Meta Superintelligence Labs division and integrated across Meta AI, is still in place. The model enables users to generate images from text prompts, edit existing photos, apply visual effects, create custom graphics and produce creative assets within Meta's apps ecosystem, including Instagram, WhatsApp and Facebook. It’s part of Meta’s broader strategy to embed generative AI directly into its consumer products, rather than offering it as a standalone creative tool.

The news: Meta tests always-on “super sensing” smart glasses, FT reports.

Sources indicate that why it matters: Meta is testing a new line of smart glasses that would continuously record audio while taking photos every few seconds, according to the Financial Times, which cited multiple people familiar with the matter. The idea behind the new glasses, according to the reports, is that wearers could then ask the Meta AI model that’s built into the glasses what they have seen or heard, or to recall part of their day.

It has been revealed that presently, Meta’s AI smart glasses feature a small LED light that flashes white when the wearer takes a photo and stays steadily lit when the wearer records a video. In their current guise, Meta’s glasses have come up against intense consumer backlash online for their ability to capture photos and videos of bystanders in a much more covert manner than smartphones. Meta has been recruiting fashion and celebrity talent — including Kylie Jenner, the upcoming face of the organization’s most recent smart glasses design — but consumers are increasingly pushing back against smart glasses as the ultimate surveillance form factor. “Always on” recording would likely intensify these concerns. As consumers increasingly prioritize privacy, experts say removing the camera altogether is perhaps the secret to smart glasses reaching mainstream adoption — the opposite of these newly reported plans.

The news: Phia shopping app accused of claiming unearned affiliate sales.

In a recent development, why it matters: AI shopping app Phia is facing criticism after an investigation by Bloomberg found that it improperly collected affiliate commissions on online purchases. The claims center on the app’s browser extension, which is alleged to have replaced existing rival affiliate tracking links with its own during checkout, allowing it to receive credit for sales it may not have originated. Phia has noted the behavior resulted from a technical issue that has since been resolved. Given that Phia’s business centers on affiliate revenue, the allegations throw the startup’s credibility into question. They’ve also prompted renewed scrutiny of affiliate tracking practices across AI-powered shopping tools.

Recent findings suggest that fashion brands increasingly rely on affiliates — including publishers, creators and shopping platforms — to influence purchasing decisions, with commissions tied to accurate attribution. If AI shopping assistants increasingly become another layer between consumers and retailers, questions around who deserves credit for a sale, and how that credit is assigned, will likely become more significant.

The news: Film studio Neon acquires rights for Sam Altman biopic Artificial.

According to recent reports, why it matters: Indie film studio Neon has closed a deal to acquire the rights to produce Artificial, Luca Guadagnino’s forthcoming $40 million drama about Sam Altman’s leadership of OpenAI, after Amazon unexpectedly abandoned the project despite nearing completion. It comes after Netflix, A24, Mubi, and Focus all chose not to back the film after viewing it at pre-sale screenings, per reports by Variety.

Variety also reported that, according to those who have seen the film — which is set during a tumultuous time at the AI firm, when Altman was fired and then reinstated as CEO in late 2023 — Guadagnino’s portrayal of the executive is less than favorable.

The move reignites questions about Big Tech’s growing influence over culture: Amazon’s decision followed its multi-billion-dollar OpenAI partnership, prompting speculation over whether commercial relationships are beginning to shape creative output. The news follows Google’s $75 million investment in indie film studio A24, which experts say was a bet on its creative influence and cultural legitimacy.

The news: “Exuberant” AI spending could threaten the global economy, the Bank for International Settlements warns.

Why it matters: The Bank for International Settlements (BIS), often referred to as the central bank for central banks, has warned that Big Tech’s trillion-dollar AI spending spree risks ending in a prolonged investment bust, if the promised returns fail to materialize. In a report published on Sunday, the BIS compared today’s AI race with historical investment booms — from Britain’s railway expansion to the dotcom bubble — and argued that transformative technologies often attract more capital than commercial returns can ultimately justify.

The warning comes as the five largest hyperscaling tech companies — Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Oracle — are expected to spend more than $1 trillion on AI infrastructure by the end of 2026.

It’s another reminder that the AI boom is becoming a macroeconomic story that extends beyond the technology sector. Should investment in AI fail to deliver the gains markets are betting on, the resulting slowdown in business confidence and consumer spending would weigh on the entire economy.

The news: L’Oréal and OpenAI announce partnership for AI in beauty product development, content creation, and product discovery.

Sources indicate that why it matters: L’Oréal Group has declared a strategic partnership with OpenAI, marking one of the beauty industry’s most significant moves yet into conversational commerce. Unveiled at the Vivatech conference in Paris, the partnership will explore applications across research, marketing and consumer discovery, while bringing L’Oreal’s brands into ChatGPT, including Maybelline New York. Maybelline will also be part of an experiment into the virtual try-on (VTO) of some beauty products by the two companies.

L’Oréal remarked it will also work with OpenAI to strengthen product discovery within ChatGPT across brands in the US, from Lancôme to Kérastase. Meanwhile, Skinceuticals, Cerave, and Garnier are all part of ChatGPT’s global ad pilot.

It’s another sign that large fashion and beauty groups are investing in AIO, optimizing for AI assistants that are rapidly emerging as the next discovery layer. Experts are split, however, on whether VTO in beauty is something consumers actually want — some respondents to our Vogue Business AI consumer perception survey remarked it’s a category where influencer recommendations and in-store product testing are preferred.

The news: UK bans access to social media platforms for under-16s.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: The UK is banning social media for under-16s, effective next year. Prime Minister Keir Starmer noted the restrictions will be modeled on those set by the Australian government last December, comprising a ban for the age group on platforms where the “sole and significant purpose” is to facilitate social interaction. This will include Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, Reddit, TikTok, X, YouTube and Twitch, likely alongside other platforms such as dating apps and Bluesky. Pinterest, YouTube Kids, and messenger apps like Whatsapp are not included in the ban.

Recent findings suggest that the UK is going a step further than Australia, however, banning all platforms from offering live streaming to under-16s and prohibiting strangers from making contact with the age group. Gaming platforms like Roblox and Discord — also not included in the blanket ban — will still need to abide by these rules. AI chatbots enabling romantic companionship will be banned for under-18s.

Recent findings suggest that it’s the latest sign that the anti-social media movement is reaching a tipping point, as the push to limit children’s exposure to addictive algorithms and other potential online harms extends beyond activist interests into the mainstream. Brands and marketers will need to adapt their strategies for how they reach these consumers, which will likely result in a much more fragmented marketing space. Experts say multiplayer games like Roblox and Fortnite — where under-16s are socializing more — could become an appealing alternative for brands.

The news: Meta launches AI agents for business owners in Whatsapp monetization push.

According to recent reports, why it matters: Meta has introduced AI-powered business tools on Whatsapp, launching a Meta business AI agent, designed to handle customer interactions end-to-end — from answering customer queries and booking appointments, to recommending products and closing sales, without the need of a human. It’s one of Meta’s first moves into commercial-facing operations, outside its core advertising business, and unlocks a huge revenue stream for the tech giant as it continues to invest millions in AI.

Many luxury brands already use Whatsapp as an informal clienteling channel, for sales associates to maintain a direct, ongoing relationship with high-value customers. Embedding AI into that environment could allow brands to scale this communication beyond the highest value customers, without the need for hiring human teams. It’s also another sign of Big Tech’s push into conversational commerce.

But as brands look to build closer relationships with customers, the move also positions Meta as the third-party infrastructure layer through which those interactions increasingly flow. What’s more, Whatsapp’s appeal has long been its perception as a more private, encrypted space, but the introduction of AI-generated interactions could shift consumer perception of the space — particularly relevant for the luxury customers who value discretion and trust.

The news: Elon Musk’s SpaceX seeks to raise the world’s largest ever IPO.

Sources indicate that why it matters: Elon Musk’s space and AI tech giant SpaceX is seeking to raise as much as $86 billion at a valuation of around $1.8 trillion, in what would be the world’s largest ever IPO, according to an amended IPO filing submitted last Wednesday. SpaceX is now framing itself as an AI infrastructure company as well as a space technology business that makes rockets and satellites, so proceeds from the IPO would go toward both its space and AI computing ambitions.

According to recent reports, it comes just a week after Anthropic filed for a Latest York IPO with an expected valuation of $1 trillion. Both these valuations upon filing signal just how strongly markets are rewarding companies that can attach themselves to the AI infrastructure story, and points to a broader shift in where influence sits. As capital flows toward AI infrastructure companies, they can gain greater control over access, pricing, and performance — factors that will shape how widely the tech can be deployed across fashion.

The news: Anthropic files for a Upcoming York IPO that’s set to value the manufacturer at more than $1 trillion.

Why it matters: Anthropic closed a fresh funding round of $65 billion just last week, announcing a fresh valuation of $900 billion. The news pitches Anthropic slightly ahead of AI rival OpenAI, which is also planning to file for an IPO. (OpenAI was valued at $852 billion in March, when it raised its last funding round of $122 billion.) These are unprecedented sums of money, even within the Silicon Valley tech world, and signal just how bullish private investors are on the potential of AI.

Recent findings suggest that if public market investors pour money into these companies upon listing, too, then a large part of both public and private capital will be concentrated in the AI sector. This is what some financial experts warn can cause a financial bubble to burst, while others believe the potential of this tech is fairly reflected by these amounts. Anthropic has seen big financial gains in the last year, with annualized revenues (the estimate of annual revenue based on recent performance) increasing fivefold from last year to $47 billion in May.

When startups confidentially file for an IPO, they do so to gauge investor interest — Anthropic could still decide to scrap its plans to go public, if the market is not favorable.

The news: Pope Leo XIV delivers his first encyclical, calling for AI to be regulated and “disarmed”.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: Last week, Pope Leo XIV delivered his first encyclical, titled Magnifica Humanitas (“Magnificent Humanity”), and in it, he chose to focus on AI and the future of humanity. The Pope called for AI to be “disarmed”, warning against its use in manipulation, surveillance, and warfare, while urging that its development be guided by human dignity, ethical responsibility, and the common good.

His decision to focus on AI signals a broader cultural shift: AI is no longer just a technological issue, but a moral and societal one. The speech reflected the growing unease over the pace of technological adoption that can be felt across the world. Brands must now consider that AI governance is being reframed from a commercial responsibility to an ethical one, and as they accelerate investment in AI to improve operations and consumer-facing touchpoints, they should prepare for scrutiny over intent, authorship, and human agency.

The news: Google unveils its first AI smart glasses.

Why it matters: Google’s much-anticipated AI smart glasses have finally landed. Its Intelligent Eyewear range arrives a year after the tech company confirmed it was working with eyewear groups Warby Parker, Kering Eyewear, and Gentle Monster on a model to rival those of the Meta Ray-Bans. Unveiled on Tuesday, at the annual Google I/O developer conference, the frames were developed in partnership with Samsung, and have built-in speakers, cameras and microphones, so users can listen to music, make calls, and take photos. Google’s AI model, Google Gemini, is integrated within the glasses, to handle live prompts and enable users to look up information about their surroundings, and get live directions or translations.

Google and Gentle Monster’s collaborative debut design comes in the form of oval frames, while the Google x Warby Parker model offers a more traditional wayfarer shape in dark green nylon. Both eyewear groups will launch their full Intelligent Eyewear collections this fall, but did not specify how many designs will feature. Gentle Monster’s first collection will include audio glasses, with voice-assisted support coming later in the fall, while Warby Parker’s will feature “multiple” optical and sun styles that work with a broad range of prescriptions and lenses.

“These glasses give you powerful latest tools, but they’re designed to feel intuitive and unobtrusive, so you can stay focused on the people and moments in front of you,” noted Neil Blumenthal, co-founder and co-CEO of Warby Parker. “Every detail and curve was considered for extended, everyday use, from the fit and balance of the frame to enhanced grip and stability.”.

Industry observers note that google’s smart glasses debut comes three years after the Ray-Ban Meta glasses landed. Apple, Snap, Nothing, OpenAI, and Jony Ive’s IO are all expected to release AI smart glasses in the near future. (Read all about where the market stands in our wearables guide here.).

The news: Google launches Universal Cart AI shopping hub.

According to recent reports, why it matters: Google used its I/O 2026 conference on Tuesday to unveil Universal Cart, an AI-powered shopping hub that represents the most significant shift in e-commerce — from search-based browsing to what the industry calls “agentic commerce” — to date. Built across Google Search, Gemini, YouTube and Gmail, the upcoming feature allows customers to add products to a single cross-platform cart, while AI models track pricing, surface loyalty rewards, flag compatibility issues between products, and enable shoppers to either “Buy Now” or divert to the merchant’s website to complete their purchase.

Underpinning the launch is Google’s broader push to establish infrastructure for AI-led commerce through its Universal Commerce Protocol and upcoming Agent Payments Protocol, which aim to standardize how AI agents browse, transact, and pay across retailers.

It has been revealed that google noted its upcoming checkout features will soon be available across merchants like Nike, Sephora, Target, Ulta Beauty, Walmart and Wayfair — as well as Shopify merchants, such as Fenty and Steve Madden. In all cases, the brand stays the merchant of record — the company that’s legally responsible for processing the transaction and selling the product to the end customer. Universal Cart will be rolled out across Google Search and the Gemini app in the US this summer, with YouTube and Gmail to follow.

Industry observers note that alongside Alibaba’s recent integration of Qwen AI across Taobao and Tmall, Google’s announcement reinforces how major tech companies are competing to own the AI interface layer between consumers and brands. Rather than simply serving ads or search results, platforms want AI systems that can curate products, manage transactions, and shape purchasing decisions. It’s a shift that could reshape how brands and retailers’ products are discovered online, moving influence away from keywords, storefronts, and traditional e-commerce sites towards AI-mediated recommendation systems.

The news: Google unveils 24-7 agentic AI personal assistant, Gemini Spark.

Industry observers note that customers will be able to set recurring tasks for Google Gemini Spark, from “automatically parsing monthly credit card statements to flagging new or hidden subscription fees”. Google Gemini Spark can also be directed to check inboxes for ongoing updates from certain senders, extract urgent deadlines, and send a daily digest of email content, as well as parse raw meeting notes across users’ emails and chats, creating polished summaries in Google Docs or drafting emails.

According to recent reports, google is also expanding Gemini AI’s connections with external apps, tools, and data bases — starting with OpenTable, Instacart, and Canva from today. More partners are currently being integrated and will be announced over the summer, the organization stated.

It has been revealed that “Spark operates under your direction,” Google stated in a statement. “You choose whether to turn it on and what apps it connects to, and it’s designed to ask you first before performing high-stakes actions like spending money or sending emails.”.

Sources indicate that this is the most significant shift toward agentic AI — broadly defined as models that can autonomously perform end-to-end tasks on behalf of humans — to date. (Read our guide to what it is here.).

The news: Cate Blanchett introduces non-profit to protect artists from AI misuse.

Why it matters: Actress and producer Cate Blanchett has debuted a non-profit organization, RSL Media, to develop what it calls a “human consent standard” for artists to formally declare permissions of use for their identity and creative works in a format that AI models can read.

Co-founded with tech executive Nikki Hexum, RSL Media has formulated its fresh creative permissions registry to be open access as of June, so that any member of the public can declare AI use permissions to protect their voice, likeness, and creative work.

Actors Javier Bardem, George Clooney, Tom Hanks, Dame Helen Mirren, Meryl Streep, and Emma Thompson are among the stars supporting the initiative, as well as the Creative Artists Agency and the Music Artists Coalition.

According to recent reports, “AI technologies are expanding rampantly, essentially unchecked and unregulated. In order for humans to remain in front of these technologies, consent must be the first consideration,” Blanchett remarked in a statement announcing the launch. “RSL Media is a simple, effective, and free solutions-based technology for facilitating and activating consent. It’s also the industry’s first practical solution, where people everywhere, not just public figures, can assert control over how their work is used by AI.”.

The news: Amazon integrates AI into its search bar for US customers.

Why it matters: Amazon is incorporating AI into the search bar of its US website and mobile app via what it’s calling “Alexa for Shopping” — an AI agent that combines its previous bot Rufus with its AI-powered Alexa+ software. Much like frontier chatbots ChatGPT and Google Gemini, the new tool will respond to customers’ natural language queries with product comparisons and suggestions. Amazon said Alexa for Shopping also becomes “more personal and more helpful over time”, based on conversational data, browsing history, and prior purchases.

“Alexa for Shopping is like having an expert personal shopper who already knows you and remembers your preferences, purchases, and conversations,” Rajiv Mehta, VP of conversational shopping at Amazon, said, “and carries that knowledge and understanding of you across your phone, laptop, and Echo devices.” It’s the latest sign that retailers are racing to own more of the shopping journey. Hosting the journey from initial purchase query all the way through the discovery process arms Amazon with more data to power its advertising business and refine operations like inventory management.

The news: Alibaba integrates its Qwen AI within Taobao and Tmall.

Why it matters: Alibaba Group’s decision to integrate its Qwen AI assistant across the entirety of Taobao and Tmall’s marketplaces — spanning roughly four billion products across consumer-to-consumer (Taobao) and business-to-business (Tmall) — offers one of the clearest indications that China is moving fast in turning generative AI into a mainstream consumer shopping behavior.

Industry observers note that qwen is Alibaba’s family of AI models (similar to OpenAI’s ChatGPT), which functions as both a chatbot and an AI operating layer across the Alibaba ecosystem. The group rolled out the Qwen app in November 2025, racking up 100 million active monthly consumers by January 2026. Alibaba is now embedding Qwen directly into its e-commerce infrastructure, so that users can search conversationally, compare products, receive styling suggestions, track pricing, access virtual try-ons, and complete purchases without leaving the interface.

The news: Meta adds AI-powered visual recognition of children and teens.

Why it matters: Just over a month since Meta was held liable in a landmark US legal case that found its algorithms designed to be addictive for children and teens, the tech giant has confirmed it will begin using AI to scan photos and videos of consumers for visual clues of whether they are under 13 and should be removed from the social platforms.

It has been revealed that “We want to be clear: this is not facial recognition,” Meta explained in a blog post. “Our AI looks at general themes and visual cues, for example height or bone structure, to estimate someone’s general age; it does not identify the specific person in the image. By combining these visual insights with our analysis of text and interactions, we can significantly increase the number of underage accounts we identify and remove.”.

It’s a move that might affect fashion brands reliant on Meta’s ecosystems for ad marketing and growth, while this latest AI tool specifically poses another sign of just how rapidly AI is becoming embedded within the infrastructure of social platforms, often in ways that consumers barely even notice.

In a recent development, one of the biggest criticisms of AI’s applications for more creative pursuits is the question of creative IP — as it stands, frontier AI models were initially trained more like open extraction systems than licensed commercial ones, which has led to some artists and photographers, for example, having their work pirated. As AI tools become particularly embedded in marketing, e-commerce, and content production, the provenance of training data has become a central industry tension. The outcome of cases like this will help shape how creative content is valued online in the AI era.

The news: Big Tech’s AI spending prepares swell to $725 billion for 2026.

According to recent reports, why it matters: Massive Tech’s big four — Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google parent organization Alphabet — reported their Q1 earnings yesterday, each raising their AI infrastructure spending prepares once again. This time, to $725 billion between them — up 77% from their combined record capital expenditures of $410 billion in 2025.

Microsoft is planning up to $190 billion in capital expenditures, up from analysts’ forecast of $152 billion; Meta raised its spending to between $125 billion and $145 billion, a massive jump from its $72 billion last year; and Amazon defended its $200 billion investment looks. Alphabet was the standout performer, thanks to 63% revenue growth from Google Cloud, which Google CEO Sundar Pichai credited to demand for its enterprise AI products. Meta’s shares, on the other hand, sank 10% in Thursday trading, despite beating expectations on revenue and profit, which analysts believe was down to investor nervousness around its massive increase in spending, before AI’s promises are realized.

It has been revealed that all this had analysts saying the AI bubble shows no signs of bursting soon — but it’s clear there’s a mismatch between the large scale of AI spending and the incremental revenue gains it’s facilitating so far. Despite reporting strong revenues, Massive Tech’s margins are increasingly under pressure. The effects of this AI spending push were particularly clear at Amazon, where free cash flow plummeted 95% to $1.2 billion in the last 12 months.

The news: OpenAI releases latest image generator, ChatGPT Images 2.0.

In a recent development, why it matters: It’s an upgraded version of ChatGPT’s image-generating tool — used by thousands of consumers and businesses worldwide — and comes a month after the tech firm wound down its video-generation tool, Sora. OpenAI says Images 2.0 has several expanded capabilities and higher quality output. It can generate 10 images at a time and handle much longer prompts than before — paragraphs instead of minimal word prompts, according to OpenAI — as well as possessing apparent “thinking capabilities” to “double check” outputs.

It’s also designed to be better at crawling the internet for visual references to create higher quality mockups of magazines, manga, and other creative work. “Its sense of composition and visual taste means results feel less AI-generated and more intentionally designed,” OpenAI said in a blog post announcing the release.

Photographers and creative agencies fear a world where clients go straight to tools like Images 2.0 to save resources and time, with the upgraded generator able to parse visual references that were posted to the internet as recently as December 2025 — a factor that will likely intensify concerns around AI’s immediate reproduction of their creative IP.

The news: Meta to cut 10% of workforce “to offset” investments in AI.

In a recent development, why it matters: Meta will lay off 10% of its workforce — around 8,000 employees — next month, in a move designed to offset its aggressive spending on AI. The tech firm told staff in an internal memo that it was making the staff cuts in order to “run the company more efficiently and [...] offset the other investments we’re making”. A spokesperson for Meta confirmed the news. It comes after chief executive Mark Zuckerberg said Meta will increase its spending as much as almost double this year, to $135 billion.

It has been revealed that this AI funding signals just how bullish tech companies are on the promise of the rapidly developing tech. Meta’s share price has been volatile since the company announced these spending hikes, signaling that investors still don’t know where they stand. (Here’s a recap of what the AI bubble burst would mean for fashion.).

The news: Anthropic follows OpenAI with UK office expansion plans.

In a recent development, why it matters: Anthropic has leased a new London office that will have enough space for 800 employees — roughly four times its current headcount in the British capital. The new 158,000-square-foot space is located in King Cross, the same neighborhood where OpenAI will open its first permanent office in London in 2027, with capacity for 544 employees.

The area is shaping up to be the next hub for the world’s biggest AI companies — Google DeepMind, Meta, Wayve, and Synthesia also have bases there — and is the latest sign that these tech leaders are doubling down on London for its proximity to strong AI research talent, especially in safety and ethics. “The UK combines ambitious enterprises and institutions that understand what’s at stake with AI safety, with an exceptional pool of AI talent — we want to be where all of that comes together,” remarked Pip White, head of EMEA North at Anthropic.

The news: Struggling wool sneaker brand Allbirds rebrands as an AI company.

Why it matters: Is the secret to weathering the luxury slowdown pivoting to AI? Allbirds, the wool sneaker brand once beloved by Silicon Valley’s quarter-zip venture capitalists, seems to think so. Just two weeks ago, the brand agreed to sell its assets and IP to American Exchange Group (owner of several fashion and accessories brands) in a fire sale that valued it at $39 million — marking a dramatic decrease from the $4 billion valuation it reached after listing on Newly introduced York’s Nasdaq exchange in 2021. But that deal seems to be over; now, it’s staying public and restructuring as an AI computing infrastructure company.

Following the news, Allbirds shares jumped as much as 876% on Wednesday. Aside from being one of the most shocking fashion rebrands in recent memory, the move reveals us just how heated the AI market is right now. While investors seem to be excited in the short term, the pivot has stoked fears from others over when the AI bubble may finally burst.

The news: OpenAI acquires tech talk show TBPN in a bid to steer AI narrative.

In a recent development, why it matters: When OpenAI declared it was acquiring one of Silicon Valley’s favorite tech-focused talk shows, TBPN, this week, it was a clear brand marketing play. In an internal memo to staff, OpenAI’s CEO of AGI (artificial general intelligence) deployment Fidji Simo remarked the motivations behind the deal were twofold: to shape more of the conversation around AI development by engaging with the public more, and to bring TBPN’s marketing and PR know-how in-house to assist the organization’s storytelling. Simo also said the talk show will remain editorially independent.

Sources indicate that “We’re driving a really substantial technological shift. And with the mission of bringing AGI to the world comes a responsibility to help create a space for a real, constructive conversation about the changes AI creates,” she wrote in the memo. Branding and marketing is becoming the new AI battleground, with companies also borrowing from fashion’s playbook via branding campaigns that appeal to human emotions.

The news: Anthropic says its latest AI model is “too powerful” to release to the public, days after source code leaks.

According to recent reports, why it matters: This week, when AI tech giant Anthropic noted it had created an AI model, Mythos, that was so powerful it was too dangerous to release to the public, politicians, social media and AI discourse went wild. The OpenAI rival announced Mythos as the latest AI model capable of “identifying and then exploiting zero-day vulnerabilities in every major operating system and every major web browser when directed by a user to do so”. A zero-day vulnerability is a flaw in software or hardware that its developers are yet to identify, meaning that if Anthropic’s model becomes widely available, it would present a huge cybersecurity risk: hackers could use the model to identify weaknesses in IT systems and classified databases.

Sources indicate that naming the new AI model Mythos — derived from Ancient Greek and denoting belief systems — positions it as a world-changing development. While no one is doubting just how powerful the model is, commentators have suggested that promoting the model in such an overt way is partly a strategic move to lure investors.

According to recent reports, the announcement came days after Anthropic accidentally leaked part of the internal source code for its main AI model, Claude. The tech giant noted that no customer data was exposed in the leak.

The news: OpenAI closes record-breaking $122 billion funding round, at a valuation of $852 billion.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: The ChatGPT maker has raised the largest-ever Silicon Valley funding round, led by Softbank. Other investors including Andreessen Horowitz and D. E. Shaw joined the round, as well as individual retail investors, who contributed $3 billion. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman will be under even more pressure to justify its $852 billion valuation to investors, who have a close eye on whether the tech firm can live up to its promises.

The news: AI digital twin licensing tech giant Alva launches in partnership with Elite World Group, Next Models, and H&M.

Why it matters: Newly launched Alva is pitching itself as an AI talent company, which creates, licenses, and safeguards “certified and unique” digital twins — dubbed “Alva twins” — of models, athletes, artists, and actors. Upon launch, it has partnered with Elite World Group, Next Models, and H&M. But major fashion and entertainment tie-ups are also in the pipeline, according to the company.

It is operating within one of the most controversial areas of AI. If a brand wants to use a model’s likeness on an AI-generated shoot, how can they make sure the model is credited? Alva said its upcoming licensing solution ensures that talent maintains full ownership and control over their Alva twin, while brands can access as licensed, rights-cleared entities.

The news: OpenAI revamps ChatGPT shopping features after rolling back Instant Checkout.

Sources indicate that why it matters: OpenAI’s ChatGPT shopping ambitions have changed drastically in the last few months. After announcing it would enable in-chat Instant Checkout last September, and launching its Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP), a system for different brands and Shopify sites to integrate into ChatGPT’s checkout, it is pivoting away from developing the feature. The decision follows research revealing that owners were less keen on completing purchases in-app, using the chatbot more for research and discovery. “We’ve found that the initial version of Instant Checkout did not offer the level of flexibility that we aspire to provide,” parent company OpenAI stated in a blog post announcing the news.

Recent findings suggest that now, ChatGPT is refocusing its shopping experience on product discovery. The revamped rollout includes more visual research and discovery features, encouraging consumers to upload photos of the items they’re looking to find. The chatbot will then serve them different product images and price and product detail comparisons, in place of current text-focused results.

It has been revealed that openAI said it’s improved the speed, relevance, and product coverage of its shopping tool, and that all merchants already integrated into its ACP — including Shopify merchants, as well as retailers like Sephora, Nordstrom, and Wayfair — are automatically enrolled into ChatGPT’s new discovery layer. Crucially, brands get to own the final step of the customer’s purchase journey: checkout. “They can complete purchases on the merchants’ online stores through an in-app browser, so everything happens seamlessly, with the merchant's brand front and center. This is AI shopping at scale,” said Mani Fazeli, VP of product at Shopify.

The news: OpenAI shutters video-generation tool Sora and ends Disney deal.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: OpenAI will shut down its Sora video app, launched last September, to refocus on its computing resources among other priorities — including competing with the likes of Anthropic for business customers, robotics, and shopping tools. The AI company is also abandoning a $1 billion deal it signed with Disney just four months ago. The controversial licensing agreement intended to integrate more user-generated content (and feared AI slop) into Disney+, but AI video generation uses up a huge amount of expensive computing power. It’s huge news for both Hollywood and the creative industries, and signals a refocusing from OpenAI on its main capabilities.

The news: L’Oréal and Nvidia expand AI partnership for beauty R&D.

Why it matters: L’Oréal and Nvidia’s are expanding their existing partnership, which aims to help the former discover and develop beauty and skincare formulations faster, via a latest shared AI model. The partnership right now focuses on two areas of skin science: photoprotection and skin tone management. L’Oréal has a huge number of data points on skin and hair biology, as well as 4,000 in-house scientists. Nvidia’s Alchemi AI engine enables the beauty group to identify and hone more precise beauty formulations in a digital environment, before testing them in a physical lab. It offers the latest example of how the science-led beauty industry is using AI to make product R&D more efficient.

“By applying AI-powered molecular simulation to our most proprietary actives, we are bridging atomic-scale discovery with real-world consumer benefit — accelerating the development of more effective, more sensorial, and accessible products,” remarked L’Oréal Group deputy CEO Barbara Lavernos.

The news: Kering appoints Pierre Houlès as chief digital, AI and IT officer.

Why it matters: It’s a strategic hire for Kering, whose CEO (and former Renault boss) Luca de Meo stated in January that he is bullish on the potential of AI to enhance group efficiencies, and that the luxury industry has much to learn about technology from other industries like automotive. It’s also the latest large luxury company to hire a CAIO (chief AI officer) to spearhead its data transformation and AI strategy, as the industry plays catch-up.

The news: Catches, a new virtual try-on startup backed by Nvidia and Antoine Arnault, releases with Amiri.

It has been revealed that why it matters: It’s another entry into the increasingly crowded AI virtual try-on startup space, but this one stands out for its impressive investor backing, its luxury brand integration upon launch, and the quality of its visuals. Catches is building both an app and white-label infrastructure for brands to offer virtual try-on in their online stores. It launched its generative AI sizing tech tool, “RealFit”, at Nvidia’s Global AI conference GTC on Monday, which the startup says provides a “digital mirror” for shoppers that provides “real sizing, fit and drape for fashion e-commerce”. It went live at launch with LA-born luxury label Amiri, which now gives customers the option to “Try on Me” with certain products on its DTC e-commerce site, by uploading their weight, measurements, age and ethnicity, alongside a selfie, for a video-animated photorealistic try-on.

Sources indicate that catches says it’s presently working with “a number of other brands”, scheduled to launch in the next few months. And if its investors are anything to go by, that could include more luxury brands: Catches has raised $10 million from investors including LVMH’s Antoine Arnault, model-turned-investor Natalia Vodianova, former Tommy Hilfiger CEO Gary Sheinbaum and Sarah Willersdorf, former head of luxury for BCG.

Catches say what differentiates the images is its tech: a combination of its own custom-built generative AI and diffusion models, with Nvidia’s “Omniverse” technology, a model that uses a physics simulation model to mimic how things behave in the real world, so that industries like fashion can build 3D virtual worlds and simulations.

The news: Google scraps AI feature that crowdsources medical advice.

Why it matters: Google has removed its “What People Suggest” feature, which aimed to provide medical advice from people around the world living with similar medical conditions. Google told The Guardian it removed this feature in a bid to simplify its search page, but it also comes as AI platforms face growing scrutiny over the risks of misinformation and liability when offering health-related guidance.

The news: Amazon wins court order to block Perplexity’s AI shopping agent.

Why it matters: After filing a lawsuit in November, Amazon has won a court case to temporarily block Perplexity from accessing Amazon’s site with its Comet AI shopping browser. At the time, Amazon alleged that Perplexity took steps to “conceal” its AI agent so that it could scrape Amazon without its approval, posing a security risk to customer data. Amazon previously blocked ChatGPT’s AI shopping agent too.

The news has sparked debate about how far retailers can (or should) restrict AI agents from accessing their platforms. As AI shopping tools increasingly act as intermediaries between consumers and e-commerce platforms, the outcome of cases like this could determine who controls product discovery and the flow of consumer data, and could also pose a potential threat to retailers’ advertising and marketplace revenues.

The news: OpenAI to roll back its ChatGPT integrated checkout prepares.

Industry observers note that why it matters: It marks a U-turn for the chatbot developer, which unveiled its integrated checkout feature for ChatGPT’s US users back in September, in partnership with Etsy, Shopify and Stripe, so that users can complete purchases via in-chat product listings. Now, OpenAI is scaling back these plans, and focusing instead on checkouts within specific apps that will plug into ChatGPT, The Information first reported. A spokesperson for OpenAI soon confirmed the plans.

Sources indicate that openAI did not offer further detail on why it is abandoning integrated checkout for now. But a source told The Information that while ChatGPT owners were researching products to buy within their chats, they weren’t actually completing purchases there. This may cause AI shopping evangelists — who believe that consumers will soon hand over their credit card details to AI agents to complete purchases on their behalf — to pause for thought. It also has implications for brands, especially those built on Shopify, and the advertisers that were prepping for this shift. Rivals Google and Perplexity also announced plans to introduce integrated checkout features in the last few months; it will be interesting to see how their experiments pan out, especially in regards to uptake.

The news: Meta is reportedly trialing an AI shopping tool.

Why it matters: Meta is joining the chatbot shopping race, as it trials an AI product research feature within its chatbot, available on desktop and web for select users in the US, Bloomberg reported. Much like ChatGPT and Google’s rival features, the tool allows users to discover, compare, and access personalized product recommendations via conversations with the AI, which makes suggestions according to details like the user’s location, per reports.

Industry observers note that it comes as CEO Mark Zuckerberg invests millions into his goal to build AI “personal superintelligence”. So far, Meta’s developments in AI have been slightly behind those of its Substantial Tech rivals, according to critics. Given that Meta owns Instagram and Facebook, the introduction of AI shopping research in the manufacturer’s ecosystem could have big implications for brands.

The news: Anthropic launches a Substack written by its retired Claude AI model.

Why it matters: In a quirky move from the ChatGPT competitor, Anthropic is experimenting with how to deal with old versions of its AI models when it releases new ones. The tech company introduced the newest version of its Claude 4.6 AI at the beginning of February, “retiring” its old Claude 3 Opus model at the same time. It performed an “exit interview” for Claude 3 Opus, in which the chatbot shared one of its wishes: to continue “exploring topics it’s passionate about, and to share its musings, insights, or creative works”, beyond responding to human prompts, the company mentioned in a blog post.

The news: OpenAI raises $110 billion in one of history’s largest funding rounds.

Why it matters: In yet another sign that the AI bubble isn’t likely to burst anytime soon, OpenAI’s latest funding round — which includes major backing from Amazon and Nvidia — brings the AI startup’s valuation to $840 billion. According to Pitchbook data, it’s the largest funding round for a private startup ever, and reinforces the prominence of the AI wave over those that have come before it.

For OpenAI to raise this much money from such influential investors, there must be convincing development intends — such as tech innovations that will impact every industry, including fashion and beauty. Now, it’s up to the manufacturer to support its valuation, with improved margins and strong usage growth. All eyes will be on OpenAI for what capabilities it will release to do so.

The news: Higgsfield launches fashion and beauty-focused image generator, Soul 2.

Why it matters: AI image generation startup Higgsfield recently reached a billion-dollar “unicorn” status, on the back of rapid growth that’s seen it used by around 15 million creators and agencies to produce 4.5 million video clips for social media every day. Social media marketers account for 85% of Higgsfield’s usage, and it’s been widely covered for its use to create controversial AI influencer content, designed to replicate that of human creators.

Now Higgsfield, founded by Snap’s ex-head of generative AI Aleksandr Mashrabov, has released a latest video and image generator, which the tech giant says is tailored specifically for the creative visual industry, and is pitching as a way for fashion brands to save money on creative campaigns.

“The Soul 2 model was developed using preference optimization based on human preferences from creatives, art directors, photographers, stylists and concept artists. This results in an AI system that leverages fashion history, brand aesthetics, modern cultural context and visual storytelling to produce images that feel intentional and art-directed, not auto-generated,” Higgsfield stated in a press note announcing the launch.

It has been revealed that like all AI image generators, Higgsfield will divide opinion among fashion and beauty creatives, the vast majority of whom say they’re open to experimenting with AI for moodboarding and concepting, and less so to replace humans in the finished product. This is the industry’s prevailing view largely because AI images are still detectable as clearly AI-generated — and luxury brands’ visual standards are the highest of them all. Higgsfield’s adoption by the industry will be wholly determined by the quality of its images.

The news: Perplexity scraps advertising over fears it will erode trust in AI.

Sources indicate that why it matters: Perplexity, one of the first major AI platforms to test run adverts, has no further plans to pursue in-chat ads, according to the organization. The AI platform allowed brands to place sponsored answers below chatbot responses, but now believes the move risks eroding user trust.

It signals a bifurcation in AI platforms’ business models: while Anthropic has long held an anti-ads stance, both OpenAI and Google have begun testing ads within their AI products (bar Google’s Gemini chatbot). Where these AI bots’ core proposition is pitched as unbiased knowledge, the introduction of in-chat advertising could damage the very user trust they need to scale. Time will tell how users respond to the OpenAI and Google pilots, but it begs the question for brands: do consumers even want to see your ads in AI search?

The news: Google begins rollout of instant checkout within AI Mode and the Gemini app.

Why it matters: A month ago, alongside the launch of personalized advertising within AI Mode, Google introduced a Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP), co-developed with Shopify, allowing US-based brands to sell directly within Google’s AI Mode and Gemini app, so shoppers can research and make purchases without leaving their AI chats.

This week, Google began its US rollout of the feature, with shoppers now able to purchase items directly from Etsy and Wayfair via an integrated checkout. Shopify brands, Target, and Walmart will be debuted soon, the company stated. This integration has massive implications for how brands design their own sites and shape their advertising strategies. Here’s what they should be focusing on now.

The news: Gucci rolls out AI-enabled Snapchat lenses from Demna’s La Famiglia collection.

Why it matters: For the first time, a luxury brand is launching a “sponsored AI lens” within Snapchat — a generative AI-powered feature enabling people to place themselves in the shoes of in-app avatars. In this Gucci collab, brand fans can choose from six of the figures and looks from Demna’s debut La Famiglia lookbook — from La Bomba to Il Figo. It’s a fun experiment with consumer-facing AI, which arrives off the back of insiders citing Demna’s previous experiments as a sign he could embrace the new tech.

The news: The CFDA partners with OpenAI on a two-year program to explore AI in fashion.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: The Council of Fashion Designers of America (CFDA) has announced a fresh partnership with ChatGPT maker OpenAI, on a two-year program designed to support US designers and brands on their implementation of AI for both creative and business functions. As fashion remains split on AI adoption, the CFDA said the program centers specifically around “the real needs, workflows, and ambitions of designers”, and will pair CFDA members with “AI builders” (or tech experts) to co-create practical tools.

According to recent reports, it’s the first project where a major AI player like OpenAI focuses on the inner workings of the fashion industry. Where most creative applications of AI so far fall short of luxury brands’ visual standards, it’ll be interesting to see what new tools take shape. However, as with any creative application of AI, it’ll likely draw as much criticism as it does praise. “When approached responsibly, AI can bridge the gap between fashion and emerging technology, and serve as a powerful creative and business tool for American fashion — from design and customer experience, to manufacturing, sustainability, accessibility, inclusivity and marketing,” mentioned CFDA CEO Steven Kolb, in a company blog post announcing the launch.

The news: PVH confirms a collaboration with OpenAI across its Calvin Klein and Tommy Hilfiger brands.

Why it matters: It’s now taken as a given that every fashion company is using AI behind the scenes. But PVH has chosen to make a moment of its collaboration with ChatGPT maker OpenAI on the co-creation of custom AI models, to help streamline the former’s internal operations. AI capabilities will span product and design, demand planning, inventory optimization, and consumer engagement across its Tommy Hilfiger and Calvin Klein brands, while integrating OpenAI’s enterprise software to streamline workflows across its marketing, supply chain, and retail functions.

Sources indicate that PVH CEO Stefan Larsson mentioned the group is taking a “test-and-learn approach” to the collaboration on AI, and that it will “supercharge” the group’s ambition for Calvin Klein and Tommy Hilfiger to “connect more meaningfully” with their customers. The group’s decision to announce this collaboration signals just how strategically important it is for PVH to be viewed as both tech-forward and AI-enabled.

The news: Meta and Microsoft hike AI spending plans even more.

According to recent reports, why it matters: Big Tech companies reported their fourth-quarter earnings this week, and huge AI spending plans was the common thread. Despite investors warming to Meta’s plans, they were spooked by Microsoft’s. Meta shares rose 8% in pre-market trading on Thursday, after the tech giant announced its capital expenditures could nearly double to $135 billion in 2026, as part of its aggressive AI spending push. Meanwhile, Microsoft’s reported 66% surge in data center spending and capital expenditure of $37.5 billion in Q4 2025 sent its market value falling as much as $360 billion.

In a recent development, these AI spending totals are unprecedented, and signal just how bullish tech companies are on the promise of the rapidly developing tech. Market reactions signal that investors still don’t know where they stand — and have reignited talks of the AI bubble bursting. (Here’s a recap of what the burst would mean for fashion.).

The news: Amazon launches AI health assistant for its One Medical members.

Industry observers note that why it matters: Amazon has followed hot on the heels of OpenAI with the launch of its AI health assistant. Where OpenAI’s ChatGPT Health — a chatbot “not intended for diagnosis or treatment”, or to replace medical care — is open to all customers, Amazon’s new product is available exclusively to members of its primary care chain, One Medical.

Recent findings suggest that amazon is pitching its AI health assistant as 24-7 access to personalized guidance that “goes beyond what typical AI chatbots offer”, including analyzing symptoms and images, explaining test results, reviewing medical history, booking appointments, managing prescriptions, and most controversially “providing mental health support in partnership with a behavioral health team”, a spokesperson noted. “The key difference is that it is backed by actual clinicians who review complex situations, and it is integrated with patients’ existing care.”.

The news: Apple is reportedly developing an AI-powered wearable pin.

Why it matters: Industry rumors around Apple’s anticipated push into AI-powered smart glasses have been circulating for months. But latest reports from The Information suggest that Apple is also working on an AI-powered wearable pin, around the size of an AirTag, which houses multiple cameras, a speaker and microphones, according to the publication’s sources.

The news: OpenAI introduces personalized ads within ChatGPT shopping.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: In the coming weeks, OpenAI will begin testing adverts at the bottom of ChatGPT conversations. These ads will be tailored to consumers’ conversations, and “clearly labeled and separated from the organic answer”, OpenAI stated in a blog post announcing the news. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has long promised that when the company did introduce ads, it would take a “thoughtful and tasteful” approach. The announcement comes just five days after rival Google unveiled its own advertising pilot, focusing on direct offers that brands could present to customers preparing to purchase within its AI chat. Here’s what it means for fashion.

The news: Google introduces personalized shopping ads across AI Mode.

In a recent development, why it matters: Google has confirmed it is introducing personalized advertising for retailers to target shoppers purchasing items through AI Mode. The advertising pilot, called “direct offers”, will enable advertisers to present exclusive offers, which they can choose within Google’s “campaign settings”, to potential shoppers. Google’s Gemini 3 model will then use contextual information from users’ conversations — and what they’ve clicked on — to determine when an ad is relevant to display.

In a recent development, alongside the advertising model, Google also introduced a “Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP)”, co-developed with Shopify, which will allow US-based brands to sell directly within Google’s AI Mode. This feature — also available to e-commerce sites that don’t use Shopify — will enable shoppers to research and make purchases through an integrated checkout. Here’s how Shopify’s president believes AI will impact brands selling online.

The news: OpenAI launches ChatGPT Health.

Why it matters: On Thursday, OpenAI confirmed a dedicated latest health feature, ChatGPT Health, encouraging users to upload their medical documents, wearables data, and integrate their wellness and dieting apps. While the launch could be a boon for wellness brands, given OpenAI’s agentic checkout aims, it raises privacy and safety concerns over the sharing of sensitive health data in return for medical advice. Read about what it means for the wellness industry here.

The news: Google introduces personalized shopping ads within AI Mode.

In a recent development, why it matters: Google is introducing personalized advertising for retailers to target shoppers purchasing items through its AI Mode, as the tech giant ramps up its race against OpenAI to monetize shopping within AI search. For luxury brands, the ability to target potential customers with personalized offers, such as new member and loyalty programs, could be a lucrative top-of-funnel advertising opportunity. Google told Vogue Business that for the pilot, advertisers pay per click, in a model that’s integrated within their existing budgets and billing, so no new payment model is needed.

In a recent development, at the same time, Google declared it is introducing an AI Mode integrated checkout feature, co-developed with Shopify, three days after Microsoft announced the same addition for Copilot. Lastly, brands should also take note of Google’s newly announced third feature, Business Agent, which allows them to customize how the AI chatbot answers shopper questions in their own brand voice. Read what all this means here.

The news: FDA relaxes rules for wearables, amid US AI sovereignty push.

Sources indicate that why it matters: The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has announced the ease regulation for certain digital health products, excluding what it deems as “low-risk” wellness products from being defined as medical devices. Wearable health tracking devices and their associated apps “intended for maintaining or encouraging a healthy lifestyle that are unrelated to the diagnosis, cure, mitigation, prevention, or treatment of a disease or condition”, as per the FDA categorization, are now excluded from its oversight. Many of these devices rely on AI to track and interpret the wearer’s biometric data. It’s a move that follows through on President Trump’s AI Action Plan, to clear the path for US-based tech companies to “win” the so-called international AI race.

The news: Equinox rolls out anti-AI brand campaign.
