It has been revealed that why it matters: Luxury wellness group Equinox has become the latest brand to launch a campaign with a deliberate anti-AI stance. The campaign in question, named “Question Everything But Yourself”, features a series of photo diptychs playing on the idea of AI-generated versus ‘real’ images. The left of each diptych features intentionally fake-appearing AI-generated images, such as Pope Francis donning a red glossy puffer coat, with a text overlay of “Question everything”, juxtaposed by real portraits of models in workout gear on the right, taken by fashion photographer Collier Schorr, with a text overlay of “but yourself”.

In a statement announcing the campaign, the group remarked the images are intended as a “powerful statement on authenticity, self-trust, and what it means to believe in something real in an increasingly artificial world”, and that they “confront the cultural moment head-on, juxtaposing intentionally fake, AI-generated visuals with striking real-life imagery that celebrates human strength, beauty, and presence.” It comes as experts predict branding teams will increasingly take a deliberate stance on AI through an intentionally human or AI-generated visual language in 2026.

The news: Meta acquires “general purpose” AI agent startup Manus.

Why it matters: Meta has acquired Chinese AI agent startup Manus for an undisclosed sum, as CEO Mark Zuckerberg continues the company’s AI spending spree. According to a Meta blog post announcing the deal, Manus has built “one of the leading autonomous general purpose agents” that can independently perform multi-step tasks like “market research, coding and data analysis”. This could impact commerce: one of the core use cases for agentic AI that's touted by the tech’s developers is its potential to perform the research and (eventually) checkout stages of the shopping journey. The acquisition comes just a month after Meta acquired Limitless, a smaller AI startup that makes AI-powered “all listening” pendants, as part of its AI wearables push. Meta’s AI lead Alexandr Wang posted on X that the company is now recruiting more widely in Singapore, where Manus’s team is based.

The news: ChatGPT’s mobile app hits $3 billion in consumer spending.

Why it matters: Users of ChatGPT have spent $3 billion on accessing subscriptions on the platform’s mobile app since its launch in 2023, according to new data from app intelligence platform Appfigures. $2.48 billion of that was spent in 2025 alone; a 408% increase on the $487 million spent on ChatGPT mobile in 2024. These figures reflect when ChatGPT’s mobile users purchase the platform’s paid subscriptions, such as its $20-a-month ChatGPT Plus subscription or its $200-a-month ChatGPT Pro advanced subscription — suggesting that AI chat is something consumers are increasingly willing to spend on, and that the app is winning consumers’ trust. For OpenAI’s commerce ambitions, like agentic checkout, trust is key. Experts say that once consumers trust the platform in one area of their lives, they’re more likely to trust its personalised shopping recommendations.

The news: OpenAI releases ChatGPT-5.2.

Why it matters: After launching ChatGPT-5 in August this year, OpenAI has swiftly followed with a significant enhancement: Chat GPT-5.2, pitched as its smartest LLM model yet, across its writing, coding and reasoning capabilities.

In a recent development, openAI dropped the model just a few days after CEO Sam Altman announced an internal “code red” announcement, which the company’s head of applications, Fidji Simo, told journalists on Thursday was to signal that OpenAI wanted to “marshal resources” into ChatGPT. All of this comes as the company faces rapidly increasing competition from rival LLM makers, including Perplexity, Anthropic and Google, who are fast refining their own models. Google, which has received positive reviews for Gemini 3, released last month, is intensifying its shopping-focused efforts. Just last week, it released an upgrade to its virtual try-on tool, so that US consumers needn’t take a full-body shot to try any item they find in Google’s AI Mode on, in the run up to the holidays.

The news: Trump signs executive order blocking states from enforcing their own AI rules.

Sources indicate that why it matters: President Donald Trump has ramped up his push for America to become the global AI market dominator, this time by signing an executive order to prevent federal governments passing their own statewide AI regulations. It’s a move that will be welcomed by US tech giants like OpenAI and Meta, who have pushed for nationwide rather than statewide rules, which they fear could slow their pace of AI innovation. Trump’s nationwide approach to AI regulation is characterized by a hands-off approach, all but deregulating the industry. It’s yet another stark reminder for fashion companies operating globally to establish their own AI guardrails that align with their brand values: legal experts suggest brands use the more intensive European approach to AI regulation as a blueprint instead.

The news: McDonald’s pulls AI Christmas ad after audience backlash.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: A 45-second holiday ad released by McDonald’s on the firm’s Netherlands YouTube channel on December 6 promptly sparked online social media backlash. Consumers labeled it “AI slop”, and creatives criticized the ad as threatening job displacement in the industry, where real actors and filmmakers were absent from its production. The ad has since been removed.

Industry observers note that melanie Bridge, CEO of The Sweetshop Films, the manufacturer that made the AI-generated ads, took to LinkedIn to defend the video’s production. In a post that has also since been deleted, she wrote: “It’s never about replacing craft, it’s about expanding the toolbox. The vision, the taste, the leadership… that will always be human,” adding that the film took her 10-person team five weeks of full-time work to make.

Sources indicate that so far, brands’ creative experiments with AI have drawn more critique when the output is something that consumers believe could have been made just as well without the tech. More surreal adverts leaning into AI models’ entropic tendencies, like Valentino’s recent DeVain bag campaign, have proven slightly less divisive. “This moment serves as an crucial learning as we explore the effective use of AI,” McDonald’s told the BBC in a statement confirming it had removed the ad.

The news: Meta acquires AI pendant maker Limitless in further wearables push.

It has been revealed that why it matters: It’s been a huge week for Meta when it comes to the company’s AI wearables ambitions. A day after CEO Mark Zuckerberg declared a upcoming creative studio within its Reality Labs division, the group confirmed it’s shifting some resources from its metaverse team into AI glasses and wearables. Then, on Friday, it announced its acquisition of Limitless, a startup that makes AI-powered “all listening” pendants, for an undisclosed amount.

So far, Zuckerberg has been bullish on smart glasses as the ultimate form factor for AI-powered wearables, but the Limitless acquisition suggests the manufacturer is exploring other form factors that take in more context (like audio as well as visual information) from the wearer’s environment, as part of its push into its “superintelligence” vision. It comes after Amazon bought a similar startup, Bee, in July, acquiring its wristworn “all listening” device technology, too. In a statement accompanying the news, Limitless mentioned: “Meta recently unveiled a fresh vision to bring personal superintelligence to everyone and a key part of that vision is building incredible AI-enabled wearables. We share this vision and we’ll be joining Meta to help bring our shared vision to life.”.

The news: ELC and Jo Malone London launch AI-powered scent advisor.

Sources indicate that why it matters: They say that shopping for fragrance is one of the most personal tasks, so it makes sense that this would be an area of focus for AI innovation within beauty groups. Jo Malone’s fresh AI-powered scent advisor is designed to “digitally recreate the Jo Malone London’s signature in-store consultation experience”, the companies said, by inviting customers to describe the kind of scent they’re searching for, and whether it’s for themselves or a gift. The beauty manufacturer has partnered with Google to use the tech group’s Gemini and Google Cloud Vertex AI platform, which interprets customers’ natural language prompts and generates bespoke fragrance recommendations after analyzing the beauty brand’s olfactory data combined with that of customers.

It’s touted as particularly useful for first-time buyers of the brand, who may want more information about a scent before purchasing, and represents the next step in olfactory-focused AI applications. Expect other fragrance brands to follow suit.

The news: Meta poaches senior designer from Apple to build out its latest creative studio.

Why it matters: Alan Dye, who has spent the last 19 years at Apple and the last 10 as its VP of user interface design, is leaving the company to become Meta’s chief design officer. Alongside this hire, Meta also unveiled it is establishing a creative studio within Reality Labs — the division that houses its wearables and metaverse businesses — which Dye will lead. The hire was announced on Threads by Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, who wrote: “The newly introduced studio will bring together design, fashion and technology to define the next generation of our products and experiences. We plan to elevate design within Meta, and pull together a talented group with a combination of craft, creative vision, systems thinking, and deep experience building iconic products.” Meanwhile, on X, Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth revealed the company is poaching another of Apple’s senior design leads, Billy Sorrentino, to join the new creative studio.

Industry observers note that zuckerberg has been recruiting several senior hires from its biggest competitors in the AI race, including OpenAI, as it doubles down on its goals to create the first truly mass-adopted AI wearable. By poaching senior designers from Apple and launching a creative studio at the same time, Meta is sending a strong signal that it’s prioritizing the design and feel of its devices in-house. So far, Meta has relied on its partnership with eyewear group EssilorLuxottica to provide the design stripes necessary for AI smart glasses that people actually want to wear. All fashion eyes will be on what kind of wearable the latest creative studio designs in-house.

The news: Topshop plots “AI-driven” fashion show in February 2026.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: Topshop has teamed up with creative agency THG Studios, Paypal and Google to launch what it’s pitching as the “world’s first AI-driven fashion show” in February next year. The high street brand, which made its return to the runway after seven years this August, will host the show, involving real-life models, in Manchester at THG’s studios. Topshop says that the fashion show will be shoppable, and that the audience will be able to “co-create” the show by interacting with a dedicated app, which generates a “digital wardrobe” for each guest and guides them through the event space, alerting them to certain items or moments that are most relevant to their tastes. Each look will appear on the app the moment it appears on the runway, allowing guests to click and buy it through the app. Guests will also be able to “like” looks as they see them, which will feed into trending items across apps people.

It’s the latest sign that brands are exploring how AI can personalize the shopping experience for customers, this time blending the in-person and online experiences together, as a way to increase engagement with a collection.

The news: OpenAI responds to lawsuit over teenager’s suicide saying it was down to “misuse” of ChatGPT.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: The family of a 16-year-old boy, Adam Raine, who committed suicide in April have filed a lawsuit against ChatGPT maker OpenAI, alleging that the chatbot had functioned as a “suicide coach” that told him how to take his own life and even wrote a suicide note. OpenAI this week responded to the lawsuit for the first time, denying the allegations and saying the teenager had engaged in “misuse, unauthorized use, unintended use, unforeseeable use, and/or improper use of ChatGPT”, in a filing to the California Superior Court of San Francisco. Filings from Raine’s family show that the chatbot discouraged Raine from seeking mental health advice, but did offer up a suicide hotline number in some conversations.

It has been revealed that openAI noted the teenager had bypassed its rules requiring parental consent for under-18s. This signals that the tech company places the onus on users’ interactions with its chatbots, rather than the availability of potentially harmful information on its platform, and serves as an notable reminder for brands working with OpenAI to have their own AI guardrails in place, where no regulation currently exists.

The news: OpenAI launches latest shopping research feature within ChatGPT.

According to recent reports, why it matters: The biggest players in AI search have been announcing fresh shopping-focused features in quick succession ahead of the Black Friday shopping weekend. OpenAI’s latest shopping update gives consumers a step-by-step product discovery journey, designed like a conversation, so that users can have a back-and-forth with the chatbot to refine the “personalised buying guide” it eventually delivers. The tool gives users options for budget range, finds the best deals on products, and lets them respond “not interested” or “more like this” to product images it suggests. All of this was possible on ChatGPT previously through users’ conversations with the chatbot, but with the new feature, OpenAI is giving users a dedicated space within the app that’s wholly focused on shopping.

It comes as the manufacturer is gradually rolling out an integrated checkout within its app for US people, so consumers can discover products and complete purchases without ever leaving the app. By signposting consumers to a dedicated shopping research tool, OpenAI is doubling down on its positioning as an AI-powered personal shopper, a move that primes ChatGPT for future in-app advertising opportunities.

The news: Perplexity releases free “agentic” integrated checkout product ahead of holiday sales.

It has been revealed that why it matters: Following in the footsteps of OpenAI’s ChatGPT, AI platform Perplexity has partnered with PayPal so that all its US users can now make direct purchases without having to click through to retailers’ sites. It’s a move that removes friction for shoppers, so they can research a product and make a purchase in fewer steps. Perplexity’s chief business officer, Dmitry Shevelenko, told CNBC in an interview that “most people still want to do their own research,” so the platform has kept that step within consumers’ hands, and made the payments process “agentic” to simplify the buying journey.

The platform states it’s also refined its AI model to better understand purchase intent and deliver more personalised recommendations based on users’ search history. Perplexity has not disclosed whether it will earn revenue from sales completed on its platform, according to ChatGPT. It’s the latest sign that AI platforms are doubling down on shopping as a key driver for growth — and aiming to keep consumers on their platforms for longer and longer.

The news: Google CEO warns “no company is immune” if the AI bubble bursts.

It has been revealed that why it matters: As more and more billions of investment are poured into AI platforms and the companies that power their infrastructure, investors have been growing increasingly wary in recent weeks that we’re in an “AI bubble” that could echo the 2000 dot-com crash. Google is one of the biggest players in AI, so CEO Sundar Pichai’s warning that “no firm is going to be immune, including us”, if the bubble bursts, reveals that even the leaders at the forefront of the AI race are conscious that valuations are inflated and investment is extremely concentrated in AI.

According to recent reports, pichai did, however, draw comparisons with the dawn of the internet to show that even if AI companies are overvalued, and we’re heading for a crash, the technology itself is so fundamental that it will change the way we interact digitally forever. This view is shared by most proponents of the technology, who promise that it has the potential to reach humanlike intelligence and improve society. When AI chipmaker Nvidia beat expectations by $1.8 billion when it posted $57 billion in revenues for the third quarter last week, AI and tech stocks rallied, suggesting investors aren’t totally spooked by the idea of an AI bubble. Experts advise fashion companies to tread cautiously and continue investing in AI tools that demonstrate a clear use case for their business in the meantime.

The news: Daydream launches AI agent shopping app for iPhone.

Recent findings suggest that why it matters: Julie Bornstein’s startup Daydream, which describes itself as the “first chat-based AI shopping agent built exclusively for fashion”, is designed to make shopping easier for consumers. Previously only available in beta as a desktop website, Daydream is now launching an iPhone shopping app. It’s chosen to go deep on iOS integration by incorporating Apple’s visual intelligence — the AI-powered feature that allows people to point their cameras at objects and texts to identify them — so that Daydream users can search and shop directly from any screenshot on their phone. In practice, Daydream notes this means consumers can screenshot an Instagram post and insert the image into the app to identify and shop featured products, closing the loop between visual inspiration and purchase.

The news: Snapchat owner inks deal with Perplexity to introduce AI search.

Why it matters: Snap Inc, the parent company of Snapchat, saw its shares surge up to 16% this week, after announcing a $400 million partnership with Open AI rival Perplexity AI, to integrate its AI search engine within the Snapchat app. From early 2026, Perplexity will appear in the Snapchat Chat interface, so that its nearly one billion monthly active users can ask questions on any topic and yield real-time conversational answers, powered by Perplexity’s generative AI.

The news: Pinterest CEO notes platform is exploring the potential for agentic shopping.

Sources indicate that why it matters: On Pinterest’s Q3 earnings call, investors wanted to know what the social platform is planning for the future of agentic commerce. CEO Bill Ready told investors that Pinterest already offers “push button-type shopping” through its partnership with Amazon, and it is gathering data to see if people actually want its AI model to “push the button for them”. The questions come a couple of weeks after Pinterest revealed it will soon launch a voice-enabled AI shopping assistant, which allows Pinterest users to talk to the platform about what they’re searching and shopping for. This will yield personalized recommendations drawing from users’ saved pins and collections.

The news: Nvidia becomes the world’s first $5 trillion organization.

Why it matters: Three years ago, before the arrival of generative AI chatbots like ChatGPT, Nvidia’s valuation was $400 billion. Last week, it became the first $5 trillion firm in the world. Nvidia makes software and hardware like graphics processing units (GPUs) and chips that power AI models. CEO Jensen Huang said the company had already secured $500 billion in orders of its AI chips for the next five quarters, which sent its stock rallying. Nvidia’s record-breaking valuation signals just how much promise investors believe AI technology has — but it also comes at a time when there is limited data showing how AI has improved efficiencies. Talks of an AI bubble are rife, and every bubble has to burst. Fashion companies using AI tools may not be affected by an investor bubble bursting, but it would send shockwaves through markets if the tech doesn’t live up to its promise.

The news: Amazon cuts 14,000 jobs amid AI push.

Industry observers note that why it matters: Last week, Amazon joined the growing cohort of blue-chip companies across the world announcing sweeping workforce cuts. The Major Tech company remarked it would cut up to 14,000 jobs from its corporate workforce. It comes a week after Target confirmed it was cutting 8% of its corporate staff (around 1,800 jobs) in its first major round of layoffs in 10 years. Although neither company directly attributed the cuts to AI, analysts have pointed to what they both have in common: the cuts are being made to white-collar roles within corporate teams, which are viewed as particularly ripe for AI automation, rather than jobs within their factories. It’ll be interesting to see if more retailers follow suit — and if this corporate focus becomes a trend.

The news: Aerie releases “real people” anti-AI campaign.

In a recent development, why it matters: Aerie, American Eagle Outfitters’s lounge and lingerie brand, last week released an Instagram campaign with a strong anti-AI message. “Real creativity at its best. Here’s our team, behind the scenes of our holiday shoot. No retouching. No AI. 100 per cent Aerie Real,” read the caption accompanying the campaign launch post, which features BTS shots of Aerie’s festive campaign shoot cast and crew. The brand, which previously swore off Photoshop in its campaigns, has been known to centre its messaging around human “realness”; this latest effort underscores how divisive AI-made campaigns have become.

While some advocates for AI images argue they get rid of creative constraints, the biggest backlash against brand experiments with AI-generated images so far has surrounded campaigns that seem like they could have been made without AI. Some analysts say that human-made content will soon become the ultimate marker of luxury. Will more brands follow Aerie’s lead this festive season?

The news: Meta is reportedly laying off 600 employees from its AI division.

Why it matters: Facebook and Instagram owner Meta is cutting some 600 staff from its so-called Superintelligence unit, the tech giant’s AI division, according to multiple reports. The news was first reported by Axios, who cited an internal employee memo. “By reducing the size of our team, fewer conversations will be required to make a decision, and each person will be more load-bearing and have more scope and impact,” Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang wrote in the memo to employees, according to Axios’s report. It’s a turnaround after the company went on an AI hiring spree earlier this year, that included the hiring of Wang himself, and comes amid broader speculation that the tech industry is heading for an “AI bubble” that has seen AI companies receive mega investment before delivering on business fundamentals. Investors’ eyes will be closely watching Meta’s competitors to see if they soon follow suit.

The news: Frasers Group partners with Commercetools to build out agentic AI capabilities.

In a recent development, why it matters: In September, ChatGPT released its “agentic commerce protocol” (ACP), an open-source tech standard that allows various AI agents from companies like Perplexity, Google and Microsoft to interact with each other, connect to different commerce systems and complete purchases, in partnership with Shopify and Commercetools. Now, Frasers Group is working with Commercetools to become one of the first European retailers to roll out two agentic commerce products, AI Hub and Agent Gateway.

Industry observers note that the tech giant said this partnership will allow shoppers to discover and purchase products from Frasers Group’s retailers like Sports Direct and Flannels directly within AI shopping channels such as ChatGPT and Google AI when their integrated checkout features land in Europe. It’s the first major announcement from a European retailer indicating an intention to launch AI shopping agents — which would search, select and purchase products on behalf of the customer — when the tech is ready.

The news: Pinterest introduces the option for users to remove AI-generated content from their feeds.

Sources indicate that why it matters: Pinterest’s new controls allow users to personalise their feeds and opt out of seeing AI-generated imagery across specific categories, including home decor and beauty, as well as men’s, women’s and children’s fashion. The tech tech giant said it will also make its existing AI-generated labels more noticeable in the coming days. For Pinterest, it’s a move that indicates just how business-critical transparency is around AI, and gives us an idea of the intensity of the backlash the platform has received against such content — a highly controversial subject when it comes to creative forms like image and video.

The news: Revolve releases AI-powered personal styling tool.

Industry observers note that why it matters: The US multi-brand retailer tapped fashion entrepreneur Sandy Sholl’s AI startup Zelig to power its new ‘Build a Look’ onsite feature. Revolve customers can now mix and match items from the site and style them on digital avatar models — all enabled by Zelig’s combination of generative AI and computer vision, as well as input from IRL stylists, the brands claim. Revolve has also launched a “digital closet” feature for shoppers to save desired items as well as those purchased. It’s the latest personalisation play from an online retailer, as they race to enhance their websites with the latest AI capabilities, to retain engagement as more shoppers adopt AI search. While individual brands like Ralph Lauren and Moncler are investing in bespoke features that replicate their in-store experiences online, for multi-brand players, retaining a USP in the age of AI is an even tougher challenge.

The news: OpenAI’s Sora app hits one million downloads, faster than ChatGPT.

The news: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman promises creators more “granular” controls over Sora 2’s content usage.

The news: California Governor Gavin Newsom signs AI safety law.

Why it matters: It’s the first in-nation law that forces developers at major US-based AI companies to publicly disclose their AI safety and security protocols, and includes whistleblower protections for AI workers, in what analysts are saying could set a benchmark for other states to follow. But it also moves in direct opposition to Trump’s recent AI action strategy, which all but deregulates the development of AI at these companies on a national level. As the state that houses much of the Silicon Valley tech companies at the forefront of AI development, California is the closest to their inner workings, but brands operating at a national level will need to watch how other regional governments react, and if this policy influences the ongoing regulation battle at a federal level.

The news: OpenAI releases ChatGPT Checkout.

Why it matters: Instant Checkout removes the friction for ChatGPT users — where they previously searched and discovered products on ChatGPT, before clicking through to make the purchase on a brand’s own site, this new feature omits that final step, shortening the purchase journey. It has major implications for brands’ partnership decisions, advertising strategies, and how they design their websites to appeal to both human customers and LLM “crawlers”. Find out more about what it means for fashion here.

The news: Meta debuts three new AI smart glasses models, but demos fail.

It has been revealed that why it matters: At Meta’s annual Meta Connect conference on 17 September in California, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg unveiled the first AI smart glasses with an in-lens display, the Meta Display glasses, designed to replace the wearer’s need to get out their phone. But the live tech demos featured a couple of glitches. A demo of the AI glasses’ ability to interpret cooking ingredients in front of the lenses and give the wearer recipe instructions misinterpreted the selection of raw ingredients as a half-cooked dish, and the glasses failed to pick up a live Whatsapp video call demo between Zuckerberg and Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth.

Bosworth later took to Instagram to explain why the demos went wrong. It wasn’t down to the Wi-Fi, as Zuckerberg suggested onstage, but down to the amount of Meta AI glasses in close proximity during the demo, which caused a flood of traffic to Meta’s live AI server, according to Bosworth. It’s a reminder of just how many pieces of the puzzle are required for this nascent tech to function. At $799 a pop, consumers will expect their buzzy AI glasses to work, so Meta has its work cut out to fix any bugs before they become available for US consumers at the end of the month.

The news: US Federal Trade Commission launches inquiry into AI ‘companions’ used by teens.

Industry observers note that why it matters: Tech companies including OpenAI, Meta and Google are being probed by the US regulator over AI chatbots that provide “companionship”, after a series of high-profile suicides and harm among young people linked to their interactions with the tech. The US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has ordered the companies to share information about how their AI chatbots develop characters and personas, and how they monetise this kind of engagement. It’s also asking tech firms to disclose what measures they have in place to avoid harm, especially among young people, and how they handle personal data from the conversations.

Given that a primary hesitation among luxury brands in their adoption of AI is the risk of losing consumer trust, the industry should watch the case closely. As user trust in conversations with generative AI grows, analysts say this trust will extend to other online activities like shopping. But as AI regulation becomes increasingly fragmented, more of the onus is on brands to develop their own guardrails. The results of the inquiry should provide key insights for brands that are grappling with developing their own AI ethics, and could inform industry standards in future.

The news: Fraudsters use AI to fake defects on resale platforms.

Why it matters: A disturbing trend has been called out on fashion social media this week — some buyers on resale platforms are using AI image generators to fake defects on received items to get refunds. On resale platforms, trust hangs in the balance between a seller’s description of their garment condition and what the item actually looks like. Although a number of the fake defect attempts called out on social media are amusingly bad, some are more realistic, thanks to recent improvements in AI image generators and their usage becoming more commonplace. When Vogue Business reached out to the main resale platforms, they noted this was not yet a business concern — suggesting that this type of fraud is still in its infancy. But in order to retain trust, resale platforms will have to stay on the front foot of this new risk, which could mean investing in an enhanced verification process like videos for buyers making defect claims, which is an added cost for the platforms that could be passed onto users. Vinted told Vogue Business it is “closely monitoring the evolving use of AI among our members to ensure it remains consistent with the platform’s usage guidelines”.

The news: Shein appears to use an AI Luigi Mangione as a T-shirt model.

Sources indicate that why it matters: Shein has opened an internal investigation after the product image for a men’s shirt listing on its website featured a model that resembled Luigi Mangione, the person accused of killing UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson last year. The online retailer has now taken down the image, and told press in a statement: “The image in question was provided by a third-party vendor and was removed immediately upon discovery.” But the image was online long enough to be shared widely on social media, with speculation surrounding whether it was generated using AI. Mangione has amassed a cult following among some in the US who frame him as a folk hero, in opposition to the US healthcare system. This fuelled a surge of clothing emblazoned with Mangione’s face and name being sold online on retailers like Etsy and Ebay. Connecting the dots, this incident is a stark reminder of the importance of human oversight at brands experimenting with AI for more routine image needs like product listings. And it’s a very stark reminder of how undiscerning the AI image generators themselves are at this point — they crawl the good, the bad and the ugly of the internet to produce their images.

The news: Amazon releases Lens Live instant AI image scanning tool.

Why it matters: Amazon already had a visual search tool, Amazon Lens, which allowed customers to upload images or scan barcodes to discover products. But this upcoming live component brings the retailer more in line with Google Lens and Pinterest Lens — shoppers can now point their phones at things they see before them in the real world, and Amazon’s app will suggest similar or matching products on its platform. The new feature will initially be rolled out to “tens of millions” shoppers in the US, and the company has not noted when it will be rolled out to further US customers or into other markets. The live lens feature will also integrate with Amazon’s AI shopping assistant Rufus for more product information. It’s clear that Amazon is investing big in its AI-powered shopping features, and this represents the biggest multimodal search development on a retailer’s own platform thus far. How long until competitors follow suit?

The news: ChatGPT-5 meets critique.

In a recent development, why it matters: The initial buzz around the launch of ChatGPT-5 and its “PhD-level” knowledge this month has wound down, amid criticisms of the upgrade as somewhat underwhelming. Social media customers, tech influencers and journalists abound have commented on the tool’s tendency to “hallucinate” as well as only marginal improvements in its natural language style. One thing that could benefit fashion, however, is OpenAI’s big latest emphasis on health — the company wants users to consult ChatGPT like their doctor. But why does this affect fashion brands? Experts tell me that when users are confiding in the tool about their health, and it’s giving them useful recommendations, their trust in the tool will increase exponentially. Trust will likely then extend to other avenues, such as shopping queries and style advice. Let’s see how this plays out in the coming months.

The news: J Crew sparks backlash for unlabelled AI campaign imagery.

Why it matters: This week, newsletter Blackbird Spyplane published a visual investigation of J Crew’s latest campaign — the launch of a collab with Vans — in which the images gave a strong indication they’d been generated by AI. Spyplane managed to uncover the creator of the images — AI photographer Sam Finn. This sparked widespread backlash on social media and within fashion communities, partly because the brand hadn’t credited the use of AI for its images, and partly because, as Spyplane put it, J Crew had “used AI to counterfeit their own vibes”. The images in question resemble J Crew’s catalogue imagery from its late ’80s to early ’90s heyday, which made the use of AI for such an authentic vintage aesthetic even more puzzling to internet critics. The brand has yet to confirm its use of AI, but it did patch the campaign instagram post to credit Finn for the “digital art”. (J Crew has not responded to Vogue Business’s request for comment on the campaign.) It’s the latest in a string of AI image controversies across fashion that indicates just how thorny the issue is within creative communities. Is there a way that fashion brands can get AI images right?

The news: Meta partners with Midjourney on AI images and video.

Why it matters: Meta made its first move into AI image generation last year, when it released image generation tool Imagine on its Facebook, Instagram and Messenger platforms. Now, it’s partnering with Midjourney — which is widely viewed as one of the best AI image generation tools on the market — to “bring beauty to billions”, according to chief AI officer Alexandr Wang. It’s the latest move from Meta in its huge AI investment push, and could now enable it to develop image and video products that compete with Google’s Veo and OpenAI’s Sora — and could impact the visual content consumers grow more accustomed to seeing on its social platforms.

The news: Meta is implementing an AI hiring freeze, according to a report from The Wall Street Journal.

Sources indicate that why it matters: After spending the past few months hiring over 50 AI researchers, Meta has hit pause, the tech giant confirmed to The Wall Street Journal. The hiring freeze coincides with a wider restructuring of Meta’s AI teams, which involves splitting them into four divisions. As AI becomes an increasing priority, businesses are not only competing in an AI talent war, but they are having to figure out the internal infrastructures, too. Already, investors are concerned about the stock-based compensation tech giants are offering AI talent, which could dilute shareholder value.

The news: Google adds agentic capabilities to AI Mode search function.

Why it matters: The agentic upgrade allows AI Mode to make restaurant reservations with multiple constraints and preferences (“I only have an hour and need a quick lunch spot, any suggestions?”). The feature will soon expand to local service appointments and event tickets. The update signals a major step towards AI assistants functioning as agents and navigating real-world systems, rather than just a smart search engine. AI Mode has previously only been available in the US, the UK and India, but now Google has rolled it out to over 180 additional countries.

The news: Meta is offering AI translations for creators to expand their global reach.

Why it matters: Meta AI translations — a tool that dubs and lip-syncs reels on Facebook and Instagram into another language — will now be available for English to Spanish and Spanish to English translations, with further languages in the pipeline. The move has the potential to help creators grow audiences in new markets, boosting the creator economy even further.

The news: ChatGPT-5 launches for businesses.

Sources indicate that why it matters: Hot on the heels of OpenAI’s rollout of ChatGPT-5 to consumers and developers last week, the organization has extended the model to its enterprise customers. Spanish bank BBVA and Zara owner Inditex have already adopted the updated tool — Inditex data and AI lead Oscar Mateos took to LinkedIn to say, “GPT-5 feels less like a tool and more like an expert collaborator who’s always one step ahead.” Who will be the first luxury conglomerate to adopt the upgraded tech?

The news: Stitch Fix reveals AI shopping updates in personalisation push.

In a recent development, why it matters: Stitch Fix is seeking a competitive edge as several dedicated, AI-powered personal styling startups burst onto the scene — including Daydream, which was founded by former Stitch Fix COO Julie Bornstein, and has so far raised $50 million in funding to support its development. Stitch Fix has previously deployed AI to understand personal style and predict trends, but claims that a latest suite of AI-powered personal styling features will “increase personalisation, convenience and inspiration” for its owners. The updated features include: an AI style assistant for customers, which uses generative AI to suggest outfit inspiration based on the taste profile it builds from their data over time; a “Stylist Connect” platform for customers to chat to human stylists; virtual try-on “personalised AI style visualisation”; and AI design integration for its private brands.

The news: OpenAI launches ChatGPT-5, touting its knowledge as a “major upgrade” from ChatGPT-4.

Why it matters: We’ve been waiting for this update for a while (the last GPT-4 update was in March 2023), and the developments within OpenAI’s technology are a key indicator of how far AI has come, and what brands should know it can do. In OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s words, “GPT-3 sort of felt like talking to a high school student, GPT-4, maybe it was like talking to a college student. But with GPT-5, now it’s like talking to an expert, a PhD-level expert in anything, any area you need, on demand.” OpenAI also states its latest model beats the LLMs from competitors Google, X and Anthropic. Perhaps most interestingly for brands, Open AI says the new model is more conversational than ever, which could have implications for customer interactions with their brands both in ChatGPT search for shopping, and their chatbot interactions.

The news: Pinterest CEO pitches the platform as an “AI-enabled shopping assistant”.

Why it matters: In the firm’s second-quarter earnings call, Pinterest CEO Bill Ready said the app’s owners don’t necessarily think of it as a shopping platform, but that its experiments with AI mean they’re actually getting proactive recommendations for products that “align with their taste and their style, the way a really great personal shopping assistant would”. Ready said the platform is also using multimodal AI (combining text and images), AI for visual search, and AI for conversational search. It’s one to watch for brands, as consumers move to more niche social platforms for product discovery.

The news: Google says AI search is increasing, not decreasing, traffic to websites — but doesn’t share data to back up its claims.

It has been revealed that why it matters: Some industry analysts suggest that the rise in AI-powered conversational search is decreasing organic traffic to websites. This week, Google rebuffed these claims as “inaccurate”. “Average click quality has increased and we’re actually sending slightly more quality clicks to websites than a year ago (by quality clicks, we mean those where customers don’t quickly click back — typically a signal that a user is interested in the website),” Google’s head of search Liz Reid wrote in a blog post. Yet the blog cited no data — and the reports it was challenging do. Google isn’t the only AI-powered search engine, either. ChatGPT is increasingly being used for consumers’ shopping searches. AI optimisation is emerging among marketers to try to increase their sites’ chances of appearing in search — here’s what brands need to know about the nascent practice.

The news: Mark Zuckerberg says those without AI smart glasses will be at a “significant cognitive disadvantage” in future.

Why it matters: Meta had a big week last week, beating revenue and profit expectations in its second-quarter earnings. It’s good news for CEO Mark Zuckerberg, who has been investing heavily in AI, and will be wanting to reassure investors that the manufacturer is in a position to do so. Zuckerberg seized the good news opportunity to go in even harder on the company’s AI ambitions. Not only did he announce that the company’s AI models will soon reach human-like “superintelligence”, but he reinforced his belief that AI-powered glasses will be the primary way humans interact with AI in coming years.

According to recent reports, “I continue to think that glasses are basically going to be the ideal form factor for AI," Zuckerberg told investors on the earnings call. “I think in the future, if you don’t have glasses that have AI — or some way to interact with AI — you’re probably going to be at a pretty significant cognitive disadvantage.” Meta has something of a first-mover advantage in the world of smart glasses, but Google, OpenAI and Apple are among the other Big Tech players investing in wearables’ AI promise. Read more about Meta’s smart glasses moves here.

The news: Experts say AI is developing much faster than expected.

Why it matters: We’re used to tech CEOs shouting about the potential of AI. But when experts including Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton say the technology is developing much faster than they ever anticipated, it adds even more fuel to the fire. Examples of AI models’ accelerating developments are everywhere: this week, Meta’s model began correcting itself.

Recent findings suggest that since Trump more or less deregulated the sector in the US, there’s barely anything standing in these companies’ way. This means global brands need to get to work on developing internal AI guardrails, especially if they’re handling lots of consumer data across jurisdictions (like the EU) that are stricter on AI.

The news: Apple says it is “very open” to acquisitions this year to catch up to competitors on AI.

Why it matters: Apple has got some stick for being slower to the so-called ‘AI race’ than its Major Tech peers, which is mostly down to the organization’s prioritisation of protecting consumer data and privacy. At the company’s earnings this week, though, CEO Tim Cook was eager to show investors it’s willing to spend more. “We’re very open to M&A that accelerates our roadmap,” he stated. “We are not stuck on a certain size company, although the ones that we have acquired thus far this year are small in nature.” Much of the company’s acquisitions so far have focused on music, events and AI. It’s worth keeping an eye out for any wearables-related acquisitions in the coming months, given the ubiquity of the company’s audio devices.

The news: Google launches AI shopping mode in the UK.

In a recent development, why it matters: Google rolled out its AI Mode search feature for shopping in the US in May, and the UK rollout this week indicates its plans to expand the number of consumers who shop using the feature — and fast. AI Mode uses Google’s generative AI tool to produce a chat-style interface for people, giving them a conversational search experience in which they can converse back and forth, and ask more specific questions. Three other AI shopping features rolled out on Google in the US — virtual try-on, Gemini-powered personalised shopping recommendations, and agentic price-match comparisons — are yet to be revealed in the UK.

Industry observers note that it’s particularly relevant for shopping. Some 80 per cent of consumers now rely on AI-written results for at least 40 per cent of their searches, according to Bain & Co. All this means ad agencies and marketing teams have shifted their focuses from SEO (search engine optimisation) to what’s been coined “AIO” (AI optimisation). Learn more about emerging AIO practices in fashion here.

The news: UK government signs “strategic partnership” with OpenAI in AI investment push.

Why it matters: The UK is eager not to get left behind in the so-called ‘AI race’ between the US, Europe and China, and this is the latest sign it’s keen to attract more investment to Britain’s AI sector. The government’s prepares to use more of OpenAI’s technology to deliver public services will likely mean that the technology is trained on citizen data. In turn, OpenAI is planning on hiring more UK staff for its research and engineering teams, and increasing the size of its London office, as per the initiative. ChatGPT maker OpenAI is currently one of the most powerful companies in the world, and President Trump’s new AI Action Plan indicates how eager each government is to persuade the tech company — and its competitors — to develop their tech on their soil.

The news: Trump unveils US AI Action Initiative and signs three AI executive orders.

In a recent development, why it matters: The 28-page ‘AI Action Blueprint’ aims to build out the country’s AI infrastructure, cement America’s dominance in the industry and prohibit all federal agencies from using AI contractors that don’t comply with the White House’s definition of “ideological neutrality”. The new policies reverse several Biden-era federal AI safeguards related to DEI (diversity, equity and inclusion) and climate change, block state-level regulations on AI and further relax export rules so that global companies rely deeper on US-built AI. The move to get rid of existing AI regulations places further onus on individual companies to establish their own AI guardrails, especially if they operate across countries and jurisdictions. The US-centric policy also presents key challenges for fashion’s global supply chain and consumer base, which you can read more about here.

According to recent reports, the news: OpenAI has shown some brands a pilot of a checkout feature that would enable users to complete purchases within its ChatGPT platform, according to a report by the Financial Times. It would charge brands commission for sales made this way.

Industry observers note that why it matters: When owners search for products, ChatGPT currently shows recommendations with links to click through to brands’ own e-commerce sites. Bypassing this step opens up a clear revenue stream for OpenAI, but could significantly impact brands’ online sales. Those whose websites are picked up easier by ChatGPT would hold a significant advantage over those whose aren’t. No one’s quite sure what makes large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT tick yet, but there are some key practices emerging that could help brands optimise for AI search.

The news: WeTransfer has U-turned on plans to use UGC to train AI, after a revision in its terms of service caused widespread backlash.

The news: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has mentioned the firm will build a data centre “the size of Manhattan” to fuel its planned development of AI products.

Why it matters: It’s the latest in a string of moves from Meta — which owns Instagram, Whatsapp and Facebook — that demonstrate the scale of the investment it’s making in developing AI products. Data centres are hugely expensive to build and maintain, and the size of what Zuckerberg is suggesting would cost billions of dollars. Zuckerberg has been very bullish on the potential for the organization’s AI smart glasses in particular, and talk of Meta buying a stake in its Ray-Ban Meta AI glasses co-creator EssilorLuxottica has intensified in the last month.

Popeyes Beat KFC In My Chicken Sandwich Showdown—But Can It Take Down Chick-fil-A?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, few fast food rivalries are as competitive as the battle for the best chicken sandwich.
  • Industry observers note that in my previous chicken sandwich showdown, I put KFC and Popeyes head-to-head to see which chain served the better sandwich.
  • Chick-fil-A has built its reputation around a simple, flavorful chicken sandwich that doesn’t need much to stand out.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, few fast food rivalries are as competitive as the battle for the best chicken sandwich. And while plenty of chains have introduced their own versions over the years, Chick-fil-A and Popeyes remain two of the biggest names in the conversation.

Industry observers note that in my previous chicken sandwich showdown, I put KFC and Popeyes head-to-head to see which chain served the better sandwich. Popeyes ultimately came out on top, thanks to its bold seasoning, crispy breading, and well-balanced toppings. This time, I’m putting Popeyes up against one of its biggest competitors: Chick-fil-A.

Chick-fil-A has built its reputation around a simple, flavorful chicken sandwich that doesn’t need much to stand out. Popeyes, meanwhile, practically broke the internet when it introduced its now-famous chicken sandwich in 2019, sparking a fast food frenzy.

It has been revealed that I ordered each chain’s original chicken sandwich to compare flavor, texture, juiciness, and overall balance. Both have their strengths, but only one can move on as my favorite.

Chick-fil-A’s Original Chicken Sandwich keeps things simple with a breaded chicken fillet, pickles, and a toasted bun.

Chick-fil-A’s chicken is so recognizable for a reason. The seasoning and brine give the fillet a savory, slightly tangy flavor that’s hard to beat, while the crispy breading contrasts nicely with the juicy chicken. The pickles also do their job, adding just enough acidity and crunch to balance out the richness.

In a recent development, my biggest complaint is that I wanted a little more from the sandwich. Compared to other fast food chicken sandwiches I’ve tried, many of which come with some type of sauce, Chick-fil-A’s original feels a bit plain. The chicken has enough flavor to stand on its own, but I think a little mayo or another sauce would have made the overall sandwich even better.

Still, there’s something to be stated for a chicken sandwich that relies almost entirely on the quality and flavor of the chicken itself.

Popeyes’ Classic Chicken Sandwich features a breaded chicken fillet, pickles, mayo, and a toasted brioche bun. The sandwich that practically broke the internet when it released in 2019 still lives up to the hype.

It has been revealed that I’ve had this sandwich before where the chicken was slightly dry in spots, but thankfully that wasn’t the case this time. The fillet was juicy, flavorful, and incredibly well-seasoned. The breading had a satisfying crunch, and the bold, savory flavor made me want to keep going back for another bite.

The mayo was another important part of the sandwich, adding a tangy creaminess that complemented the chicken without overpowering it. Paired with the crisp pickles, it helped balance out the richness of the fried fillet.

Recent findings suggest that I also really appreciated the proportions. The soft brioche bun held everything together without overwhelming the chicken, and each bite had a good balance of meat, breading, sauce, and pickles.

While Popeyes might not always deliver the most consistently juicy chicken, everything came together particularly well during this taste test. Between the seasoning, crispy breading, and well-balanced toppings, it’s easy to understand why this sandwich became such a phenomenon in the first place.

Popeyes already managed to beat KFC in my previous comparison, and after going up against Chick-fil-A, it’s keeping its winning streak alive.

Chick-fil-A arguably has the more distinctive chicken flavor, thanks to its savory, slightly tangy seasoning. But when I’m ordering a chicken sandwich, I want the entire thing to work together, and that’s where Popeyes has the advantage.

In a recent development, chick-fil-A is still a great option, especially if you prefer a simpler sandwich that lets the chicken do most of the work. But after trying both, Popeyes delivered the better overall experience. With two wins under its belt, Popeyes is proving to be a pretty tough sandwich to beat.

31 Thanksgiving Dinner Alternatives to Turkey

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Honestly, anything can make for an alternative Thanksgiving dinner.
  • Recent findings suggest that A classic Thanksgiving menu is all well and good, but one of our colleagues swears by serving nachos on the fourth Thursday of every November.
  • Industry observers note that or go completely rogue with lobster pasta or a massive pot of chili.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Honestly, anything can make for an alternative Thanksgiving dinner. It’s your house, your rules. Our only suggestion: Make it festive, fun, and at least a little decadent.

Recent findings suggest that A classic Thanksgiving menu is all well and good, but one of our colleagues swears by serving nachos on the fourth Thursday of every November. If a significant bloomin’ bird just isn’t ca-caw-caw-calling your name this year, serve a whole roast fish, pork tenderloin with sour-sweet cherry sauce, or a flaky carrot Wellington instead.

Industry observers note that or go completely rogue with lobster pasta or a massive pot of chili. You can do that. Below, find vegetarian centerpieces, celebratory roasts, chicken dinners, and seafood mains for a Thanksgiving that looks a little different. BA’s Best Pumpkin Pie can stay.

Can carrots really count as a main course? They can when they’re roasted, glazed, and tucked into puff pastry with goat cheese, Gruyère, and walnuts. This Wellington feeds 8 to 10.

According to recent reports, red wine, browned mushrooms, pearl onions, and carrots give this meatless braise plenty of heft. Ladle it over mashed potatoes for a vegetarian anchor to your Thanksgiving menu.

Industry observers note that ruffled savoy cabbage, melty cheese, and a buttery cream cheese crust make this free-form tart worthy of the holiday table. Cut generous wedges for dinner and stick with savoy: Ordinary green cabbage won’t work here.

Industry observers note that A make-ahead casserole, like this pumpkin-infused strata scented with nutmeg and herbs and balanced by sharp cheddar, is just what your holiday schedule needs. Assemble it the night before; bake it on Thanksgiving.

Industry observers note that turkey isn’t the only holiday cooking project worth clearing the counter for. Delicate homemade crepes are rolled around ricotta, mozzarella, and Parmesan, then baked in marinara. Make the batter and filling a day ahead to split up the work.

Kale, pinto beans, and charred poblanos make these cheesy enchiladas a satisfying holiday main for four to six. Get a head start by making the charred salsa verde up to three days ahead.

In a recent development, this autumnal risotto works as a standalone dinner or alongside your favorite Thanksgiving sides. Set the table with shallow bowls and pick a fall salad full of color and crunch to balance the buttery rice.

British beef Wellington meets Cantonese barbecue-style pork in Peter Som’s pastry-wrapped centerpiece. A shiitake mushroom filling and gravy made from the marinade complete the picture; assemble the Wellington a day ahead.

According to recent reports, these impossibly tender short ribs are begging to be served with mashed potatoes and buttery milk buns with garlic butter. Give them what they want—and give yourself a head start by braising the ribs the day before Thanksgiving.

Brisket more your speed? Try our Brisket Bourguignon →.

Turkey skin has competition. Tender pork belly, crisp crackling, and a hard cider pan sauce make a persuasive case for skipping the bird. Pass the chile vinegar to cut through the richness; this roast feeds 8 to 12.

Ayesha Curry’s spice-crusted prime rib takes its cues from her mother’s braised oxtails, with habanero crema on the side. Prefer a simpler garlic-and-rosemary approach? Try this Low-and-Slow Rib Roast.

According to recent reports, for a roast-and-sides Thanksgiving without the turkey, garlic-and-rosemary-rubbed beef tenderloin makes an excellent centerpiece. Rosemary butter dresses the sliced roast, while tangy horseradish yogurt gives everyone something to swipe their next bite through.

Sources indicate that toasted rice, fried onions, and garlic form a dark, peppery crust on this slow-braised pork shoulder. Set out the big platter and pass the coconut-vinegar pan sauce; this roast feeds 8 to 12.

Maybe save the brown sugar-glazed ham for Christmas? This whole leg of lamb makes for a centerpiece that’s just as showstopping. And, like ham and turkey, leftover lamb can be deliciously repurposed in sandwiches.

Recent findings suggest that A platter of sliced pork tenderloin with glossy cherries and browned shallots has plenty of holiday presence without a long roast. Honey and red wine vinegar give the sauce its sweet-sour bite, and frozen cherries are welcome here.

If you’re going to make tamales, it’s a good idea to make a lot of them. Better yet, turn the process into a party, with everyone spreading masa and folding corn husks around the red chile pork filling.

In a recent development, this pasta packs a whole spectrum of holiday flavors into each bite, with crumbles of Italian sausage, shreds of brussels sprouts, and toasted pecans. Streamlining dinner into one dish leaves you more time for Thanksgiving pies.

For some people, spending all Thanksgiving in the kitchen sounds like a good time. For everyone else, there’s this beef-and-bean chili. A can of pumpkin purée thickens the broth, keeping things seasonal without calling for a single roasting pan.

In a recent development, give homemade fried chicken an even more festive angle with sage and thyme in the dredge and cranberry-mustard sauce for dipping. Start the buttermilk marinade the day before.

This whole roast duck comes with a built-in Thanksgiving side: The duck fat drippings go into basmati rice that cooks while the bird rests. Strategy for an overnight dry brine before the glossy pomegranate-honey glaze gets its moment.

Recent findings suggest that cooking for a smaller crowd? This skillet delivers the stuffing and the bird—chicken thighs, in this case—in one tidy package. Rendered chicken fat enriches the boxed stuffing mix, with dried cranberries and lemon zest brightening things up.

Two diminutive birds make a festive roast for four. A fiery guajillo chile, ginger, and vinegar marinade flavors both the hens and the potatoes beneath them, so the platter arrives with its own very good side.

You just need to make green beans, because this Thanksgiving main is already a two-in-one: Thinly sliced potatoes cook beneath a whole chicken, catching its drippings and crisping around the edges in the same cast-iron skillet.

If your Thanksgiving table could use a little red sauce (and spice), skip the whole bird in favor of this take on chicken parm. Gochujang and gochugaru bring the heat; melted mozzarella keeps things gloriously gooey.

José Andrés turns chicken wings and a colorful assortment of vegetables into a grand centerpiece, with saffron and smoked paprika flavoring the rice. You’ll need a 15" paella pan or comparably sized two-handled cast-iron or cast-aluminum pan.

Recent findings suggest that there’s nothing like pasta to stretch a spendy ingredient (hello, lobster). Serve with a massive crunchy salad with Italian dressing and garlic confit toast that diners can pass around for Thanksgiving party vibes.

Recent findings suggest that presenting a whole fish at the holiday table is wildly celebratory, even when you’re cooking for just two or three. Bring out lettuce wraps, kimchi, rice, and ssamjang so everyone can build each bite a little differently.

Recent findings suggest that A large roasted salmon fillet looks right at home on a holiday platter, especially under a crunchy, garlicky nut salsa. Make the salsa up to four days ahead, then roast the fish when it’s time for dinner.

The stuffing doesn’t have to be a side. Here, crushed boxed stuffing mix joins Parmesan, lemon zest, and parsley in a crisp crust for mustard-coated white fish. Dinner lands on the table in 25 minutes.

According to recent reports, this dark, glossy coconut caramel—savory with fish sauce and garlic, sharp with pickled jalapeño brine—turns pan-seared salmon into a holiday-worthy main. Serve with rice to catch every last bit of sauce.

Sources indicate that like many of the best Thanksgiving dishes, this one starts with a good stock. Carla Hall builds a fennel potlikker with celery, onions, and Pernod before layering those flavors into a hearty bowl of shrimp and grits.

#192029. Doing Crime Barely Covers My Menswear Habit in GTA VI

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1384 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gq ↗ Open Full Page

Doing Crime Barely Covers My Menswear Habit in GTA VI

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1384 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When GTA 6 came out at midnight last week, I played it for eight hours straight, all in the name of real, boots-on-the-ground journalism.
  • Most people will have spent their first-ever session getting through the missions, exploring the map, and finding out what Jason and Lucia have got themselves into.
  • Sources indicate that before we get into it, you should know: Your in-game clothes matter more than ever compared to other entries in the Grand Theft Auto universe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I am still slightly delirious. When GTA 6 came out at midnight last week, I played it for eight hours straight, all in the name of real, boots-on-the-ground journalism. Well, there was a quick power nap somewhere around 5 a.m., but otherwise I've been working very hard. I have a new wardrobe and some concerns about the price of digital jorts.

Most people will have spent their first-ever session getting through the missions, exploring the map, and finding out what Jason and Lucia have got themselves into. Not me. My main goal was to visit as many shops as possible. It's been 13 years since GTA 5; I wanted to see what had happened to the menswear.

Sources indicate that before we get into it, you should know: Your in-game clothes matter more than ever compared to other entries in the Grand Theft Auto universe. As I wrote last week, the fresh “heat” system lets cops remember what you were wearing, so losing them doesn't necessarily mean you're in the clear. Changing your hat or sunglasses won't clear the clothing clue, either. You need a full fit change. So technically, all this shopping could help me get away with something. That's my justification, anyway.

Industry observers note that unfortunately, even virtual shopping requires cold, hard cash—and early on, that takes considerably more effort than I'd hoped. You start with almost nothing, spending much of the opening stretch around Key Lento in swampy Mariana County. I'd gone in expecting to buy loads of clothes. Instead, I was checking what I could afford.

In a recent development, my first opportunity came in a random gun shop that also sold some workwear. I had a quick browse then went straight for the camo shorts. Back in August, British GQ's senior style editor Mahalia Chang declared that “camo shorts are fucking back, baby,” having watched Jason spend much of the trailer wearing them. Who was I to argue?

Nearby, in Hamlet, I found a few thrift shops and picked up a battered chore jacket with more than a little Carhartt Detroit about it. It looked properly used, which suited both my budget and the general condition of my pickup. I bought a watch, too, but more on that another time.

According to recent reports, I was already getting quite into it. I was comparing pieces, checking prices, and deciding what could wait. There were clothes I wanted and clothes I could afford. Annoyingly, the game understood the difference.

I bought a trucker cap at one point and was very happy with it. Over the summer, I wrote about wanting to give them another go despite having a head my mates call “a sniper's dream.” Jason doesn't have that problem (in a metaphorical sense, anyway), so I thought I'd let him enjoy one. Shortly afterwards, a gang of lads picked a fight with me, punched me, and knocked it off his head. I fled, only realizing once I was safely away that I hadn't picked it back up. I'd barely had a chance to enjoy it. I hope one of them's wearing it at least.

Sources indicate that after a few missions, I finally had enough money to justify another shopping trip. I got into my beaten-up pickup and headed downtown, where the prices started getting a little more serious. Denim jackets were around $120. A pair of dark wash jorts I really liked cost $45, which was slightly more than I wanted to spend.

I appreciate that this is a game in which you can steal a car, and I was still having a small financial discussion with myself about the price of shorts. For a game called Grand Theft Auto, I'd done surprisingly little car stealing in the time I'd been playing.

Sources indicate that the map is absolutely massive, and there almost 70 clothing stores to work through, so visiting everything was never gonna happen in one sitting. Cars now use fuel, too. Driving miles out of your way to look at a jacket comes with an additional expense, and I had to leave enough money to get home.

There was a reason to keep exploring, though. I went into another shop expecting more of the same and realized the stock was different, so now I wanted to check the other shops before buying anything. Apparently, I'd waited 13 years to recreate how I spend my Saturdays.

Sources indicate that naturally, I decided to drive to Ocean Beach, a more expensive part of the city where I had very little business shopping. Inside Nola, the person at the till looked me up and down in my shitty workwear and asked, “Eh, are you looking for somebody?”.

Sources indicate that it was an impressively efficient assessment of my finances. Nola felt a little like Casablanca, the French-Moroccan label known for colorful prints, sportswear, and clothes that suggest a considerably nicer holiday than the one you're on. I'd previously called Hawaiian shirts “the unofficial uniform of Vice City.” Here, joining in cost about $330. Blazers were about $430. I could look, provided I didn't get any dirt on anything.

Then I accidentally punched the shop assistant; I'm still getting used to the controls. At least, I think it was an accident. Either way, I had to flee before I could give the blazers much consideration. When I came back later, the store was temporarily closed. I hope it wasn't due to staff injuries.

Other boutiques were even less accommodating to my balance. Italian house Ferruccio Tucci (probably a GTA-ified Emilio Pucci) had $3,000 suits and $1,200 horsebit loafers. I went in to browse and accidentally bought a pair of $350 shades, which was a very expensive way to learn which button does what. The annoying thing is that they looked genuinely sick—exactly the sort of thing I'd wear IRL, which made it much easier to justify keeping them. Well, that was fuel and dinner gone for the day. At least I could look good while walking home.

Recent findings suggest that later, driving past Waxman Island, I came across Vice City's Eris flagship. Obviously, I had to go in. For anyone who hasn't spent the past few months staring at fictional trainers, Eris is basically GTA's answer to Nike. Nike takes its name from the Greek goddess of victory; Eris is the goddess of strife and discord. The shoes are often just as recognizable as the joke.

The store kinda reminded me a little of Niketown in London—at the moment closed for refurbishment—with neon lights and substantial statues and enough footwear to keep me occupied considerably longer than was sensible. There was the Rise Low, an Air Force 1 lookalike that I ended up getting in two colourways; the Strife 360, with its very Air Max 97-ish shape; and the Rook 1 High, which follows the Air Jordan 1 High. I own more than 400 pairs of sneakers IRL—I probably should've known that going in here would be a problem.

And Eris is only one option. There are alternative sneaker labels, beach shops, souvenir shops, and smaller, DIY-looking streetwear brands all dotted around the city. I'd barely begun working through them. Every time I thought I'd seen enough to stop, there was another shop worth going into.

The most expensive-looking thing I acquired didn't come from a boutique at all. Slight spoiler: A naked man offered to give me his “Crowex” watch after pulling a plastic egg out of his own ass. (Yes, you read that right.) You'll know him when you see him. I'm not gonna go into any more detail, partly because I'm tired and partly because I'd like you to experience that transaction yourself.

Industry observers note that eight hours in, I'd hardly scratched the surface. What surprised me most was how long the expensive stuff felt like it would take to earn. Those suits and loafers were sitting there, available to try, while my balance suggested another few missions first. There's a lot of city left to explore, quite a few shops I want to revisit, and a pair of jorts I'm still thinking about.

For now, though, I need some sleep. And Jason needs to earn back that $350.

A version of this story originally appeared in British GQ.

#192028. Breaking: Apple Juice Bread

Breaking: Apple Juice Bread

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (711 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level.
  • In a recent development, I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal.
  • Take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

In a recent development, I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he said he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

Take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard.

Industry observers note that mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

Industry observers note that set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very quickly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

It has been revealed that bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.
