#192026. Latest Update: The Year Fashion Fakes Became Too Real

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1779 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Vogue ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: The Year Fashion Fakes Became Too Real

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1779 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, fashion has a reality problem.
  • Earlier this month, the embattled Nvidia co-founder and now reinstated CEO Jensen Huang became an unlikely menswear sensation when the Instagram account @hidden.ny posted images of him wearing an archival, silver-studded Saint Laurent leather jacket from Hedi Slimane’s tenure.
  • The internet rushed to crown Huang a Hedi boy, but he’d never worn the jacket.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, fashion has a reality problem. Celebrities can be seen wearing clothes they’ve never touched, luxury houses may appear to release products they’ve never designed, and, in some cases, even clothes that actually exist don’t quite look like themselves online.

Earlier this month, the embattled Nvidia co-founder and now reinstated CEO Jensen Huang became an unlikely menswear sensation when the Instagram account @hidden.ny posted images of him wearing an archival, silver-studded Saint Laurent leather jacket from Hedi Slimane’s tenure. The post came just a day after Nvidia opened an investigation into Huang’s alleged affair with a suspected Chinese spy. “Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in Hedi Slimane SLP Studded Leather Jacket after admitting to affair with alleged Chinese spy,” read the caption.

The internet rushed to crown Huang a Hedi boy, but he’d never worn the jacket. As CNN first revealed, the images were fake; Vanity Fair subsequently verified they’d been generated or altered using AI. The originals, in fact, showed Huang wearing Dior at an airport in Seoul in June. The post was subsequently taken down, but the fantasy had already traveled.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang waves to the media as he arrives at Gimpo airport in Seoul on June 5, 2026. Photo: Jung Yeon-je / AFP via Getty Images.

It has been revealed that days later, designers including Reese Cooper and Gerrit Jacob called out luxury retailer Ssense over product imagery that misrepresented their clothes, from distorted construction details to inaccurate branding. Unlike Huang’s fictional fashion moment, these were real garments available to buy.

According to recent reports, cooper, founder of Reese Cooper and RC Outdoor Supply, discovered the inaccuracies while browsing the website himself. He had not been consulted about the imagery, which depicted his brand’s signature trademarked hook at twice its actual size.

“There’s a lot of sewing and design detail inaccuracies but the important issue is misrepresenting my trademarks — our hook is a major part of our branding, and of course all of the logos,” Cooper indicates. “The initial reaction is disappointment and frustration. It takes an overwhelming amount of time and resources to protect your brand legally with these trademarks, not to mention the work going into designing the clothes themselves.”.

Recent findings suggest that the errors were subtler than AI signifiers of the past, like extra fingers or missing limbs. But when shopping online, details matter. Fashion commentator and journalist Odunayo Ojo identified missing design details and Gerrit Jacob trousers with an invented waistband, additional seams and altered lettering.

“AI pulls everything toward an average, but design lives in the details that depart from that average,” Ojo says. “Generative models are built to make something that looks plausible, not something that’s precise. Plausible is fine for a moodboard. On a product page, plausible is misrepresentation.”.

In a statement to Vogue Business, a spokesperson for Ssense acknowledged the errors: “Accurate representation of our brand partners and their products is fundamental to Ssense. We recognize that some recent e-commerce imagery did not meet that standard, resulting in inaccuracies in product details. We take full accountability and have taken steps to resolve this problem with urgency.”.

According to recent reports, it comes after local media reported over the summer that Ssense had laid off its full-time photography and retouching teams as it invested in AI Virtual Try-On (VTON) in August to support content production and has since strengthened quality controls. The spokesperson for Ssense confirmed to Vogue Business that “in preparation for the transition to Virtual Try-On (VTON), Ssense made organizational changes in June that affected certain roles within its visual content department.” Ssense did not explicitly confirm that the AI technology caused the inaccuracies last week.

Together, the incidents exposed two sides of fashion’s growing synthetic image problem: AI can make an imaginary garment look real, and a real garment look imaginary, with both able to put brands in a difficult spot.

It has been revealed that the Huang images were far from an isolated incident. In April, AI-generated images indicated celebrities including Megan Fox and Robert Pattinson wearing fictional Balenciaga designs made from cardboard shipping boxes, while another fake imagined the Olsen twins in a Louis Vuitton campaign.

It has been revealed that nor was Ssense the only case of AI imagery creating confusion around real products. In May, after Swatch and Audemars Piguet teased a collaboration, AI-generated images of a colorful Royal Oak wristwatch circulated online. The actual release was a collection of Bioceramic pocket watches, disappointing fans who had come to expect a product that never existed.

Sources indicate that while the average person has struggled to distinguish many AI-generated images from real photographs for a couple of years, experts say things seem worse now because it’s become so much easier to produce them. “It’s now at the point where it’s really easy to create highly realistic content with minimal knowledge of how to optimize for the tool you’re using, and there’s plenty of tools to choose from,” claims Henry Ajder, a synthetic media expert and founder of Latent Space Advisory, pointing to their integration into popular chatbots and the growing availability of open-source alternatives.

It has been revealed that fashion is particularly exposed. “With fashion imagery, because there’s so much highly stylized, high-quality content associated with the industry, there’s been a huge amount of training data for these tools to utilize,” Ajder says, arguing that we’ve reached a tipping point. In 2026, unofficial campaigns can now look practically indistinguishable from a house’s own advertising, even as brands experiment with AI themselves.

Industry observers note that for Cooper, the Ssense episode has created a commercial dilemma. “Simply put, it’s brand damage,” he states. “RC Outdoor Supply is a new firm and all we have is our trademarks and reputation of design aesthetic and quality. To have these things put in question by the customer, it really erodes trust for the brand as a whole.”.

Sources indicate that he points out that retailers judge brands on sell-through, and inaccurate listings can deter purchases or generate returns, while removing them means losing sales altogether. “Ssense has removed the images, which I’m thankful for. However, it also removed the ability for anyone to purchase those items, which will result in low sales when looking at this season’s data,” Cooper claims.

According to recent reports, experts say the problem is particularly acute in luxury, where small design decisions and fit often underpin a garment’s value. “In luxury, the details are the price,” Ojo notes. “If the image erases them, you’ve erased the reason the garment costs what it costs — the problem isn’t AI as a tool, it’s using it for the one job where accuracy is the whole point.”.

Sources indicate that an accurate image of Reese Cooper’s Outdoor Supply Sierra Puffer Jacket. Photo: Screenshot, rcoutdoorsupply.com, courtesy of Reese Cooper.

In a recent development, wholesale contracts, meanwhile, haven’t caught up. “When a retailer’s AI imagery misrepresents a garment, the designer absorbs the returns and the reputational harm, and most of the wholesale agreements I review do not address AI-generated product imagery,” says Shermin Lakha, founder and managing attorney at Lvlup Legal.

Industry observers note that for luxury brands, the legal questions become more complicated when AI-generated images of their products circulate online without anything being sold, as in the Huang case. Lakha argues that luxury brands have fewer remedies against these non-commercial viral fakes than many might assume. “Existing law is effective against commercial actors and leaves a gap for the viral fake that nobody monetizes,” she says. Susan Scafidi, founder of the Fashion Law Institute at Fordham Law School, agrees legal options are limited. “There is no single, universal cause of action that a brand can invoke to target unauthorized imagery that includes its products, whether that imagery is created by AI or not,” she says. Trademark and false advertising claims may apply where recognizable products or logos are involved; other claims may arise from reputational harm.

The calculation changes if an account uses a brand’s identity to sell services, promote counterfeit goods or generate revenue. The Balenciaga cardboard box images, for example, were associated with an account promoting a course on creating viral AI visuals. But even when brands have grounds to challenge unauthorized imagery, the distinction between infringement and creative expression is rarely straightforward. “Luxury brands have for decades chafed against the imprecise nature of parody and other forms of ‘fair use’ under US law,” says Scafidi.

Daniel Shapiro, a brand protection executive at Red Points, which helps brands detect counterfeits and online impersonation, notes traditional monitoring tools that look for logos are increasingly inadequate. Newer systems analyze entire images for unreleased colorways, inaccurate hardware or recognizable patterns, even when logos have been removed.

But policing the internet is only part of the answer. Scafidi urges brands to distinguish harmful images from passing memes to decide whether to take action. When necessary, brands can work with platforms on removals and respond through their own channels. Lakha also recommends tighter contracts and internal verification before brands share viral images.

Recent findings suggest that on brand and retailer sites, Ojo wants human review against physical garments, designer approval and disclosure of AI alterations. “If what’s on the page isn’t a photograph of the real garment, they [a designer] should say so,” he says. “A small [AI] label costs nothing. Finding out later is what causes scandals and also costs Ssense the customer,” he says.

According to recent reports, the deeper challenge may be cultural. Luxury has traditionally relied on controlling its image, from campaign casting to the placement of a logo. AI makes that harder, while increasing the value of visual credibility. Lizzie Wheeler, founder of archival bridal salon Studio Dorothy and the resale expert behind the Instagram account @shit.u.should.buy, sees consumers becoming more discerning and brands returning to human craft as a ‘realness’ signal.

“Aside from the legal problems, luxury is moving back toward more organic, human work (like the hand-drawn Prada holiday campaign) and showing AI shortcuts will dissuade a luxury client,” she indicates. “Ssense does rely heavily on the luxury client and I imagine this type of error will impact them seriously,” she adds.

The irony is that fashion’s most elaborate fakes have often been powered by some of its most recognizable signatures: a Balenciaga provocation, an archival Saint Laurent jacket, an instantly identifiable luxury watch. As these signatures become easier to imitate, the ability to prove what’s real is becoming a more valuable part of luxury itself.

It has been revealed that “The consumer is becoming increasingly educated,” Wheeler says. “So I’d advise all retailers against pulling wool over the customer’s eyes.”.

The Best Air Fryers For Faster, Crispier Cooking (2026)

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that buzzy as they’ve become over the past several years, air fryers are really just small ovens with fans built into them, i.e., convection ovens that circulate hot air around your food.
  • It has been revealed that air fryers can take a few forms; the robot-esque basket-style models are probably what come to mind when you think of an air fryer, but there are versatile countertop convection ovens that add bake, broil, toast, and slow-cook options to the air fryer functionality.
  • The best for all varieties of air fryer needs are below.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that buzzy as they’ve become over the past several years, air fryers are really just small ovens with fans built into them, i.e., convection ovens that circulate hot air around your food. Our years of testing air fryers (and we’ve used over two dozen in that time) have taught us that there are plenty out there that can give you crispy-enough results—but the very best air fryers churn out not only golden brown French fries and crispy-skinned chicken wings, but tender fillets of salmon and even whole roast chickens at the touch of a button.

It has been revealed that air fryers can take a few forms; the robot-esque basket-style models are probably what come to mind when you think of an air fryer, but there are versatile countertop convection ovens that add bake, broil, toast, and slow-cook options to the air fryer functionality. Some even dehydrate and steam too. And most recently, more bowl-style air fryers have started to hit shelves, which swap a slide-in basket for a glass container and top-down, air-frying lid.

The best for all varieties of air fryer needs are below.

Updated 11/23/26: There may not be a more popular Black Friday sale item than an air fryer. And all our favorites have discounts this week, including our overall top Cosori pick for less than $100. High-tech options from Breville, Cuisinart, Instant Pot, and Ninja are deeply discounted, too.

Clearview 4-Quart Glass Basket Air Fryer.

Vortex Plus 6-Quart ClearCook Air Fryer.

Ninja SL401 DoubleStack XL 2-Basket Air Fryer.

Instant Vortex Slim XL 6-Quart Air Fryer.

Most air fryers fit into one of three categories: oven, basket, or bowl.

A countertop convection oven, or air fryer–toaster oven, combines most of the crisping power of the basket-style air fryers you know and love with the multifunctionality you get from a toaster oven or countertop oven. Generally, the “air frying” function is achieved with a perforated slide-in rack, which usually means lots of cooking surface, but the racks are usually shallow and can require careful tossing or flipping of whatever you’re cooking, depending on the dish. But air fryer ovens, like the Breville Smart Oven Pro with its 13 different cooking modes, can do a lot, making them bona fide do-it-all kitchen appliances.

Industry observers note that basket-style air fryers aren’t as versatile as air fryer ovens, but they’re also less expensive and take up less space. They also tend to deliver better final results on traditional air fryer stuff like crisping up small foods that require shaking (tater tots, French fries, or Brussels sprouts), for which a handled basket is far easier to maneuver. Minuses are that they can be hard to clean and are limited in square inches inside the basket. They’re also sometimes made of plastic or nonstick-coated materials, which may not appeal to some consumers.

Sources indicate that bowl air fryers offer some of the best (and worst) of both worlds and also some unique benefits. Most of these include a heat-resistant glass bowl acting as the basket. Some models operate much like basket air fryers, with the glass container sliding into the base unit, while others opt for a “lid” that sits on top and houses the air frying mechanism. The glass baskets make these very easy to clean (included crisping trays are another story), however their functionality for shaking and pausing to flip foods can be cumbersome. But many come with lids for the glass containers, letting them double as prep and storage containers too.

Capacity: 6 qt.Wattage: 172510 Cooking functions: Air Fry, Roast, Broil, Frozen, Preheat, Reheat, Dehydrate, Proof, Bake, and Keep WarmColor: WhiteWeight: 11.5 lb.Dimensions: 11.8" x 14.4" x 11.9"Warranty: 2 years.

Recent findings suggest that what we love: The 6-Quart Cosori Turboblaze Smart Air Fryer impressed us in every test, producing evenly browned and crispy frozen sweet potato fries, juicy chicken breasts, and perfectly cooked brussels sprouts. It has a straightforward digital interface that allows you to easily set the time and temperature and an impressive array of preset programs (Air Fry, Roast, Broil, Frozen, Preheat, Reheat, Dehydrate, Proof, Bake, and Keep Warm).

According to recent reports, A few things set the Turboblaze apart from the competition (including the previous longtime winner of this test, the Instant Vortex Slim). Most notably, it consistently produced the crispiest food of any air fryer we tested in record time. That may have something to do with the fact that there’s more space between the crisper plate (where the food sits) and the bottom of the basket than there is in some of the other top-performing models we’ve tried, which allows for better air circulation.

According to recent reports, another standout feature is its variable fan speeds, which adjust automatically depending on the cooking function. Unlike most air fryers that use this tech behind the scenes, the Turboblaze indicates you the fan speed right on the display. Air Fry, for example, is one of four “turbo modes,” running the fan at full blast (speed 5), while Bake uses a gentler speed 3 to avoid disrupting delicate foods. Low-temperature settings like Dehydrate and Proof drop all the way down to speed 1.

In a recent development, the Cosori Turboblaze is also a real value pick. The top performer in its price range (100–150) by a wide margin, it’s powerful, versatile, quiet, lightweight, and easy to clean (the brand notes both the nonstick basket and cooking tray are dishwasher-safe, though we recommend hand-washing anything with a nonstick coating).

In a recent development, the model we tested includes smart features, meaning you can control it remotely or use voice commands via the VeSync app. If that’s not your thing, Cosori also sells a non-smart version for about $10 less.

Recent findings suggest that what we’d leave: Our gripes with this model are minor. It’s slightly annoying that you have to press a release button to pull the basket out. And while the greater amount of space between the crisper tray and basket bottom contributes to better airflow (and thus better browning), it means food is more likely to fall through while cooking.

Capacity: 2.1-qt.Wattage: 9004 cooking functions: Air-Fry, Bake, Roast, ReheatColors: Gray, red, white, greenWeight: 4.9 lb.Dimensions: 10.1" x 8.3" x 10.5"Warranty: 2 years.

If you’re on a tighter budget, have very little counter space to spare, or are mostly crisping up food just for yourself, consider the Cosori Lite 2.1-Quart Mini Air Fryer.

What we love: This compact air fryer did a beautiful job crisping and browning small servings of frozen tater tots and fries, sliced zucchini, and veggie burger patties (two at a time, max). Depending on where you buy, it will only costs $50–$60 (as of publish time)—not at all bad for a lightweight, quiet, digital air fryer with four easy-to-use presets (air-fry, roast, bake, and reheat). It’s easy to tuck into a cabinet and to clean. Like the Cosori Blaze, the Lite has a nonstick basket. Again, while the manual claims the nonstick basket is dishwasher-safe, we always recommend hand-washing anything with a nonstick coating.

What we’d leave: Per its name, it’s quite small—don’t expect to be cooking enough food for more than two people in this thing. It also won’t remind you when it’s time to shake your food, so you’ll need to keep an eye on the timer yourself (luckily, the digital display makes this pretty easy).

Sources indicate that if you want an air fryer with maximum versatility and have some counter space to spare, spring for the Breville Smart Oven Air Fryer Pro. Breville makes a few different models (which can be found in the kitchens of many of our editors), but this one is the best combination of performance and value.

What we love: This midrange model has been our top pick for years now because of its versatility, build quality, intuitive design, and consistently strong performance in testing.

In testing, the Smart Oven Air Fryer Pro delivered reliably great results. It excelled at foods that need to be laid in a flat, even layer across the crisper tray (think veggie burgers or salmon fillets), but also handled frozen fries, tots, and sweet potato fries well. Its interior is roomy enough to fit a quarter sheet pan or 13x9" casserole pan, which means it can effectively double your oven space (or eliminate the need to turn on your full-size oven altogether).

Recent findings suggest that this model is also a favorite among BA staffers and Test Kitchen editors, as well as award-winning cookbook author Nik Sharma, who developed some of BA’s favorite air fryer recipes. “I prefer toaster-oven-style to basket-style air fryers, because they’re easier to use for more common tasks like baking, toasting bread, and roasting more efficiently,” Sharma notes.

Sources indicate that what we’d leave: As with most oven-style air fryers, it’s harder to toss or shake small foods mid-cook compared to a basket-style machine. We also found that, in general, food benefited from a higher cooking temperature (and often slightly longer cook time) relative to the basket-style winners.

Capacity: .5 cubic feetWattage: 18005 Cooking functions: Toast, Bagel, Broil, Pizza, Bake & Roast5 Air-frying functions: Air-Fry, Fries, Wings, Bacon, Crispy ReheatColor: Stainless steelWeight: 15.8 lb.Dimensions: 15.7" x 16.9" x 10"Warranty: 2 years.

If you like the idea of going the air fryer–toaster oven route but (1) don’t have the space for the Smart Oven Air Fryer Pro or (2) don’t want to shell out $400 in pursuit of crispiness, here’s some good news: Breville offers the Smart Oven Air Fryer Compact, which is essentially a smaller, cheaper version of our top pick.

What we love: As with most Breville products, the Smart Oven Air Fryer Compact feels thoughtfully designed, with stainless-steel finishes and a solid build. There are fewer niche modes than the Pro—no Dehydrate or Proof—but it does include four air-frying-specific presets in addition to a standard Air Fry setting.

We found using the Compact intuitive (the guide printed on the inside of the oven door helped). We also appreciated the “bit more” button, a feature borrowed from Breville’s toasters that adds a touch of extra cooking time when your fries are looking just a touch underdone.

Recent findings suggest that this model performed comparably to the Smart Oven Air Fryer Pro in most of our tests, producing juicy chicken, evenly browned cubes of tofu, and crispy veggies. We still prefer the larger model for its versatility and additional functionality, but this little oven would make a worthy addition to any smaller kitchen.

What we’d leave: While the Compact did well in most tests, it struggled a bit with frozen sweet potato fries. This largely came down to overcrowding due to the smaller capacity: While we tried to fit an entire bag’s worth on a single tray, the unevenness with which the fries browned is a good example of the fact that, unlike a basket fryer, countertop oven-style air fryers are best used to cook things in a single layer.

As mentioned, there’s a guide to oven inserts and placement on the inside of the oven’s door, but this is easy to miss, and these suggestions did not appear in full in the manual. Because of this, one tester accidentally cooked chicken with no tray underneath the wire basket to catch the drippings, which resulted in a smoking-hot mess.

It’s also worth noting that one of the major benefits of opting for an oven-style air fryer tends to be capacity, but the Compact wasn’t able to fit more food than our top basket-style pick.

The Breville Smart Oven Air Fryer Compact (L) is much smaller than the Smart Oven Air Fryer Pro (R).

Clearview 4-Quart Glass Basket Air Fryer.

Capacity: 4 qt.Wattage: 16005 Cooking functions: Air Fry, Bake, Broil, Recrisp, Keep Warm, plus custom settingsColors: Black, Toasted Oat, Sage, TahiniWeight: 12.75 lb.Dimensions: 13.75" W x 12.75" D x 11.25" HWarranty: 3 years.

New on the market in 2026, Cuisinart’s ClearView series of air fryers truly delivers on its name with the introduction of a glass basket model that also sports a viewing window on the top of the unit (the line also features a larger, 9-qt. non-glass model). Unlike other glass air fryers we tried, this one operates more like the basket-style most people expect when they think of an air fryer.

According to recent reports, what we love: The ClearView got high marks across the board in our tests comparing glass air fryers head-to-head, almost always offering up the winning results. The controls are easy to navigate, and the functions are intuitive with beeps to remind you to flip or shake your food when your cook is halfway through. In addition to the usual Air Fry, Bake, and Reheat functions, Cuisinart’s also offers a Keep Warm. Plus, there are two programmable custom presets if you’re cooking the same foods frequently.

The crisper plate is nonstick, coated in PFAS-free ceramic, making it a breeze to clean with a little soap and water (or just throw it in the dishwasher). The glass basket is also dishwasher-safe. The ClearView doesn’t have any kind of mesh or grate covering the heating mechanism. We’ll continue to see how this fares over time, but in the meantime it’s nice not worrying about another greasy, perforated plate to clean. Lastly, the ClearView 4-Quart Glass Basket Air Fryer also comes in four colors—Black, Toasted Oat, Sage, and Tahini—and, as with all countertop appliances, it’s nice to have some kind of choice behind black plastic and stainless steel.

Sources indicate that what we’d leave: The cord wrap post noticeably sticks out from the back of the unit. While this is probably great for airflow safety, it adds inches to a machine that’s also tall. And unlike some of the other glass air fryers we tried, Cuisinart’s bowl is oven or microwave safe. Granted, the point of the bowl is to air-fry, but if you’re using to carry your lunch into the office after cooking the night before, reheating is a little trickier.

Capacity: 6.5 qt.Wattage: 17256 Cooking functions: Air Fry, Roast, Bake, Dehydrate, Proof, and ReheatColor: Stainless steelWeight: 14.1 lb.Dimensions: 11.8" x 11.8" x 11.6"Warranty: 5-year limited.

We won’t go down the PFAS rabbit hole and get deep into the concept of “nontoxic” cookware right here and now (we've got other articles for that), but given the way the concept has come front and center we know some people want an air fryer with a PFAS-free nonstick basket—and for that, we recommend the Cosori Iconic.

It has been revealed that what we love: It has similar features and produces similar results to our top pick, the Cosori TurboBlaze, churning out crispy-skinned salmon and beautifully browned Brussels. Like the TurboBlaze, the Iconic allows you to choose between five different fan speeds, which means it's equally adept at turning delicate kale into crispy chips without blowing them around the basket as it is cooking hefty bone-in chicken breasts to bronzed perfection.

And for those looking to eliminate PFAS from every inch of their kitchen, it has both a PFAS-free ceramic nonstick-coated basket and crisper plate.

It has been revealed that what we’d leave: Aesthetically, it may not be for everyone as this stainless-steel air fryer looks a bit spaceship-like. But the real downside is the price, which is practically double that of the TurboBlaze.

In the long run: The Cosori Iconic has seamlessly fit into the life of BA’s head of video, Dan Siegel. The speed is what won him over: “I shave 25% or more off any package-recommended cooking time and achieve perfect browning and crisping on every cook. The nonstick surfaces of both the basket and the included rack are remarkably easy to clean, making this my go-to appliance. My toaster oven probably misses me.” He mostly uses it for his two kids, occasionally scaling up to cook chicken breasts for his family of four, which takes two batches. (“It’s not huge.”) Despite the mirror-like stainless-steel finish, upkeep has been simple: “I haven't had any problems; I really only touch the top and the basket.” And then there’s the look. "It looks grown-up, like an actual appliance and not a big plastic toy without looking industrial. The MacBook of air fryers.".

It has been revealed that we have spent hours and hours over the past few years researching, testing, and retesting popular air fryers from top-name brands, including Breville, Cuisinart, Ninja, Philips, and Cosori. Here's how we put each appliance to the test:.

When evaluating each model, we looked for a few key qualities:.

4-Quart Vortex 6-in-1 Mini Air Fryer.

Industry observers note that this model from Instant Pot is a great option if a full-size (6-qt. or more) air fryer feels too massive for your space or lifestyle, but our winning mini model (2-qt. limit) is too small. There’s a lot to love here, including the intuitive controls and presets, the viewing window and built-in light, and the ceramic nonstick interior coating. In testing, we found it did a decent job crisping everything we threw at it, though its performance didn’t quite match the winning Cosori Turboblaze.

Instant Vortex Slim XL 6-Quart Air Fryer.

Recent findings suggest that this model from Instant was a previous top pick, and we still think it’s an excellent air fryer. Its design, although compact, offers a significantly larger cooking surface area than comparably sized air fryers thanks to the shape of its basket. In practice, this meant our tester was able to fit an entire extra veggie burger patty (six total) compared to models of a similar size and generally cook more food in each batch without sacrificing any of the airflow that makes air-fried food so crispy.

Vortex Plus 6-Quart ClearCook Air Fryer.

If a basket-style air fryer is what you’re after and you like the idea of being able to monitor what you’re cooking, the Instant Pot Vortex Plus ClearCook is definitely worth considering. This model performed nearly identically to our old top pick, the Instant Vortex Slim (probably because it’s a very similar build). The major difference—besides the ClearCook’s dimensions—is that it has a cooking window located at the front of its basket, plus a button that switches on an interior light, sort of like a traditional oven. This makes tracking the progress of your tots, fries, or chicken wings possible without removing the basket and disrupting the cooking process. Considering that providing a certain level of brownness is one of the chief concerns in air fryer cooking, this really comes in handy. A few more bonus points for the ClearCook: It adds Dehydrate to its list of functions and can hold temperatures as low as 95°F (the low end of the Vortex Slim’s range is 120°F). The ClearCook also happens to be $30 cheaper than the Slim at full price. On the downside, the square shape of the ClearCook’s basket fits one less veggie burger patty than more elongated baskets. It’s also a bit bulky.

Recent findings suggest that the Typhur Dome 2 is notably spacious compared to other basket-style fryers, with 139.5 square inches of cooking surface that fits a 12" pizza, 20 chicken wings, or 11 large chicken thighs per batch, and a digital panel with 15 presets plus a companion app offering more settings, self-cleaning, and one-touch recipes. We used to recommend the original Typhur Dome as a top pick for extra-large capacity, but after testing the Dome 2, which replaced it, we felt its performance didn’t quite merit a spot on our top picks: When filled to capacity, it took much longer to properly cook and crisp food than most other basket air fryers, and 11 bone-in chicken thighs took upward of 45 minutes to get truly golden, a major red flag given that cutting cooking time is a major reason to choose an air fryer over the oven. That noted, the Dome 2 cooks food evenly and does eventually get very crisp, so if you’re feeding a large family and have counter space to spare, it may still be worth the investment.

Sources indicate that the Philips almost took a top spot—almost. It’s got a generous capacity, the control panel is easy to navigate, and it performs well with minimal user intervention. In other words, you won’t have to do a lot of shaking or stirring to get crispy fries from the Philips. This model did have a smaller yet heavier basket, and it’s loud and harder to clean due to a bunch of interlocking parts. It’s a good air fryer, but with its higher price tag, we feel like there are better deals on this list.

Recent findings suggest that this newer model from Philips has a lot going for it: sleek touchscreen interface, helpful viewing window, and a whopping 16 settings. It did very well in our testing, producing crispy tots, tofu, and fries, but we preferred the design and the interface of the Cosori and Instant models. If you’re looking for an air fryer with a window feature, we’d recommend going with the Instant ClearCook (slightly cheaper at the time of writing) unless you find this model at a discount.

The Dreo ChefMaker isn't just an air fryer—it's also got probe cooking capabilities and app compatibility that make cooking proteins pretty effortless, and is a personal favorite of senior editor Olivia Tarantino. For the purposes of this article, though, we mainly tested its air frying abilities. We found that while the Dreo performed well, the winning TurboBlaze produced crispier, more evenly-cooked results all while ringing in at a third of the price. That said, if the probe cooking feature intrigues you, this fryer might be worth a try.

In a recent development, our Place partnered with James Beard Award–winning chef and cookbook author J. Kenji López-Alt on this updated version of the Wonder Oven, which features eight cooking functions, a touchscreen interface, and a roomy three-tier 30-liter capacity. Like all of Our Place's products, this little oven is an aesthete’s dream—but looks aside, it impressed us. It’s incredibly powerful, able to crisp brussels sprouts, tofu, and fries up to twice as fast as the winning Breville. It produced tender salmon with potato-chip-like skin in just seven minutes. Despite its smaller footprint, it’s large enough to fit a quarter-sheet pan, making it a good option if you want to save a few inches of counter space.

According to recent reports, all that said, while the Wonder Oven Pro is generally well-designed, a few features were annoying to use. The touchscreen isn’t the most responsive. But the bigger issue we had was with the preheating cycle. Preheating this oven to 400°F took 8–9 minutes from cold, which is already slower than the Breville’s 4–5. But more importantly, the Breville (like most regular ovens) takes less time to preheat when it’s already at temp. The Wonder Oven Pro, on the other hand, seemed to kick off a whole latest several-minutes-long preheat cycle even when it had just been heated, only after which the timer would start.

Cuisinart Air Fryer Oven 6-Qt Basket Stainless Steel Air Fryer.

Industry observers note that the Cuisinart was easy to use, didn’t whirr too loudly, included a nice preheat feature, and was about the same price. We also really liked the viewing window you could use to check the progress of your food. However, its deeper square-shaped basket has less surface area than something like the Instant Vortex Slim’s rectangular one, which limits its capacity.

Ninja SL401 DoubleStack XL 2-Basket Air Fryer.

Sources indicate that the DoubleStack takes the idea of a dual-basket air fryer to a whole newly introduced level—literally. Like the Vortex Slim, the DoubleStack’s design prioritizes using vertical space. It’s skinny with the baskets stacked on top of each other instead of side by side like most other dual models. This makes it narrow and tall instead of wide, but not so tall that you can’t nestle it under your cabinets. Despite its space-saving design, you don’t lose out on actual cooking space. The baskets are substantial enough to fit a chicken, and the wire racks in each mean you can really maximize how much you’re cooking. (Though you do need to remain mindful of not overloading it with food, otherwise you’ll block the airflow and mess up the whole air-frying process.) You can also program the baskets separately and utilize the machine’s Smart Finish feature—which delays the start of the basket with the shorter cook—to have a whole meal ready at the same time. The one thing we didn’t like was the somewhat confusing interface.

AeroLucen 5-quart Glass Air Fryer.

According to recent reports, like the Cuisinart ClearView we recommend above, this glass air fryer operates like a traditional basket air fryer, in fact even more so as it features a front-mounted basket handle with slide-in operation. It’s a sleek-looking machine with a glossy top that illuminates when powered on with all of your touch-surface buttons. And we like that’s is relatively compact at just over 9.5" tall, making it great for in-cabinet storage. In the glass category, it performed nearly as well as the Cuisinart across the board with just a few cases of less even results, but we’re really nitpicking. What we didn’t like was the mesh-style crisping plate, which is tedious to clean and sits awkwardly on some jutting posts inside the basket, (though its design does offer a high and low position for maximizing space or airflow). That mesh is repeated on the underside of the heating element, something we don’t look forward to cleaning after a few dozen oil-evaporating cooking cycles. The internal light is intended to help you see what you’re cooking, but it glows red, which isn’t so helpful when you’re trying to keep an eye on browning.

Industry observers note that of the lid-style glass bowl air fryers we tested, this one was the easiest to maneuver with a fold-away handle that makes removing the top easy for flipping or shaking in the middle of cooking. With fine-tunable controls, it nailed crunchy skin on chicken thighs and crispy brussels sprouts with tender centers. More delicate dishes like salmon didn’t get where we wanted on the first try, and tofu cubes required more time than the recipe allotted to get anywhere near crispy enough. It fell short, as a lot of the glass bowl fryers did, on frozen fries, yielding uneven results and underdone portions when using the settings suggested on the back of the bag. We wish the “flip” alert was more than just a light, and it’s a little odd that the “Dehydrate” setting is listed as a bonus because you have to long-press another button to use it. The attached feet also mean the glass bowl can’t be put in the oven or microwave, but it is dishwasher-safe and comes with a lid. Plus, the whole fryer and basket setup is designed to nest inside itself for storage. And of this style of meal-prep-friendly air fryers, it’s the best version.

Instant Vortex Plus 4-Quart Air Fryer.

Recent findings suggest that this Instant Pot air fryer model is if you need something with a smaller capacity. The rectangular shape of its basket made it easy to fit plenty of food inside. It is sleek and has a short profile, which are nice features too. The Vortex Slim just offered better performance.

Recent findings suggest that this is Ninja's basic basket air fryer. It’s lightweight and simple to use, and it does a nice job crisping up fries. The round shape of its basket, though, makes it less versatile than other models on this list. If you’re trying to cook raw proteins or a tray of vegetables, you give away a lot of space with a round basket.

It has been revealed that while the Dash looks cute with its retro silhouette and poppy colors, it just didn’t perform that well. Sweet potato fries came out soggy and greasy. Tofu cubes got crisped on one side but were raw on the other, and the round basket could only fit one veggie burger. The two dials, controlling time and temperature, also prevented us from getting more specific in the cook settings.

Panasonic FlashXpress Air Fryer Toaster Oven.

It has been revealed that this oven-style air fryer from Panasonic performed well in our testing, but we found it frustrating to use for a few reasons. It has 12 different functions, but they come with very little on the display as to what each of these functions truly means. The Air Fry mode only allowed us to select temperatures between 410℉–445℉, which seemed quite high for certain foods. We also disliked the automatic preheating period that we couldn’t bypass even if the oven was already hot (this was particularly annoying when we just wanted to tack on an extra few minutes after finishing a cooking cycle). If you want to do that, you have to take the extra step of once again pressing the start button after the preheating process in order to start the timed cook cycle.

In a recent development, like all of DTC darling Our Place’s products, the original Wonder Oven is cute. Unfortunately, it failed to impress us enough to earn a recommendation here. While it did fine at cooking tater tots and french fries, it produced unevenly browned, ultra mushy zucchini and tofu that never quite got the crisp exterior we were looking for. The analog controls are aesthetically pleasing, but make selecting an exact temperature impossible (and knowing when the unit is at temperature impossible too). It did, however, make a shockingly good fillet of crispy-skinned salmon.

Rather than a typical basket system, the Crispi consists of a glass container and a PowerPod that sits on top. The idea is that you can store your food directly in the glass containers, and Crispi sets include as many as three basket sizes (with more available). While most food did get crisp in the Crispi (you’d hope so with a name like that!), it took longer to do so than in a standard basket air fryer, and we found that food cooked somewhat unevenly. We tested this unit twice, the second time head-to-head with other glass air fryers, and our biggest gripe remains that there’s no precise temperature control—instead, you must choose between four preset modes (Max Crisp, Bake, Air Fry, and Recrisp). We thought that lack of precision made this model less versatile, and remembering which mode to use for which temperature number recommended on the bag of frozen fries or other foods wasn’t very user-friendly.

Recent findings suggest that the Typhur Sync has lots of bells and whistles, like a wireless probe thermometer (with a built-in charging port), app compatibility, a PFAS-free basket, and nine total programs (including the three found only in the app). In testing, though, it failed to produce as impressive results as the winning Cosori. The fries browned, but many remained soggy, the salmon skin failed to crisp, and the Brussels sprouts didn’t quite get as golden as we’d have liked. While some of this might be solved by tinkering with time and temperature, at $160, we just didn’t feel this air fryer was worth the splurge.

Recent findings suggest that in its defense, Magnifique’s Glass Air Fryer has some thoughtful features: two sizes of glass baskets (4.5-qt. and 2.5-qt.), each with lids, and a silicone base that’s easy to remove for cleaning and oven or microwave cooking (something Cuisinart and Ninja can’t match). It’s also the only glass air fryer we tested in this round that could possibly hold a small pizza with an 8.5" diameter crisper plate. However, there are more than a few aspects that weren’t as user-friendly. The stainless-steel crisper plate (no nonstick coating whatsoever) was the most difficult to clean by far, not only because of that lack of coating but because of the perforation pattern as well. The instructions specifically say don’t use scouring pads, but a gentle scrub with a plastic pad was the only way we could remove all the residue. There’s no reminder to flip or shake your food halfway through, a pretty standard-matter beep on many other units, and when you do take the lid off, you have to actually hit Start again to keep going, something other fryers do automatically. Results, especially with frozen foods like fries, were uneven, and fine-tuning is near impossible as its interface only allows for four preset cooking modes with no customization. If you’re following a recipe, you’ll have to remember which mode gets to which general temperature range and hope for the best.

What is an air fryer? Is it just a convection oven?

An air fryer is a countertop oven that uses hot air, circulated by a fan, to give foods crisper textures than you can achieve in a regular oven or toaster oven. What makes an air fryer a “fryer” is a built-in convection fan that blows the hot air around the food to crisp it up. It’s the combination of heat and moving air that produces the kind of crispy exterior you’d otherwise get from deep-frying or pan-frying. But unlike a deep fryer, an air fryer requires far less oil to achieve the desired effect—and it doesn’t leave your house smelling like a grease trap for days or weeks. So, technically speaking, yes, air fryers are just small convection ovens, but the most classic form of air fryer isn’t usually oven-shaped, rather more like egg or block with a slide-out basket on the front.

Whether you’re a purist and only consider products that contain baskets to be true air fryers, or you find the term air fryer to be stupid marketing jargon for a convection oven is up to you to decide. For the purposes of this review, we’ve included both toaster ovens that contain convection or “air fryer” settings and basket or bowl air fryers.

What accessories should I buy for my air fryer?

Recent findings suggest that there are a few extras you can buy to optimize your frying experience—things like an olive oil sprayer (so you can crisp without spilling oil on the heating element), parchment paper liners, and an instant read thermometer. For more of our favorite air fryer accessories, head right this way.

Alaina Chou: I’ve been testing air fryers and other small appliances for Bon Appétit and Epicurious since 2023. In that time, I’ve cooked countless batches of salmon, brussels sprouts, and frozen fries in pursuit of an air fryer that delivers on the lofty promise of deep-fryer-level crispiness without the need for a vat of hot oil. And I’ve blown out the power in the Test Kitchen numerous times in the process (sorry, Test Kitchen editors).

The Real-Life Wardrobe of Michael Bennett, Who Traded the NFL for Furniture Design

💡 Key Takeaways
  • When you’ve won a Super Bowl ring, made three Pro Bowl appearances, and played a key role on one of the most dominant defensive squads ever—the Seattle Seahawks’ 2010s-era Legion of Boom—what do you do next?
  • Industry observers note that after completing his 11-year NFL career in 2020, the 41-year-old enrolled at two institutions—the University of Hawaii and Seattle’s Heritage School of Interior Design—to study architecture and interior design, respectively.
  • Through his design practice Studio Kër, Bennett debuted an 11-piece collection of avant-garde furniture inspired by the African diaspora in 2024, which was well received by critics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When you’ve won a Super Bowl ring, made three Pro Bowl appearances, and played a key role on one of the most dominant defensive squads ever—the Seattle Seahawks’ 2010s-era Legion of Boom—what do you do next? For Michael Bennett, the answer was to head back to school.

Industry observers note that after completing his 11-year NFL career in 2020, the 41-year-old enrolled at two institutions—the University of Hawaii and Seattle’s Heritage School of Interior Design—to study architecture and interior design, respectively. “I’m a student of whatever I do,” Bennett tells me. “My best quality—and probably my worst quality—is that the things I love to do, I try to become the best. I play tennis five days a week. I’m trying to go to Wimbledon. And design and architecture are like that.”.

All that effort is paying off. Through his design practice Studio Kër, Bennett debuted an 11-piece collection of avant-garde furniture inspired by the African diaspora in 2024, which was well received by critics. He’s now hard at work on his sophomore line, alongside a spoken-word album and the occasional bespoke garment.

That last side quest should come as no surprise, because Bennett has some of the most distinctive personal style I’ve ever seen on a pro athlete–current or former—with a particularly clean headwear and accessories game. Here, Bennett tells me all about the skills he carried over from football into his upcoming career, what fatherhood has taught him about masculinity, and the song he listens to every day.

Michael Bennett: I’ve been playing football my whole life, man. After winning so much, I dug deep. I had already conquered the body. How do I conquer the mind? At what point am I being selfish? I’m missing so much of my kids’ lives. I’ve already been to the highest of the high. Am I going to leave my family with a broken man? That was really the question. Am I chasing ego or am I chasing something else? In reality, a lot of us are just chasing the ego, to be remembered, scared of the death of what [your life] was rather than [embracing] the growth that can be.

People want to keep others in a certain box because that’s the way that they understand them. That’s in any relationship. If you started to date somebody when they’re 20 and you turn 40 and they start to change, you’d be like, “You used to like your eggs like that.” People don’t allow others to transition; won’t allow people to actually experience growth. Often you’re meeting people in a time where they’re just starting to learn who they are. Over time you start to really develop who you are.

In a recent development, the truth is it doesn’t matter if people take you seriously, [as long as] you take yourself seriously. What are you doing to practice your craft? Artists are like, “Oh, my practice, my practice.” I never really understood what that meant until I started doing my own practice. I practiced on the field and I can practice the body. But really, if you want to be taken seriously intellectually, then you have to practice the mind. Sometimes practicing the mind is also connected to the body. In football, yeah, you are connected to the mind in a certain way. But it isn’t always like learning to be a lawyer or an architect or an artist—to be a thinker, you’re doing something completely different. And it’s just allowing yourself to transition. Man, truthfully, you got to say fuck everybody.

I think it’s one of the most intellectual sports in general. Tennis is one of those sports where it’s about the angle, the quick twitch. You’re by yourself. With football, it’s the amount of moving parts. People overlook the amount of detail that it takes to run a team—practicing and going through a play 3,000 times before you actually get it. The best players I ever met were the smartest when it came to the sport. They were the PhDs of their craft.

It’s taught me vulnerability. It made me a better human. In some ways, my daughters have allowed me to mature. The sport of football requires so much masculinity. I’m not saying that all masculinity is toxic, [but] it’s more about, how do you hunt but still be gentle? The true samurai doesn’t strike, but knows he can.

Industry observers note that what my daughters have allowed me to do is develop my whole humanity. To have a daughter is so special—women are very special. As an athlete, people come back from injuries, but to see a woman come back from giving birth is a whole other level of love. My daughters have been my greatest accomplishments in my life. I never made a Super Bowl trophy. There’s always another winner. But there’s only one Peyton, there’s only one Blake, and there’s one Ollie. As a maker, those are the most special things that I could make.

Sources indicate that in 2019, I was really into Booker T. Washington and W.E.B. Du Bois and [their debate over] the “Talented Tenth.” [Booker T. Washington believed that] intellectualism should never get away from the idea of making. I got into design because I’ve always been involved in politics, and politically, I started to realize that everything came down to design.

Sources indicate that shirt and pants by Studio Kër. Shoes by Collegium.

Whenever I spoke out about police brutality or on critical complications in America, that was really where I started to think about design as this language—this form of resistance. How can I change the system? It starts with design. Where I grew up, a non-gentrified area that was low income, it’s like you could see that there was no empathetic way of thinking about design. The definition of architecture for me is empathy for space. That’s what led me to this idea of these African diaspora forms and languages that I will use as my form of resistance.

In a recent development, I’m working on a new collection of furniture. The first collection I did was called “We Gotta Get Back to the Crib,” which to me was really about getting back to the essence of Blackness. A lot of times we talk about Blackness and it’s always connected to traumatic experience. But to me, it was more about how can I connect to these true levels of love, these things really shaped my culture, my family, my mother, my grandmother, and everything that was beautiful about being Black? This next collection is about African brutalism. How can I bring these things that are seen in the ghetto in America and in West Africa and then turn those into ideas about furniture? A lot of times what I’m dealing with as a designer is this idea of abstraction. How can I pull and reference something in such a sweet way? Like how Virgil designed shoes with references, leaving crumbs to this unspoken past. As a designer, that’s what I’m trying to do.

Yeah, I got a spoken word project.

According to recent reports, as an athlete, if you talk about your cars or you talk about your jewelry, the way that you gained it doesn’t have that kind of Jay-Z effect—you didn’t hustle to get that. You played to get that, which is different from somebody hustling to get that. With spoken word, I think about Gil Scott-Heron or The Last Poets. They’re talking about critical challenges. My perspective is really about humanizing the Black experience and the Black man. My stories and what I’m trying to tell with this music, E-Nigg-Ma, is so much about Black culture, Black design, Black features, this idea of what America is trying to suffocate about Blackness and not let it breathe.

It has been revealed that cuff by Dries van Noten. Ring by Olithica. Watch by Patek Philippe.

Music. When I’m designing, beautiful sounds are really important to the way that I think. My number-one song that I always listen to is Miles Davis’s “Flamenco Sketches.” It’s my daily listen. Those are the sounds that I need to hear: the horn, the riffs, the in-between.

According to recent reports, my studio inspires me, just the way light hits. It’s the simplest things. Seeing my family movies. My wife inspires me with what she’s designing.

According to recent reports, my great-grandpa, Hall Mack, everybody talked about his fashion. People still talk about his style. He was the first person I saw dry cleaning everything. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that chicken noodle soup just got way more interesting. Inspired by Egyptian bird tongue soup, this warming spice-tinged chicken broth is as comforting as it is flavorful. The real star here is the orzo. Toasted in butter until it’s deeply golden and nutty-fragrant, the pasta takes on a latest personality. Unlike plain noodles, which quickly go limp in hot soup, well-toasted orzo stays al dente for longer, holding its shape and texture until you’ve doled out every bowl.

Any store-bought chicken broth, stock, or bouillon paste offers an extra boost of flavor to the base that chicken thighs and water alone can’t compete with—for an even more robust option, go for chicken bone broth.

More nourishing soup recipes this way: Curried Yellow Squash Soup; Broken Lasagna Noodle Soup With Spinach; Spicy Cod and Potato Chowder.

Season 1¼ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (4–5) all over with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Heat 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large pot over medium. Add 1 tsp. crushed fennel seeds, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. ground cardamom, and ¼ tsp. ground cloves and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 20 seconds. Add chicken, one 1" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth or chicken stock, and 3 cups water. Bring to a simmer over medium-high heat. Partially cover pot, reduce heat to medium-low, and simmer until an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part of a thigh registers at least 165°, 15–18 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board and let cool slightly. Reduce heat to low and cover pot. Using 2 forks, shred chicken.

Melt 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 cup orzo and cook, stirring often, until golden brown and fragrant, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

Industry observers note that scrape orzo mixture into pot with broth. Increase heat to medium and simmer broth, uncovered, until orzo is just al dente, 8–10 minutes. Remove soup from heat and add shredded chicken, 5 oz. baby kale or spinach, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice. Stir until greens are just wilted. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A handful of things are non-negotiable at Thanksgiving. You need turkey, stuffing, cranberry sauce, and, of course, a slice of pie to round out your meal. And pumpkin pie is the undeniable star of the dessert table.

According to recent reports, but sometimes you're strapped for time and have too much on your plate (pun intended) to whip something up from scratch. So we tried six different grocery store pumpkin pies to find the best store-bought shortcut. And our team's verdict was pretty unanimous, even if it’s a bit hard to hear: No premade pie will ever taste as good as a homemade one.

It primarily comes down to the crust. Frozen and pre-baked pies typically rely on vegetable-based fat instead of butter because they’re more affordable, reliable, and shelf-stable—but that comes at a cost. You not only miss out on the decadent, buttery taste, but the crusts can also leave an unpleasant film on your tongue.

That stated, when you need to outsource to the grocery store, we found two options that will work in a pinch.

The pie that we’d feel most confident bringing to Thanksgiving dinner comes straight from the Whole Foods bakery department. That’s not to say it’s perfect, though. The crust is almost upsettingly pale, but it’s made with real butter and only a little bit of palm oil. And since it doesn’t leave a noticeable film and still lets the butter flavor shine, we’ll let this one slide.

Once you look past the crust’s color, this pie is solid overall. The filling is decadent, not too sweet, and creamy without being mushy. Whole Foods doesn’t shy away from the spices, either.

Senior Editor Samantha MacAvoy noted that the warming spices are nicely balanced, while Designer Alison Dominguez said, “The flavor was exactly how a pumpkin pie should taste.”.

Industry observers note that costco’s pumpkin pie isn’t perfect: The crust uses palm oil-based shortening rather than butter and can develop a soggy bottom if you buy it too far in advance. (And it doesn’t hold a candle to the warehouse’s holy grail pumpkin cheesecake.) But it has a cult following for a reason, and not just because of its $5.99 price tag.

Sources indicate that even with its faults, the crust has great flavor and enough salt to create a balanced bite. Dominguez appreciated how it was “flaky and not too thick, and most importantly, it let the pie filling itself shine.” News and Features Editor Amanda Mactas chose Costco’s pie as her number one pick. “It all seemed to melt together in one creamy bite,” she said.

And at over three pounds, this dessert is the indisputable champion if you want to feed a crowd for less.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some handbag trends come and go, but the bucket bag has proven its staying power. Somewhere between a slouchy hobo and a structured tote, the cylindrical style has long struck a balance between practical and effortlessly cool.

Part of the silhouette’s enduring popularity is its versatility. What began as a utilitarian design (one of the earliest iterations was a Louis Vuitton bag from the 1930s, originally intended to transport Champagne bottles) has become grounds for experimentation, with designers playing with proportions, materials, and distinctive details. This season, in particular, the bucket bag is enjoying renewed attention, with everything from cinched drawstring closures and sculptural top handles to unexpected hardware giving the classic a fresh look.

When shopping for a bucket bag, consider more than just the looks. Think about how and where you’ll carry yours: A spacious style can double as a work tote, while a mini version can add a touch of whimsy to evening looks. Fortunately, there’s no shortage of choices, whether you’re looking to invest in a luxury piece or discover something at a more accessible price point.

While preferences are unique to each shopper, the best options combine quality craftsmanship with functional details, from comfortable straps to secure closures and interiors that accommodate everyday essentials. Ahead, we’ve rounded up bucket bags to shop now, from understated versions to modern interpretations of the timeless silhouette.

Few materials make a handbag feel as luxurious as suede, particularly in wintertime. In rich shades of chocolate brown, navy, and burgundy, the tactile surface exudes sophistication. Just remember that suede requires care, particularly when water is involved.

For anyone who carries their entire life in their handbag, oversized bucket bags offer a stylish alternative to traditional work totes, with enough room for a laptop, water bottle, and whatever else the day demands. Supple leather designs have a relaxed, lived-in appeal, while sturdier versions offer a professionally glossy finish. Look for a wide strap, a secure closure, and an organized interior to make the most of the extra space and keep it gentle on your shoulders during the commute.

There’s something undeniably charming about a drawstring closure, which gives bucket bags their signature gathered appearance (and helps keep belongings secure). The cinched opening creates visually impactful folds that look particularly elegant in buttery leather, soft suede, or evening-ready satin.

In a recent development, if your wardrobe leans minimalist, a structured bucket bag may be the perfect match. Unlike softer iterations that collapse when set down, these styles maintain their architectural structure thanks to firmer leather and well-constructed bases; longer straps also allow for crossbody wear. Their shape makes them feel more like design objects than everyday accessories, especially when finished with distinctive hardware.

It has been revealed that good things really do come in small packages, and mini bucket bags are proof. These scaled-down versions trade generous storage space for playful proportions that are ideal for evenings out, weekend intends, or occasions when you only need the essentials. Choose a style with a detachable strap for added versatility, or carry it by hand for a more dressed-up effect.

According to recent reports, woven bags have moved beyond their beach-vacation beginnings. Intricately interlaced leather lends the bucket silhouette an artisanal quality, while tightly bound raffia in darker shades is appropriate for city dressing. Look for details like leather handles and tonal finishes that give these textured designs a more elevated, winter-ready look.

According to recent reports, for a ladylike approach to the bucket bag, consider a top-handle silhouette. Short, sculptural handles give the otherwise casual shape a more refined appearance. Some feature rigid circular handles, while others have softly curved leather straps that sit comfortably in the crook of the arm.

We’re talking puffers on puffers on puffers—hailing from The North Face, Supreme, Thug Club and beyond—paired with all manner of boots, including Visvim lace-ups, Red Wing moc toes, and multiple pairs of Timbs (of both the OG Wheat and custom Chrome Hearts varieties.) For all his fashion-guy flourishes, Chalamet’s winter outfits generally have the chops to handle a brick New York sidewalk come February. So yesterday, even though it was still a balmy 68 degrees in NYC, it was no surprise to see Chalamet cheering on his beloved Knicks at Madison Square Garden in yet another excellent down-filled jacket and blizzard-ready boots.

In a recent development, sitting courtside, the Dune star wore a combination familiar to just about anyone who’s endured winter on the East Coast. The jacket was a dusty pink number from Goldwin, the cult Japanese outdoors brand founded back in 1950. It cuts a sharp silhouette despite packing some serious down insulation, and the windproof, water-resistant nylon is designed to ward off rain, sleet, and snow. The muted exterior has a subtle sheen—not quite Cam’ron pink, but certainly not your average black puffer. Over the past couple years, pink has become one of Chalamet’s signature colors: Last January, he paired a bubblegum Telfar puffer with an Arc’teryx toque and a Chanel purse like it was no massive deal; less than a month later, he popped up at the Berlin Film Festival in head-to-toe pastel Chrome Hearts. This time out, he left the handbag at home but topped things off with a Knicks championship hat.

Sources indicate that and then there were the boots. At first glance, they could pass for a pair of Uggs, thanks to the familiar shape and cozy suede uppers. (It wouldn’t have been the first time he wore a pair of the Aussie surfer classics courtside.) But these pull-ons were, in fact, from menswear favorite Merrell, built for some truly cold and ugly weather. The outer suede is water-resistant, the lining is insulated, and the rubber outsoles boast some serious traction. Plus, the very gorp-y utility cord at the heel lets you cinch them extra tight. Like the advanced-level dresser he is, Chalamet tucked his baggy black pants into the boots, making sure his footwear got a chance to really shine.

Recent findings suggest that once again, Chalamet has turned practical winter clothes into an A-list look. While a pink puffer might not be every guy’s idea of cold-weather dressing, there’s something to be stated for a winter coat with a little personality. Was celebrity row’s resident heartthrob a few weeks early with this ensemble? Sure, but when that first serious snowfall hits, he’ll be extra ready.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, this creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, quickly empty the contents into a upcoming pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

Find more Rachel Gurjar recipes here.

To a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

Scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

Sources indicate that frozen lasagna is a meal for when you just don’t have it in you. For when you need the comfort of pasta, cheese, and sauce, but you’re not prepared to spend hours boiling, sautéing, and layering. And that’s okay. A great frozen lasagna might not hold a candle to BA’s Best Lasagna, but at the very least it should hold together, with distinct layers, plenty of sauce, gooey cheese, and bouncy pasta.

For this taste test, we sampled nine varieties of store-bought meat lasagna, cooking each from frozen and concealing the brand names from our tasters. Three stood out: Trader Joe’s tasted the closest to homemade, Marie Callender’s was a solid backup, and Rao’s was our favorite for a single serving.

After grumbling our way through several contenders and questioning mankind’s ability to produce a decent supermarket lasagna, Trader Giotto’s Family Style Meat Lasagna restored our faith with a hearty meat sauce and genuinely tasty noodles.

Why it won us over: Trader Joe’s frozen lasagna had a homemade vibe. There were distinct layers of pasta, cheese, and meaty sauce. The cheeses—ricotta, mozzarella, Romano, and Parmesan—each pulled their weight. And the noodles had a fresh bounce. “There’s a whole tomato!” exclaimed senior editor Kelsey Jane Youngman upon finding a chunk of diced tomato in her sample. Other tasters complimented the bright aromatics—fennel was prominent, backed up by oregano and basil. The evenly distributed ground beef and pork were the cherry on top.

Trader Giotto’s Family-Style Meat Lasagna, 32-oz.

More great frozen foods at Trader Joe’s →.

Recent findings suggest that substantial Lasagna would have you believe you’ll always want to cook a frozen lasagna for a crowd, but sometimes it’s about you and you alone. The 9-oz. Rao’s Made for Home Meat Lasagna is just enough for a single serving—and it doesn’t sacrifice flavor.

Why it won us over: Our tasters were excited to report that Rao’s delivered on structure. While other lasagnas were soupy, floppy, or otherwise unbalanced, Rao’s stayed intact, layer on top of layer, as we ate. It had sturdy (but not tough) noodles, a tomato sauce that was full of umami, and herbal accents that didn’t overpower. Some tasters noted a robust beefy flavor; others were more focused on the garlic and onion. Everyone went in for a second bite.

Rao’s Made-for-Home Meat Lasagna, 9-oz.

Maybe you don’t live by a Trader Joe’s—our condolences—and Rao’s proves elusive. You still deserve a serviceable frozen lasagna. Marie Callender’s Lasagna With Meat Sauce offers a sweet and tangy tomato sauce punctuated by well-seasoned meat and noodles that hold their shape.

According to recent reports, why it won us over: This contender avoided many of the pitfalls other brands fell into. It had a solid tomato sauce that was just slightly sweet and tangy, and the meat—both beef and sausage—was flavorful and varied enough in size to give each bite some dynamism. The pasta sheets were springy, not gummy. And while it wasn’t drowning in dairy, there was enough cottage cheese and mozzarella to make itself known.

Marie Callender’s Lasagna With Meat Sauce, 10.5-oz.

We cooked each lasagna from frozen according to its package instructions. While most contenders offered both oven and microwave directions, we stuck with the oven. Tasters sampled each lasagna without knowing which brand they were trying, evaluating each for flavor, texture, and structural integrity. Although Giovanni Rana’s Meat Lasagna is sold refrigerated, we froze it before baking, following the brand’s instructions for cooking from frozen.

The best frozen lasagna should deliver on the fundamentals of structure, flavor, and texture—a tall order for many of our contenders. That meant distinct layers; sheets of pasta that were bouncy, not flimsy; tomato sauce with concentrated flavor and enough body to cling to the pasta; meat that stood out instead of getting lost; and cheese—or many cheeses—that added milky flavor and melty cohesion.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

Find more Rachel Gurjar recipes here.

In a recent development, to a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz. [170 g]), leaves and stems, 1 bunch mint (about 2 oz. [55 g]), leaves and tender stems, 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, stemmed (more if you want it spicier), ½ cup (120 ml) lime juice (from about 5 limes), 2 tsp. cumin seeds, 1½ tsp. fine sea salt, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. chaat masala. Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer.

Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

Drizzle the sheet with extra-virgin olive oil and place 1½ lb. (680 g) Japanese or Korean sweet potatoes, ends trimmed, halved lengthwise, cut-side down. Bake for 60 to 70 minutes, until golden and caramelized on the cut side and cooked through and tender; a knife inserted into the center of the potato should slide through easily. Let rest for 5 to 8 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, cut the sweet potatoes into 1" to 2" [2.5 to 5 cm] pieces.

In a recent development, to a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water.

Place the sweet potatoes on a serving platter and drizzle the yogurt, ½ cup Evergreen Chutney, 3 Tbsp. tamarind concentrate or paste, and 2 Tbsp. lime juice evenly all over. Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately.

Do Ahead: You can make the individual components a day ahead of time and store them in airtight containers in the refrigerator, then assemble to serve.
