📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Attendees of Bon Appétit Live experienced a taste of Maine through a hands-on lobster cooking class and a demonstration of wild blueberry cornmeal shortcakes, both hosted by Visit Maine.

According to recent reports, the class, Lobster 101, was led by Bon Appétit manager of audience strategy Carly Westerfield and Krista Tripp, founder of Aphrodite Oysters in South Thomaston, Maine. Attendees learned how to break down a whole, steamed two-pound Maine lobster and transform the meat into a rich, creamy lobster dip—ideal for holiday hosting. Guests then enjoyed the fruits of their labor, sampling the freshly made dip with Ritz crackers before tasting oysters.

It has been revealed that tripp explained that her oysters, cultivated in the cold tidal waters of the Lower Weskeag River, take three years to reach maturity. Known for their distinctive fluted shells, they offer a briny, mineral-rich flavor balanced by a mellow sweetness.

Industry observers note that after years as a lobster harvester, Tripp started Aphrodite Oysters to diversify her lobster business and has since shifted her focus to oyster cultivation full-time. She’s come to appreciate the many environmental benefits of farming and consuming them. Her oysters filter up to 50 gallons of water a day, taking in nitrogen and sequestering some for their growing shells. “Eating an oyster is contributing to the environment,” she declared. Indeed, water test scores have improved at her farm, demonstrating that bivalves help create a healthier ecosystem.

In a recent development, before the end of the class, a few brave attendees volunteered to shuck their first oysters. Krista guided them through the process, demonstrating how to safely do it at home by protecting the hand holding the shellfish with a towel and gently working the knife into the hinge until the shell released. The well-earned reward was another taste of the Penobscot Bay, as fresh and pristine as the waters themselves.

Sources indicate that later in the day, guests in the Demo Kitchen were treated to Cornmeal Shortcakes with Blueberry Compote, prepared by Bon Appétit senior Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewczyk. The compote featured wild Maine blueberries from Brodis Blueberries, a multigenerational family farm in Hope, Maine, stewarded by Ron Howard and his family. Howard joined Szewczyk for the demo, where he shared that 99% of the wild blueberries grown and harvested in the United States come from Maine. Attendees learned that they have been growing since the end of the Ice Age, when the tenacious plants, fortified by ericoid mycorrhizal fungi, began to grow and colonize the newly exposed land as glaciers retreated. An notable food source for Native Americans, wild blueberries were valued by Indigenous communities for their nutritional benefits well before the modern superfood movement.

Speaking passionately, Howard discussed the many challenges facing Maine growers, including tariffs and currency exchange fluctuations, particularly the impact of a stronger Canadian dollar. Like many Maine farmers, the family has had to get creative. Howard invested in newly introduced equipment, including a more efficient type of harvester that allowed the business to scale up and sell to retailers. They created a shelf-stable, freeze-dried product with no added ingredients, allowing them to ship their product beyond the local area. Howard and his son started a distillery, where they use wild blueberries to make an eau de vie and vodka. They have also begun hosting a Wild Blueberry Weekend, opening the doors to the farm and educating the public about the unique benefits of their crop and their growing process.

Carolann Ouellette, director of the Maine Office of Tourism, emphasized that visiting Maine and engaging with local growers and producers such as Howard and Tripp was the best way to experience the state’s diverse bounty. “The relationship between people and nature is inseparable, and stewardship is an important part of the state's identity,” she reflected. Ouellette grew up in Latest Jersey but relocated to Maine over 40 years ago. Her family used to visit Maine when she was a child, and she recalls those experiences vividly: “As a kid, I remember, when you get to Maine, you can smell the pine and spruce.” It’s those potent memories that drew her to the state permanently, a place she described as “filled with hardworking, welcoming communities that depend on one another.”.

In a recent development, A few years ago, Visit Maine began placing greater emphasis on the state’s culinary identity. Ouellette stated that awareness of Maine as a food destination continues to grow, “Sea to table with local ingredients is what we were doing before it was a thing.” Beyond the lobster, Visit Maine has been intentional about showcasing the breadth of the state’s agricultural, fishing, and heritage industries. Apples, potatoes, kelp, seaweed, and grains are just a few of the local ingredients featured in Visit Maine’s newsletter and Bountiful Plate video series, which highlights food and beverage producers throughout the state. Ouellette noted that Maine’s food culture is more diverse than many people expect, and its abundance of local products has attracted an interesting mix of exceptional chefs, many of whom are deeply embedded in their communities. Ouellette cited Tripp’s practice of personally delivering her oysters to local restaurants as an example of how the hospitality ecosystem is interconnected.

In a recent development, most notable, Ouellette emphasized that sustainability and stewardship are central to the state’s approach to its food systems and relationship with the landscape. “You can’t get much fresher than food in Maine,” she concluded.

Recent findings suggest that all denim is timeless, but straight-leg jeans might be the most trend-resistant silhouette of the bunch. That stated, they’re trending! The classic style has been making a comeback (or perhaps it never really went away), cropping up in the fall collections of Dior, Stella McCartney, Toteme, and Balenciaga. Amid the revolving door of denim trends, from ultra-baggy shapes to the much-debated return of the skinny jean, there’s something about the simplicity of a straight leg that feels very much like an aesthetic homecoming.

With their clean lines and easy proportions, straight-leg jeans are a true wardrobe chameleon. They’re a key part of the model-off-duty look when worn with a white tee, leather jacket, and retro sneakers, but they also look chic dressed up with a pump or heeled boot. Their streamlined silhouette also lends itself well to winter layering, balancing out both oversized knits and heavy coats. And while the shape is relatively straightforward, there’s plenty of room for interpretation: A faded blue pair can feel laid-back, while a dark-wash style can look almost as polished as trousers; a bone-colored pair works as a palette cleanser, while a warm brown brings softness to the look.

Below, a few of our favorite styles—with ways to wear them this season.

Dark-wash straight-leg jeans can look just as polished as trousers. Lean into the sophisticated vibe with a pussy-bow blouse, a sharp leather jacket, and a pair of sleek kitten-heel boots.

Play up the Americana roots of classic blue jeans with a plaid flannel shirt and a chocolate brown suede jacket. A pair of supple leather loafers and Balenciaga’s City bag keep the look from feeling too rugged.

Take a cue from the model-off-duty set, and style your straight-leg jeans with a zip-up hoodie and retro Nikes.

Washed brown jeans make a surprisingly versatile foundation for colorful separates—like an argyle knit and a bright red suede jacket. Keep the look grounded with black leather accessories.

Sources indicate that pale blue jeans pair particularly well with various shades of brown. A belted, fur-collar suede jacket and matching ankle boots lend the look a subtle ’70s feel.

The streamlined silhouette of a straight-leg jean works well with voluminous outerwear, like a plaid, fringed-trim scarf jacket. Ivory ballet flats worn with tonal socks don’t detract from the action up top.

Style slightly more relaxed straight-leg jeans with a collared cashmere cardigan, a lived-in leather jacket, and suede moccasins for a look that strikes a balance between polished and nonchalant.

Black straight-leg jeans are a winter wardrobe workhorse. Layer a navy crewneck over a classic white tee, then add a belted wool coat for an understated look.

Recent findings suggest that during the November 18 episode of her Happy Hour with Ina Garten podcast, Garten got to talking with guest Rose Byrne about opportunities that felt too intimidating to pursue. Ina didn’t have to think very hard to come up with her own example.

According to recent reports, with which I respectfully disagree. I think quite a few of us would happily clear our schedules to see Ina Garten attempt a salsa. Still, this is a woman who’s made some pretty bold decisions throughout her career. Garten left her job working on nuclear energy policy in Washington, D.C., to buy a specialty food store in the Hamptons with virtually no experience running one. There were some early mishaps, including a batch of roast chickens nobody wanted until she changed how they were displayed, and those experiences eventually helped shape the approachable cooking philosophy behind her hugely successful cookbooks.

And Garten has certainly gotten comfortable sharing the spotlight over the years. In Delish’s recent interview with Garten and Jennifer Garner, the longtime friends traded stories about their kitchen adventures, favorite recipes, and even late-night In-N-Out Burger runs. Give Ina some good food and someone she loves spending time with, and she's in her element.

Personally, though, I can't stop imagining Jeffrey in the audience holding up a giant “10” sign in support of his wife. We really missed out on something special.

Sources indicate that place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Lightly coat a 13x9" baking dish with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Whisk 2½ cups (313 g) all-purpose flour, ¼ cup (50 g) sugar, 2 Tbsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Set aside.

Cook 2 lb. breakfast sausage, casings removed if needed, in a large skillet set over medium-high heat, stirring and breaking into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until browned and cooked through, 10–12 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer sausage to a small plate, leaving fat behind. Pour fat into a heatproof measuring glass. You want ½ cup fat; spoon out any excess or pour in vegetable oil as needed if you don’t have enough. Stir 2 large eggs and 2 cups whole milk into fat. Let sausage cool slightly, then crumble into small, even pieces with your hands.

Recent findings suggest that pour fat mixture into reserved dry ingredients and stir until just combined and no large dry pockets of flour remain (batter may be thin and lumpy; it’ll be fine). Set aside ½ cup sausage and ½ cup cheese from 8 oz. sharp yellow cheddar, coarsely grated (about 2 cups), for topping, then add remaining sausage and cheddar to batter and stirring until evenly distributed.

Scrape batter into prepared baking dish and evenly scatter reserved sausage and cheese over. Bake casserole until top springs back when gently pressed with your finger and a tester inserted into the center comes out with just a few moist crumbs attached, 20–30 minutes.

Just before casserole is done, heat 2 Tbsp. pure maple syrup and 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a small skillet over medium, stirring occasionally, until butter is melted, about 2 minutes.

Brush maple butter over casserole and let cool 10 minutes. Cut into squares. Serve with more maple syrup and butter alongside.

It has been revealed that whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours.

According to recent reports, place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too swiftly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let crust cool.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Bring 1 lb. fresh or frozen cranberries, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, and ¼ cup water to a boil in a large saucepan, then reduce heat to medium and simmer, stirring often, until cranberries soften and burst and most of the liquid has evaporated, 10–15 minutes. Let cranberry mixture cool.

Recent findings suggest that transfer cranberry mixture to a blender; reserve pan. Add ⅔ cup fresh lime juice and ¼ cup (32 g) cornstarch and blend on high speed until smooth. Scrape purée back into pan (not over heat) and add 3 large eggs, 2 large egg yolks, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Place over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture bubbles and thickens to a pudding-like consistency, about 4 minutes. Remove pan from heat. Add ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, and whisk until melted and combined. Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

Industry observers note that just before serving, beat 6 large egg whites, room temperature, ¼ tsp. cream of tartar, remaining 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy and sugar is dissolved, about 5 minutes. Increase speed to high and continue to beat until stiff peaks form, about 3 minutes more.

According to recent reports, spoon meringue over filling and swirl decoratively as desired. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue if desired.

The Tucson Restaurant Turning Cactus Into Fine Dining

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (930 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Traipsing through Tucson Mountain Park, a Midwestern blow-in might not identify much to eat.
  • In a recent development, gray, tangled brittlebush, which the average Tucsonan walks or drives by almost daily, can be pressure-cooked, caramelized until black, and baked into cake.
  • Industry observers note that don’t even get Lopez started on the dozens of cacti varieties that thrive here, which the restaurant sources from local grower Toadlet Farm and which Lopez harvests throughout the year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Traipsing through Tucson Mountain Park, a Midwestern blow-in might not identify much to eat. Plants armed with burs, barbs, and spines all but scream “do not touch.” For chef Aaron Lopez and June Chee, however, this prickly, dusty landscape stocks a pantry of possibility. The married co-owners of Ursa see the Arizona desert as a rich ground for foraging.

In a recent development, gray, tangled brittlebush, which the average Tucsonan walks or drives by almost daily, can be pressure-cooked, caramelized until black, and baked into cake. Dusty, sage-colored salt bush, when hung to dry, takes on an intensely umami, aquatic saltiness like seaweed. The sweet buds of the Seussian-green palo verde tree become briny, like olives, when suffused with lye.

Industry observers note that don’t even get Lopez started on the dozens of cacti varieties that thrive here, which the restaurant sources from local grower Toadlet Farm and which Lopez harvests throughout the year. The restaurant processes the young and mature paddles, fruit and their seeds, buds, and flowers, which are then grilled, poached, cold-smoked, juiced, dehydrated, nixtamalized, or preserved into jam, wine, and vinegar.

There are hundreds of edible plants in the Sonoran Desert. Ursa strives to showcase their potential, one 10-course meal at a time.

Industry observers note that “We treat Ursa as an art showroom, demonstrating to people what these plants can do, what sustainable means, and what was here before it got easy,” claims Lopez. The idea was inspired in part by his Sonoran grandfather, Hector Lopez, who died in the spring. “He was the first person I ever heard say they’re proud to be from the desert,” the chef said.

Ursa began as a pop-up in California in 2023. Lopez and Chee moved to a historic brick building in downtown Tucson, re-opening their doors in October 2025. It’s a homecoming of sorts for the couple, who are both from the Sonoran Desert borderlands. They met in Hawaii, where Chee was working in clean energy and transportation. Lopez, meanwhile, spent roughly 18 years cooking in fine dining and modern progressive restaurants like Redbird and Orsa & Winston in LA, and Pai Honolulu. But he was longing for the desert.

In a recent development, after helping a friend open a restaurant and hosting a few popups in Austin, Lopez and Chee bought a desert foraging guide, packed up their two dogs and began driving around the Southwest. It made sense to settle in Tucson, which was recognized by UNESCO in 2015 as a Creative City of Gastronomy for its continuous 4,000-year agricultural history and deeply rooted Sonoran Desert food traditions.

“That’s a unique thing about being here, the connection from seed to plant to restaurant that we hadn’t been able to grasp before,” Chee notes.

Consider a recent course that Ursa built around tepary beans, in which the ancient, nutty bean is refried and topped with h:al squash that’s been lactofermented. The squash’s leaves are fermented to make Japanese-style kosho and its flowers are pickled, dried, crushed with dried saltbush, then tossed with barrel cactus seeds for a desert furikake. It’s served with grilled coins of chorizo made from Lopez’s great-grandmother’s recipe and housemade flour tortillas, to all be washed down with an amazake drink made from fermented wheat and goat fat. Don’t get too attached, however. Riffs owing to finicky ingredient availability occur here almost daily.

Running a restaurant using only ingredients foraged and farmed from within about eight to 10 miles means abiding by pretty intense guardrails. The only wheat used is pima club, an ancient soft white variety cultivated for centuries by the Akimel O’odham (Pima) people. Ursa does not use cucumbers, radishes or citrus.

Recent findings suggest that “We’re not trying to substitute anything, like, ‘How do we achieve cucumber? Let’s grab a cactus,’” Lopez indicates. “We have to throw everything out, really strip it down. Sometimes we have to let the ingredients be bitter or spicy. We have to put our egos aside and let the ingredient be the star.”.

For staff who didn’t grow up or learn to cook here, the learning curve at Ursa can feel a little like alighting on a upcoming planet, even if certain flora happen to resemble prickly weeds in their own backyards.

In a recent development, “We have these really cool moments in the restaurant where people are like, Oh! I have lamb’s quarter just growing in my yard!” Chee says of the spinach-like desert green that appears all over Ursa’s menu.

A young Aaron Lopez with his grandfather Hector Lopez.

In a recent development, ursa’s approach isn’t always easy for customers to understand, so the couple came up with a more down-to-earth option. This fall, the restaurant debuted a four-course, family-style Lineage menu for $75, alongside the existing 10-course Harvest menu ($150). There’s now a pozole course inspired by the family’s annual springtime tradition of roasting goat in agave leaves, barbacoa-style, and shredding it for soup, and a red masa tamal with glazed quail and yucca blossoms in mole made with burnt mesquite bread, a technique Lopez remembers from childhood.

The idea took shape during Ursa’s extended summer break, as Lopez recovered from foot surgery and reflected on the loss of his late grandfather, the tenacious keeper of family traditions.

“I feel so much closer to my ancestors and the land; we want Ursa to be less esoteric and more soulful,” he claims. “The story of Ursa is partly of the desert, partly my family. Now we’ve advanced to the point where they’re symbiotic, and I can't tell them apart.”.

Creative strategist and Good Boy Wine co-founder Eric Bach invited her out for a picnic at Echo Park Lake with his dog, Ty, in June 2022, and the pair hit it off. “Eric asked me a lot of questions, which was honestly a revelation; men, take note,” says Lily. “Eventually, I got to flip the script and hear about his travels, his wins, his losses, and I remember thinking, ‘This is a very special person.’” Lunch led to dinner, and the two had a feeling there were more dates to come. Says Eric, “Pretty early on, I could tell there was something incredibly solid about her, and being with her just made me feel more like myself.”.

Industry observers note that their relationship bloomed over the next few years, and on February 24, 2025, Eric popped the question. It was during Frieze in Los Angeles, and Eric told Lily there was a special event at the Wolford House, which was transformed into a gallery for the week. “On the drive over, I told Eric about a conversation I’d had that day with my friend and mentor Bobby Hundreds, who asked about my boyfriend. I’d said, ‘It’s funny hearing you say ‘boyfriend,’ because Eric is so much more than that. He’s my person, for life, I hope.’ I had no idea how perfectly timed that was.”.

According to recent reports, when they arrived at golden hour, the house was completely empty. “Then, I looked at Eric, and he was tearing up. He couldn’t get a word out,” remembers Lily. “He pulled out a box, dropped to one knee, and opened it to reveal his mother’s diamond ring and necklace. He told me he wanted to spend the rest of his life with me, and I mentioned, ‘Yes! Put it on me!’” His mother had also given her blessing for Lily to take the stones and redesign them into something of her own. “I get to wear something charged with her love and legacy every day,” the jewelry designer claims.

The bride and groom decided to host their wedding over the weekend of April 3, 2026, in Newly introduced Orleans. “Eric’s family has deep roots there—four generations—and it was the first trip we ever took together,” indicates Lily of their destination choice. “We wanted to share the best the city has to offer with our guests.” The festivities would kick off with a crawfish boil welcome party at Industrial Garden, their wedding ceremony in the Sydney and Walda Besthoff Sculpture Garden, a candlelit reception in the church of Hotel Peter and Paul, a second-line parade, and an after-party at DBA on Frenchmen Street. “We wanted people to experience the city through its food, music, art, rituals, and sense of chaos, but filtered through us and the things we love,” says Eric. “Every part of it was meant to engage your senses and keep changing shape as the weekend went on. And above all, we wanted it to be insanely fun.”.

Sources indicate that the couple approached wedding planning like any other creative project: “Story arc first, details second,” Lily explains. “With Eric’s long-time background in experiential, we wanted to spearhead the planning ourselves, with Michelle Norwood and Sarah Schreiber consulting along the way.” As collectors of contemporary art, getting married in a sculpture garden felt like the perfect complement to their relationship. “When we found out the garden had Jean-Michel Othoniel’s L’Arbre aux Colliers—an oak hung with strands of his glass necklaces—we knew exactly where we’d be standing,” says Lily. “A jeweler getting married under a tree of necklaces… I couldn’t have designed that better if I’d tried.” Guests were also encouraged to have fun with their wardrobes. “We kept it loose and wanted our friends to have the freedom to express themselves: jewel tones with a Latest Orleans, formal flair,” says Eric.

It has been revealed that other intentional details were folded in throughout the weekend. “Instead of a traditional invitation, we wrote our guests a poem, framed in a hand-painted border by our dear friend, the illustrator Sarah Kersting, and inspired by vintage Newly introduced Orleans carnival ephemera,” notes the bride. The bride’s mother calligraphed all the invitations and even hand-made masquerade masks for every guest. The couple also wanted to highlight their own creative projects within the celebration. Eric made a custom Good Boy wine to be served just for the weekend, and Lily debuted Monbouquette’s bridal collection across all three days.

In a recent development, the bride’s redesigned engagement ring actually served as the inspiration for her wedding dress. On the ring, her mother-in-law’s diamond is surrounded by a spinning ballerina halo of custom-cut emerald and diamond baguettes. “Like the twirl of a tutu!” Lily indicates. While shopping at Loho Bride with owner Christy Baird, she fell for a dress from Wed Studio with a similar ethos of shape and movement. “The tiered gazar skirt with its ruffled edge is pure ballerina, like a Degas painting, and a whisper-thin tulle overlay drapes the entire dress, but the V-shaped boning and sheer side panels of the corset give it an edge,” she describes. “Christy worked closely with my mother and I to add a few customized touches to my entire look.”.

The bride curated the rest of her wardrobe to mirror the essence of her ceremony gown, which she describes as “playful, a little edgy, feminine, and timeless.” For the welcome party, she donned a Wiederhoeft slip dress beaded like a tattooed retelling of the Eurydice myth. “It’s genuinely a work of art,” Lily states. She also wore a beaded mini skirt and corset from the designer for the after-party. “I initiative to wear both for the rest of my life,” the bride adds. As for beauty, Lily had makeup artist Nicole Costanza do a look inspired by the work of Katie Jane Hughes.

It has been revealed that A longtime fan of the brand Bode, Eric chose to create a custom suit with the designer. “I wanted something a little unexpected from them while leaning into what makes them great: vintage nods, very current tailoring,” he says. The look included a cream jacket with a black lapel, which was layered over a black shirt and wide-leg pants. “I loved how the black shirt underneath almost seamlessly blended into the lapel and the unstructured satin bow tie, which read more like a neck scarf,” the groom says. “And then, of course, there was the vase brooch Lily made for me, which made it feel completely personal.”.

Recent findings suggest that the weekend kicked off in classic Fresh Orleans style with a crawfish boil. “Most of our LA friends had never been to a boil, and there’s no better introduction to the city: the Willie Green Project—Bacchanal’s house band—playing live, bibs for everyone, and a king cake that crowned the king and queen of the wedding weekend,” claims the groom. “It immediately set the tone for everything that followed.”.

The wedding day arrived and the bride and groom connected on the grounds of the Besthoff Sculpture Garden for their first look. While a stormy forecast threatened the proceedings, the sun broke through just as Lily was about to head down the aisle. “Eric’s mother passed away earlier this year, and we all felt her shining down on us at that moment,” she claims. The couple’s friend Chris Swanson officiated the ceremony. “He put so much thought into what he wrote, and he delivered it with such grace,” says Lily. “Having someone who truly knows us standing up there is what made the ceremony feel like ours.”.

In a recent development, eric describes the ceremony as surreal. “We were surrounded by incredible sculpture, beneath these beautiful draping mossy oaks, with all the people we love around us. Lily looked absolutely stunning,” he says. “Nothing had ever felt so right.” The couple also recited their own vows. “Just to add, there really wasn’t a dry eye in sight,” says the groom.

After the newlyweds said “I do,” cocktail hour was held throughout the sculpture garden so guests could experience the collection. “We did a champagne toast, Eric sabered the bottle with his uncle’s Mardi Gras sword, and then led everyone along a path through the grounds so they could wander amongst the art and the gardens,” claims the bride. “An alligator slid through the pond right as we were walking along the floating boardwalk. So rare and so New Orleans!”.

Industry observers note that the party then moved back to Hotel Peter and Paul, where the old church was lit by close to 1,000 candles. “There was classic Latest Orleans cuisine, there were epic speeches, there was a performance by the whistler Molly Lewis, and then I gave everyone a surprise: I sang ‘La Vie en Rose’ in the church,” says Lily. Most guests were unaware the bride could sing and were floored by the performance. “I knew she could sing, but damn, I had no idea how emotional it would make me,” reflects Eric. “Watching her up there was pretty unreal.”.

As dinner was complete, guests put on their hand-made masks and made their way through the city in a second line. “Instead of circling the block, we paraded all the way down Frenchmen Street,” notes Lily. “It was the most exhilarating thing: people came out onto the balconies of the jazz bars to watch us, and strangers joined in dancing in the street. We ended at DBA, where our dear friend DSD DJ-ed.” Even the groom popped on the decks for a set during the night. Adds the bride, “He absolutely crushed it!”.

According to recent reports, the next day, guests enjoyed beignets from Café du Monde and a pool party at The Country Club, a pool, bar, and garden in the Bywater neighborhood. The groom notes this was secretly one of his favorite parts. “Everyone was a little destroyed from the night before and completely relaxed,” he says. “And the drag queens were next level! It felt like the perfect comedown from the weekend.”.

According to recent reports, looking back, the couple say they have yet to get the wedding blues as they continue to celebrate. Indicates Eric, “It feels like the wedding was less of an ending and more like the beginning of this really wild, exciting latest chapter.” Adds Lily, “I’m too lucky to be married to my soulmate, and I wouldn’t change a thing.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. Like all good things, apple pie can’t be rushed. It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so initiative ahead, especially if it’s for Thanksgiving.

Sources indicate that welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling).

Whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

According to recent reports, turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

According to recent reports, place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

Stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

It has been revealed that unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

Sources indicate that place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

According to recent reports, place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

Recent findings suggest that do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that christmas might get the lights, presents, and monthlong buildup, but Ina Garten has a few thoughts about which holiday really deserves the fuss. And if a certain Thanksgiving side dish comes up in conversation, the Barefoot Contessa’s face might tell you everything you need to know.

It has been revealed that during the November 18 episode of her Happy Hour with Ina Garten podcast, the cookbook author asked guest Rose Byrne about her first Thanksgiving in the United States. The Australian actress recalled attending a Friendsgiving, with everyone contributing something to the meal, and Garten immediately wanted to know whether the whole thing had been organized in advance or “if everyone just highlighted up with string beans.”.

Things got even funnier when Byrne mentioned candied yams topped with marshmallows, something she found “pretty weird.” Garten visibly grimaced at the mention of the dish, chuckling before describing them as “very American." Judging by that expression alone, I wouldn't expect to find the dish making an appearance at her next dinner party.

Garten's feelings about Thanksgiving itself, however, are considerably warmer, especially when compared to Christmas.

Recent findings suggest that "Thanksgiving is just quiet. It's all that one day and it's all about the food," she explained, pointing out that Christmas comes with gifts, parties, and a whole lot more going on.

It has been revealed that it makes sense coming from someone who’s built an entire career around bringing people together over a good meal. And we already know Garten’s enthusiasm for Thanksgiving extends beyond what’s on the plate. Last year, she shared her favorite wines to serve with Thanksgiving dinner, including Morgon, a lighter French red from the Beaujolais region, and white Burgundies like Meursault or Montrachet to accompany the turkey. She also likes a Sonoma Valley Pinot Noir, giving the American holiday a little hometown representation in the wine department.

At least now I know that if I ever get invited to Thanksgiving at Ina’s, I'll gladly let her handle the wine—and I know to keep the marshmallow-topped yams at home.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Skyler Gisondo is getting soaked.

Recent findings suggest that it’s a wet, quasi-Floridian November afternoon in Carroll Gardens, Brooklyn; the sidewalks are plastered with layers of translucent brown and gold leaves. We’ve just met at a cafe for a bite; our plan is to walk to Brooklyn Bridge Park. But the second we step outside, we’re pelted with rain. Gisondo is dressed more for a sunny Southern California boardwalk than these soggy Brooklyn streets: white vintage-ish T-shirt (“Norwalk Seaport’s Oyster School”), canvas pants, brown boots, and the usual Rolex Submariner on his wrist. No hat to cover his thick auburn hair, no jacket, and, crucially, no umbrella.

In a recent development, jacket by Celine. Shirt by Banana Republic Vintage Archive. T-shirt by Paul Smith. Pants by Raimundo Langois. Watch by Cartier.

We rapidly unite in a single mission: to locate and purchase one. “I have a good feeling about Park Natural,” the actor notes optimistically, gesturing to the health food store across the way. We splash over to check, and an employee redirects us to a CVS down the street, prompting a nine-block journey under my single umbrella. Gisondo is a supportive partner on the scavenger hunt. He is patient as I lead us the wrong way, carefully holding the umbrella over us both while I look at my phone to course-correct, and takes the lead only with my permission. He matches each of my questions with his own, seemingly determined to maintain the cadence of a conversation, rather than that of an interview. As we walk, the rain gets even heavier, saturating the cuffs of our pants. Gisondo draws a few excited looks of recognition from people on the street, before two passersby attempt to recruit him to their church. “Oh, that’s all right—thank you,” he responds politely.

By the time we finally arrive at the CVS, I’m worried the trek was a mistake—not the type of thing you subject a Hollywood actor to, no matter how easygoing they may seem. But when I offer to buy Gisondo a $20 drugstore umbrella and charge it to GQ, his pale-blue eyes light up and a major smile breaks across his freckled face. “Hoo-ley smokes,” he states, his voice rising in astonishment. “Thank you.”.

It has been revealed that “Heck yeah,” he continues as I navigate through self-checkout. “You know what’s funny? The real ‘pinch me’ moments are this stuff.” He explains with complete earnestness how he grew up reading GQ. “Being a boy, being a young man, I was like, ‘I want to look like these guys.’ It’s almost like Stranger Than Fiction, where you hear the narration in your head or something.”.

It has been revealed that when we step outside, it’s stopped raining almost entirely. Still, Gisondo thanks me again. “Spanking brand-newly introduced umbrella,” he declares with childlike awe, as if he’s holding the key to the city.

Sources indicate that this is how Gisondo moves through the world: present, content, unflappable, well-mannered. An all-around good sport. It’s why, in a 4/20-themed Jimmy John’s campaign transparently angling for virality, he seemed not just willing to play ball but really, truly stoked to be eating a Jimmy John’s sandwich. It’s why the persistent memes that imagine Gisondo as a ’90s kid with a peanut allergy who got “hyper as fuck at recess” feel spiritually, if not always factually, accurate. And it’s those same wholesome qualities—and his ability to wield them in increasingly dark scenarios—that have turned the steady, subtle drumbeat of his acting career into an infectious stomp-clap over the course of a year.

Recent findings suggest that in 2026 thus far Gisondo has appeared as a deadbeat but emotionally literate surfer bro boyfriend in the Apple TV series Brothers, made a charming cameo in a Phoebe Bridgers music video as one of its titular adventure-seeking “Lost Boys,” and received a seven-minute standing ovation at the Venice Film Festival for his absorbing role as a sex offender decoy in Primetime. The day before Thanksgiving he’ll complete his sprint with Focker-In-Law, the latest Meet the Parents sequel, in which Gisondo plays Greg Focker’s well-intentioned but avoidant grown-up son. Next up, he’s got two lead roles in projects tentatively slated for next year: a return to the DC universe of James Gunn’s 2025 Superman, as the unwitting ladies’ man and journalist Jimmy Olsen in the true-crime mockumentary The People vs. Gorilla Grodd, and an A24 comedy called Goblin, where he stars opposite a talking puppet, in a film whose script Gisondo calls “probably the most batshit crazy thing I’ve legitimately ever read.”.

Though these projects take place in wildly different worlds, Gisondo’s characters have one thing in common: They’re nice guys in fraught situations. In a cultural moment where dark, morally slippery antiheroes dominate entertainment as well as real life, Gisondo has carved out a lane as a sincere, scrupulous bright spot. “He reminds me of Michael J. Fox in Back to the Future,” states Danny McBride, who cast Gisondo as aspiring stuntman Gideon, the grounded eldest grandchild of the dysfunctional evangelical family empire in The Righteous Gemstones. “There’s something about him that hearkens back to a simpler time and an innocent time, and it makes you root for him.”.

In a recent development, for a guy with an IMDB credit page almost as long as the CVS receipt that came with his umbrella, the blitz of red-carpet events, late-night TV spots, and awards season buzz for his role in Primetime has been especially surreal. “For the first time, at 30, I’m engaging with the part of this job I haven’t before, in a heightened way,” he says.

It has been revealed that now, with his first real shot at an Academy Award nomination, People magazine calling him the “internet’s boyfriend,” and a 2027 stacked with high-profile parts, Gisondo appears poised to prove that, even in the darkest of timelines, nice guys don’t necessarily finish last. And since his role in Primetime, he’s never been more locked in. “It lit a fire under me that I didn’t know I had before,” he states. “I heard actors say stuff like that in the past, ‘I want to do stuff that scares me,’ and I never got it. And now, light bulb. That’s it. That’s when you feel alive. That’s the point.”.

According to recent reports, up until about age 12, Gisondo wanted to be one of three things when he grew up: an actor, a professional hockey player, and/or a professional basketball player. “I was imagining playing both seasons somehow,” he tells me with a grin at Mister Cheeks, the cafe where we first meet. “I held on to that dream for too long.”.

In a recent development, he recalls really “tearing it up” in the 9-to-10-year-old hockey league—until he moved up to the next age bracket, which widened to include older kids, ages 11 to 14. “That’s the first league where full-contact was allowed,” he says. “I was 11 and the size of an 8-year-old, and there were dudes who were shaving.” This mismatch in size and ability culminated in a wake-up call on the ice: “All I remember is getting hit, and then the next thing I’m on my back, opening my eyes with my parents over me. The game had stopped and that was the day that dream died,” he says—before adding, with a laugh: “Thankfully, the acting thing kept working out.”.

It has been revealed that the acting thing included fewer instances where one might be bodychecked by a pubescent teenager, at least in the literal sense. And by that point, Gisondo was already pretty experienced in the craft. Growing up in Palm Beach, Florida, he was “obsessed with movies,” watching West Side Story on repeat until he’d memorized the entire script. Gisondo got it in his head that he could be an actor. His parents, who are process-oriented oceanic engineers, were skeptical. But when a work project brought his family to the Los Angeles area, his mother finally acquiesced and took him to an audition: a hundred-child call for a national Pizza Hut commercial. Gisondo, a precocious blue-eyed cutie pie with bangs and an underbite smile, landed the part. At the time, his dad was convinced his family was the victim of some kind of scam. In actuality, Gisondo had secured his first professional acting gig—and a Screen Actors Guild card—at the tender age of six, a whole 17 years earlier than his character Dan Plum in Primetime. Fans have since dug up and posted evidence of his acting debut, delighting over “TINY GISONDO.”.

In a recent development, thus began a string of small roles—as “Chris,” “Ryan,” or “Boy #1”—on a handful of family-friendly TV sitcoms. Gisondo’s parents relocated to Southern California and began homeschooling him to support his budding career. As Gisondo tells it, his mother specifically forbade any Disney and Nickelodeon auditions, in order to keep him far away from child stardom. “You get one childhood, so I think she wanted to preserve as normal of a childhood as she could for me,” he claims. “And I’m really grateful that she did that.”.

That freedom to be a kid helped him play one so well that he has since become a folkloric avatar for carefree adolescence—and the subject of one of the modern media landscape’s few truly benevolent memes. Captioning an old photo of Gisondo (from the press cycle for 2015’s Vacation), fans have imagined him enjoying all manner of nostalgic ’90s-kid activities—doing crazy tricks on trampolines, playing with Nerf guns, buying a Guinness Book of World Records at a book fair.

Recent findings suggest that “Some of them I’m like, Oh my God. This is uncanny,” he says excitedly. “These people tap into something.” Gisondo and his friends did, in fact, shoot Nerf guns at each other “point-blank” during sleepovers. As a kid he was “ecstatic” to be on a trampoline. And he keeps a copy of The Guinness Book of World Records on his coffee table to this day.

In a recent development, “At a certain point, with the memes,” he indicates, “I feel like they transcended and it became about something else, like it’s not about me anymore. It’s become a vessel for something.”.

Nevertheless, these posts have been passed around long enough that even his girlfriend—rumored to be Sterling Point’s Ella Rubin—seems to have internalized them. “There’s one that’s like, I just know his ass has a peanut allergy or something,” he indicates. “I don’t have a peanut allergy, but I’ve been with my girlfriend three years, okay? We’ll be at dinner. I’ll go to take a bite from her plate and she’ll very seriously go, ‘Oh no, peanuts.’ And then she’ll go, ‘Why do I always think you have a peanut allergy?’ That’s been happening for years.”.

To Rachel Brosnahan, who starred alongside Gisondo as Jimmy Olsen’s Daily Planet colleague Lois Lane in Superman, the memes speak to a larger appetite for Gisondo’s wholesome qualities. “It feels so in line with something that we were pleasantly surprised and excited by when the first Superman movie came out, which is that being earnest and caring a lot and loving really hard can also be cool,” she states. “It’s been awesome to watch a world that feels sometimes increasingly cynical and apathetic embrace that. And it’s not surprising to me that Skyler has become the face of that.”.

Recent findings suggest that even if Gisondo managed to have plenty of good old-fashioned fun as a kid, being homeschooled for nine years left him with a lasting identity as an outsider. He’d show up to camp each summer, trying to figure out what kids who’d spent the year in school together were into. “And I remember that feeling of exclusion,” he says; the older he got, the more apparent it was. “I remember being 15 and getting auditions for high school kids, and they were at a house party. And I was like”—here Gisondo shifts into a blissfully clueless impression of 15-year-old him— “‘I don’t know what the fuck this is about.’”.

That was around the time Gisondo enrolled in traditional high school, in pursuit of some quintessential experiences. But by then the kind of parts he was booking made even the most prototypical occasions extraordinary. He attended his senior prom—and brought a date he’d secured by filming a prom-posal video on the set of Night at the Museum: The Secret of the Tomb with the help of his costars Ben Stiller and Robin Williams. (Stiller even paid for his limo the night of, as a “wrap gift.”).

Recent findings suggest that gisondo would chase his dream of a normal life all the way to University of Southern California’s film school, where he pledged a frat for all of three weeks before dropping out. He managed to attend at least one real-life college party before finally accepting his fate as a full-time actor. “It was not my vibe per se,” he says, as we stroll through a dank tree-lined block of brownstones. “It’s like Lord of the Flies.”.

Industry observers note that you could argue that only tip-toeing past these young-adult rites of passage has helped Gisondo preserve a certain old-world aura—untouched by keg stands, gravity bongs, or double-digit daily screen time. “Something about Skyler reminds me of actors from the ’30s or ’40s, who had a real personality and a kind of street smarts about them,” Stiller indicates via email. “I could see him in a movie playing one of the Dead End Kids in the ’30s, like these kind of New York street kids.”.

In a recent development, gisondo did manage to collect enough real-life memories to call upon in future standout supporting roles like the rich-kid hypebeast nerd in Booksmart or Cooper Hoffman’s smarmy child-actor nemesis in Licorice Pizza. He now measures his life milestones by the types of roles he’s being called to audition for. “I remember when I got sent Fockers, I think it was my first time being a fiancé, and I was like, Oh my God, I’m a kid,” he says. “And then it hit me like, Wait a minute, most of my friends are engaged. I’m not a kid. I’m not a child bride. This is a completely appropriate age to be doing this.”.

Sources indicate that those years as an outsider have made Gisondo especially attuned to social dynamics. He says he senses when someone is quiet in a group and will be the one to go talk to the person standing alone in the corner of the party. “A lot of my friends and people I respond to are people who are, I don’t know, weirdos in some way, who maybe do have a more difficult time,” he says. “It’s funny, there’ll be moments with my girlfriend where I say something. And she’ll be like, ‘Oh my God, I forget you were homeschooled for nine years.’”.

But after turning 30 this past July, he says that he feels more self-assured than ever. “I think you spend a lot of your 20s posturing, trying to find your place, find your lane. And I almost feel like I sprung into consciousness two years ago. At 30, I feel very much like myself for the first time. You know what you like, you know who you are. It becomes almost harder to fake it. You become less interested in faking it. I guess I did always feel that, but there’s an immediacy to that feeling now.”.

It has been revealed that that self-assuredness has only grown with time, notes Beanie Feldstein, who worked with Gisondo on Booksmart and then again, seven years later, on Focker-In-Law. “Skyler has always been very pure and truthful and rooted and that has never changed, but of course we are older and have lived more life,” she states via email. “He feels like a more settled-in version of the same person I’ve always known.”.

That Gisondo has always felt more at home with the out crowd has made him all the more surprised by his current buzzy moment—much of which can be credited to Primetime and what he calls “the most challenging” role of his life. The propulsive film fictionalizes the lurid early-aughts reality series To Catch a Predator, hosted by former Dateline NBC correspondent Chris Hansen. Gisondo plays one of the decoys Hansen and his team used to lure sex offenders inside a sting house, an impressionable musical theater fan named Dan Plum—a.k.a. Decoy Dan—who’s so eager to kickstart his acting career that he’s initially oblivious to the toxic workplace and mission he’s joined.

Unlike Plum, of course, Gisondo was already a known quantity when he auditioned for Primetime, but he desperately wanted the part. As he tells it, Lance Oppenheim offered it to him within the first 10 minutes of their introductory call. “I was used to singing for my supper,” he indicates. “But he was so certain. And I remember asking him, ‘What have you seen of mine that makes you so certain?’” Oppenheim, who says he “bookmarked” Gisondo when he saw Licorice Pizza, was drawn to what he describes as “this particular combination of sweetness, humor, and slightly awkward, boyish earnestness.” The director also liked that Gisondo had experience as a child actor, but from the perspective of an older, wiser adult. “I was drawn to the idea that Skyler had spent so much of his life navigating the strange machinery of the entertainment industry himself, and what he might bring to a character who was also trying to find his place within that world,” he told me via email.

Industry observers note that gisondo recalls trying to explain the part to his father, the oceanic engineer, after he signed on to the film. “It was the most exciting opportunity of my career by far,” he states. “I remember telling my dad all of these things: So, it’s an A24 movie, starring Robert Pattinson, this guy Lance Oppenheim. And I would play a guy who’s an aspiring actor who’s used as bait to catch pedophiles in the decoy operations. And I’ll never forget, my dad was kind of quiet and he goes, ‘So this is something you’d be excited about?’”.

Sources indicate that as Dan, Gisondo parades through rented homes in puka shells and tie-dye T-shirts, directing unknowing predators toward a variety of snack foods with a high-pitched, exuberant naivete that manages to both brighten the film’s depraved subject matter and make it feel that much more sinister. (These scenes, too, were GIF’d and memed by the Gisondo hive.) But as we watch Hansen (Robert Pattinson) and his producer Andie Bender (Merritt Wever) plunge deeper into a shameless pursuit of higher ratings, Dan recoils, gradually becoming the closest thing this story has to an ethical center.

Recent findings suggest that “He plays it absolutely honestly, absolutely straight-faced with absolute sincerity,” states Wever, who calls Gisondo’s performance “perfect and undeniable.” “So when there’s comedy to be had—even if it’s uncomfortable or squirmy comedy or cringey comedy or comedy that is uncomfortable because you’re laughing because you can see the heartbreak inside somebody, the true ouch of the vulnerability and the unknowingness—it’s there because he’s not winking at the audience. He’s really inside that part. It has so many colors because he’s playing it so truthfully. That’s a sign of a very smart actor.”.

I point out to Gisondo that this isn’t the first time he’s played a character who becomes the sneaky moral compass of the story. He had something similar going as Gideon in The Righteous Gemstones, where he served as a relief to the over-the-top antics of a completely insane evangelical empire. Considered alongside all those memes about his imagined childhood, a single through line becomes obvious—in the parts he plays, but maybe also on a human level, he seems to remind people that good still exists in the world.

Industry observers note that “What’s funny is hearing you say that—it’s my first time bumping up against perception, in a way. Being perceived on that scale,” he indicates, slowing down to sort through his words for the first time in our otherwise free-flowing conversation, his eyes widening a little. “I think all any of us want is to be seen. I think to be loved is to be seen, in a way. People thinking that about me is the most gratifying possible thing. To me, it communicates I’m doing something right in my life.”.

But even as he’s astonished by the public feedback loop about his persona, he also can’t help but feel a little unnerved by it. “Usually, I feel like, only at your funeral are you meant to see so many people talking about what they think of you.”.

By this point Gisondo and I have made our way down through Brooklyn Bridge Park, looking out at the Manhattan skyline from a waterlogged pier and then wandering along a few wooded paths to arrive on the edge of Dumbo, where we’re idling as our conversation winds down. Behind him, the Brooklyn Bridge is enveloped in rain clouds. I remind him that people are saying good things.

Industry observers note that “Everybody wants to read nice things about them, whether it’s a review, whether it’s a meme,” he states. “There’s no doubt it feels good. I’m not sure I want to feed the part of me that likes how good that feels. That’s the gremlin in all of us.”.

With that, we say our goodbyes and I turn to make my way to the subway. “Thanks for my umbrella,” he indicates. I have no question he really, truly, earnestly means it. ✦.

#191988. How to Make Whipped Cream Perfectly, Every Time

How to Make Whipped Cream Perfectly, Every Time

📅 27 Jul 2017 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1416 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you love a low-effort, high-reward kitchen assignment, learning how to make whipped cream is a walk in the clouds.
  • It has been revealed that in whipped cream, and in life, the key challenge is knowing when to stop.
  • Industry observers note that to make whipped cream at home, all you need is cold heavy cream, a large bowl, and a whisk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you love a low-effort, high-reward kitchen assignment, learning how to make whipped cream is a walk in the clouds. The only ingredients are time and heavy cream. You can use an electric mixer, a whisk, or a mason jar and strong-armed devotion.

It has been revealed that in whipped cream, and in life, the key challenge is knowing when to stop. Desserts like Strawberry Eton Mess or Triple Chocolate Mousse Cake fare best with silky, unsweetened, soft-peaked whip. Others, like this show-stopping Berries and Cream Mille-Feuille, gain structure from sturdier peaks.

Industry observers note that to make whipped cream at home, all you need is cold heavy cream, a large bowl, and a whisk. You can also use a handheld mixer or a mason jar and some elbow grease (more on that later).

Sources indicate that if you’re opting for a bowl-and-whisk combo, choose your tools wisely. Cream roughly doubles in volume as you whip it, so use a bowl with three to four times the capacity of your liquid. A large balloon whisk, rather than a narrow sauce whisk, helps incorporate plenty of air into the cream.

Be strategic in the dairy aisle too. Heavy cream and heavy whipping cream contain at least 36% milk fat and can be used interchangeably. Skip anything labeled simply “whipping cream”—or, heaven forbid, “light cream”—which contains less fat and won’t hold its loft as well.

Sources indicate that for a basic batch, start with 1 cup cold heavy cream, which makes about 2 cups whipped cream. For lightly sweetened whipped cream, add 1 Tbsp. powdered sugar; for vanilla whipped cream, add ½ tsp. vanilla extract or paste.

With your equipment and ingredients in hand, there are only five steps and infinite possibilities.

Sources indicate that because whipped cream is usually eaten with or as dessert, you might not need to sweeten it at all. To keep flavors balanced, we tend to serve whipped cream au naturel with Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie or Diner-Style Rice Pudding.

But there are no hard-and-fast rules. Maybe you love sweetened whipped cream, or you’re serving it with something less sugary—like, say, a bowl of tart blackberries and torn mint leaves.

For lightly sweetened whipped cream, start with about 1 Tbsp. sugar per cup of cream. Powdered sugar dissolves easily and contains a little stabilizer (usually cornstarch), which can lend the whipped cream some extra holding power. Some cooks prefer the cleaner flavor of granulated sugar, which takes a little longer to dissolve. Either way, add the sugar before you start whipping.

If you’re gazing at a bowl of fluffy, ethereal whip and thinking, “Could I make this even more enchanting?” the answer is yes. There are two primary ways to make flavored whipped cream: infuse or stir.

Kitchen professionals and advance planners tend to cold-infuse. Combine your cream with flavorings like rice (for a creamy Horchata) or bourbon (to take a classic pumpkin pie over the top), then store it in the fridge anywhere from three hours to overnight. Strain out any solids before whipping.

Recent findings suggest that you can also add simple flavorings, like vanilla extract, a small splash of liqueur, cocoa, ground spices, citrus zest, or coffee syrup, before you start whipping. For heavier or chunky additions, such as toasted nuts or chopped chocolate, use a rubber spatula to gently fold them in once the cream is whipped.

Peaks are the shape your whipped cream takes when you pull the whisk out of the bowl and hold it upright like the Statue of Liberty’s torch.

Soft peaks are cloudlike and slump over when you lift the whisk. Stiff peaks stand upright and hold their shape. Somewhere in between are medium peaks, which have enough structure to hold a shape while remaining soft and supple.

Most Bon Appétit recipes, such as these Mix-and-Match Fools, involve whipping cream to soft peaks. That velvety texture is our go-to when we’re dolloping whipped cream atop pecan pie.

Industry observers note that but we aren’t always such softies. Medium peaks help this Ginger-Raspberry Icebox Cake keep its shape. And old-fashioned chocolate mousse involves whipping batches of cream into stiff and soft peaks: The former is folded into the chocolate mixture for structure, while the softer stuff tops the dessert.

There’s more than one way to whip.

According to recent reports, by hand: Our preferred method, whipping cream by hand requires the most time and effort, but it also gives you optimal control over its final texture. Even if you use a mixer to get your whipped cream started, switching to a whisk for the final few moments makes it easier to stop exactly where you want.

According to recent reports, in a Mason jar: No whisk? No mixer? No problem. To make whipped cream with your bare hands, put a container with a tight-fitting lid, large mason jar, or leak-proof cocktail shaker into the freezer for five minutes. Get the heavy cream very cold and make sure you have ample headspace in your vessel of choice. About one cup of liquid in a four-cup container is a good amount.

It has been revealed that secure the lid and shake it like you mean it. For the creamiest results, a consistently assertive pace is better than intermittent spurts of brute force. When the liquid stops sloshing and starts feeling and sounding heavier, open the lid and take a peek. If it looks underwhipped, close it back up and keep shaking.

Good news for meal preppers: You can make whipped cream hours in advance. Err on the side of underwhipping it during your prep. Store the lightly whipped cream, covered, in the fridge for up to four hours before serving, then give it a few energetic whisks to bring back its bounce right before you dollop it onto dessert.

Sources indicate that you can also freeze whipped cream (no, seriously). It takes a bit of effort, though. Line a baking sheet with parchment, then pipe or scoop spoonfuls of whipped cream onto it. Freeze until the whipped cream nuggets are solid, then peel them off the parchment and store them in an airtight bag in the freezer for one to two months. When you’re ready to serve, let them thaw at room temperature for about 15 minutes.

Instant vanilla pudding is the key to luscious, long-lasting whipped cream.

Industry observers note that need it to hold up longer? Instant vanilla pudding mix is one of BA’s favorite shortcuts for stabilized whipped cream. For every cup of heavy cream, add 1 Tbsp. instant vanilla pudding mix (call it pastry cream powder if anyone gives you sass) and 2 tsp. powdered sugar, then whip as usual. The modified starch in the pudding mix absorbs excess moisture and helps prevent the cream from separating, keeping it fluffy for up to 24 hours.

Recent findings suggest that for something tangier, sour cream adds both flavor and body. Our Pecan Cream Pie whisks ¼ cup sour cream into 1 cup heavy cream; the sour cream cuts the richness while helping the topping hold its shape.

In any case, your dinner party guests don’t have to sit quietly as you furiously whisk their dessert topping to order. Prep work never tasted so sweet.

It has been revealed that if your whip isn’t coming together quite right, don’t fret. Simple solutions abound.

It has been revealed that this is probably a temperature concern. Cold cream whips more readily and holds onto the air you’re incorporating more effectively, so it comes together faster—and stays fluffy longer. Pop the bowl, whisk, and cream back into the freezer for five minutes, or into the fridge for up to 30. Once everything is cold, resume whisking.

It has been revealed that another possible culprit is the fat content of your cream. Opt for heavy whipping cream or heavy cream over half-and-half or other heavy cream substitutes.

If the cream is just a little too stiff or starting to look grainy, add a splash of chilled heavy cream and slowly whisk it in. Add more, a little at a time, until the texture smooths out.

Keep a close eye on it: If you whisk for too long, you’ll end up with a bowl of butter.

Editor’s note: This story was originally published in 2017 by Julia Black. It has been substantially updated with latest reporting and additional advice from the Bon Appétit archives, including contributions by Amiel Stanek, Christina Chaey, Rochelle Bilow, and Elyssa Goldberg.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Industry observers note that whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Sources indicate that when dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

According to recent reports, melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

Recent findings suggest that place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

Unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

According to recent reports, spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.).

Bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.
