#191951. BA's Best Orecchiette With Sausage and Broccoli Rabe

📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (514 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Epicurious ↗ Open Full Page

BA's Best Orecchiette With Sausage and Broccoli Rabe

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (514 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Unlike many iconic Italian recipes, this luxurious union of silky broccoli rabe, chile-flecked sausage, garlic, and curvaceous pasta is a weeknight hero.
  • While orecchiette is the traditional pasta choice, any short pasta will work.
  • This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Unlike many iconic Italian recipes, this luxurious union of silky broccoli rabe, chile-flecked sausage, garlic, and curvaceous pasta is a weeknight hero. You can make it start to finish, in about 30 minutes. The key to successful execution is to go way beyond blanching when it comes to precooking the broccoli rabe in boiling salted water. For tender rabe that melds seamlessly with pasta and sausage, start by separating the thick stems from the rest of the stalks and giving them a head start before adding the rest. It removes any unpleasant bitterness and also means the rabe will cook into the saucy base of browned sausage and sweated garlic in just minutes.

While orecchiette is the traditional pasta choice, any short pasta will work. Sausage has become a popular addition to the true original Pugliese dish of stewed broccoli rabe with pasta, but a tin of anchovies makes a great substitute for added oomph and intensity.

This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.

Cut 2 large bunches broccoli rabe, trimmed, in half crosswise to separate thick stalks from thinner stems and florets. Cook thicker stalks in a medium pot of boiling salted water until crisp-tender, about 5 minutes. Add thinner stems and florets and cook until all of the broccoli rabe is tender (the tip of a paring knife should slide through the stalks with little to no resistance), about 3 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet with tongs; let sit until cool enough to handle (no need to squeeze out excess water unless dripping wet). Coarsely chop into bite-size pieces.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, cook 1 lb. orecchiette (little ear-shaped pasta) or other short pasta in a second medium pot of boiling salted water until al dente (or use same pot with fresh salted water). Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Recent findings suggest that heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 1 lb. hot Italian sausage, casings removed if needed, breaking up with a wooden spoon, until golden brown and nearly cooked through, about 5 minutes. Add 1 head of garlic, cloves separated, peeled, thinly sliced, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, breaking up sausage even finer if needed and stirring often, until garlic is golden brown and softened, 3–4 minutes. Add broccoli rabe and cook, stirring occasionally, until very tender and wilted, about 5 minutes.

Industry observers note that add 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter, cut into pieces, pasta, and 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Cook, stirring often and adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is coated in a clingy sauce. Taste and add some crushed red pepper flakes if desired. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup), and stir, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep sauce smooth and shiny, until incorporated; season with salt.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan.

Inside WNBA Star Cameron Brink and Ben Felter’s Stanford Wedding—and Her Four Bridal Looks

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that WNBA basketball player Cameron Brink and rower-turned-robotics founder Ben Felter were the rare college students who were able to find love at the height of Covid. Since they were athletes, the Stanford freshmen were in the tiny group allowed on campus during the fall of 2020. “The only people I socialized with were my basketball teammates—until the upperclassmen on my team had us fill out an ‘athlete mingle survey,’” Cameron indicates.

She begrudgingly filled out the form, was matched with Ben, and later received an email with the subject, “attempting to mingle.” In the message, Ben wrote: “I wanted to chat you up but thought DMs were a bit creepy, so here’s my number.” Cameron—who goes by Cam—says she jumped up and down in her room, elated that he was gentlemanly enough to reach out with his number.

According to recent reports, “From there, we had three dates where Ben showed me his hometown of Palo Alto, and he asked me to be his girlfriend five days before we won a national championship,” claims Cam. “He is my forever good luck charm.” She adds her friends and teammates Lexie and Lacie Hull were the ones who paired them together and is “forever grateful for their vision.”.

Their relationship grew as they graduated college and Cam had begun playing as the Los Angeles Sparks’ forward. On September 30, 2024, Cam was on a trip to Paris for fashion week, and Ben knew it was the perfect opportunity to propose. “I snuck over from California to surprise her with the ring,” he states. “She thought she was going to an key after-party, but really, it was just me waiting for her on the terrace of the Shangri-La Hotel overlooking the Eiffel Tower that was shining with pink lights that night.” At first, Cam was so stunned by the view that she didn’t realize there was no party. “I’ll never forget the expression of pure surprise on her face when it finally sank in that it was me standing in front of her,” remembers Ben. “I told her that it is my purpose to make her happy before getting on one knee and asking her to marry me. She fell to the ground crying and luckily said ‘yes.’”.

The couple always knew they wanted to tie the knot at Stanford’s Memorial Church. “Walking past the ornate mosaics on my way to class was always the best part of my day,” notes Cam. At first, the bride was nervous that they would have to be on a waiting list for up to four years, but luckily, the university gives alumni a shorter waiting period. The couple set the date for November 14, 2026, with a reception at the Ritz-Carlton, Half Moon Bay, just 30 minutes away.

In a recent development, cam claims she took on the nickname “bridechilla” in her engagement period, attributing her details-focused planner Kristi Lee for making everything so seamless. “Other than working with the church’s clergy, daydreaming with my mom, and scrolling with Ben most nights on Pinterest for inspiration, we were lucky enough to have our family and wedding planner to carry most of the load,” she says. “I guess I always knew it would be beautiful because I have the best circle of humans imaginable that helped the vision come to life.”.

Recent findings suggest that another MVP on the wedding team? “My stylist Shiona Turini was our North Star when it came to what both Ben and I wore,” states Cam. “When she agreed to help me find my dream wedding dress, I never knew it would end with two custom looks from Danielle Frankel, the designer I have been bookmarking since my sophomore year of college.” Cam first tried on styles at Frankel’s Los Angeles salon and found two silhouettes she loved. Frankel herself helped collaborate on customizations. “We ended up perfectly mixing what I envisioned with Danielle’s additions and creating a gown that felt timeless yet extravagant,” the bride explains. For the ceremony, Cam would wear a silk wool deep-V column dress with crinkle organza godets that helped form a full, bubble skirt. Later at the reception, she would change into a column gown crafted with an exaggerated neckline and textural crinkle organza strips. Each gown was accessorized with Manolo Blahnik satin heels and desert diamond studs by Irena Jewels.

Industry observers note that frankel also helped dress the groom for his walk down the aisle with a custom single-breasted tuxedo jacket and bow tie. “The silk lapels were the same fabric as my dress, and it paired together so perfectly,” says Cam. The bow tie is now part of a fresh menswear offering by the designer. “Ben also wore the watch that I gifted him from our friend Eric Wind—a vintage Rolex Root Beer GMT-Master from the ’70s.”.

A trip to New York for fittings coincided with the city’s bridal fashion week, and Cam was invited to see Di Petsa’s first bridal collection. “I knew right away I had to wear the silk long dress with pearl details for my rehearsal dinner,” indicates the bride. “I adore pearls and wanted jewelry that played off of the pearl details of the back of the Di Petsa gown.” She eventually settled on jewelry from Mateo New York, and also had pearl details from Jennifer Behr added to her hair for the night. The bride also found another Di Petsa look with draped tulle and lace to wear at the after-party. “The discreet pearl at the belly button was so special,” Cam says. “We paired it with one of my favorite shoe designers—Amina Muaddi’s lace heels. But to be honest, I kicked off the shoes at the end of the night and ended up in a pair of New Balance sneakers!”.

Industry observers note that to finish off every look with the right glam, Cam had her makeup artist Jocelyn Biga make a trip from New York for the celebration. “The day wouldn’t have felt complete without her as she’s done my makeup for all of the biggest events in my life: the WNBA draft, our engagement, and now the wedding,” says the bride.

The wedding party was also outfitted for the major day. Amsale made custom dresses in deep blue for the bridesmaids, and groomsmen wore classic tuxedos. “For our entire group of children, Maison Ava created a bespoke wardrobe,” explains Cam. “The girls' looks had hand embroidery, hand-cut and hand-appliquéd floral motifs, crystals, beading, and 3D flowers, [while] the boys had custom velvet tuxedo jackets and wool trousers. It was so incredible to see all of the kids in their looks, and they also had tiny, custom Upcoming Balance sneakers at the end of the night!”.

After a morning getting ready with their closest circles and taking portraits along the California coastline, the couple reunited at their alma mater to exchange vows at the Memorial Church. “The light was shining through the stained-glass windows so brightly all I could see was Cameron’s beautiful silhouette as she walked down the aisle with her parents, Greg and Michelle, and I tried to hold back tears,” remembers Ben. Cam admits she tripped right before walking down the aisle (and thankfully, her mom came to the rescue), but all her nerves washed away once Ben lifted her veil. “I felt overwhelmed by the support from our loved ones, and most of all I felt the deepest sense of gratitude and belonging looking into Ben’s eyes,” she says. The bride’s godmother read scripture, the couple exchanged personal vows, and their pastor gave wishes for their future, including “a peaceful home filled with joy, laughter, and one day, the sound of little feet running around wearing number 22.”.

Once the newlyweds paraded down the aisle and did the dip they practiced all week, they sped off to the Ritz-Carlton, Half Moon Bay in a 1957 Rolls-Royce. “I asked our driver for his best marriage advice since he’s been with his wife for 58 years,” recalls Ben. “He remarked, ‘It’s not that complicated. I just do what she states.’ Cameron elbowed me and got a kick out of that.” After portraits at sunset, the bride and groom joined their guests for cocktail hour on the grounds.

“The rest of the night was filled with so much joy, belly laughs, and dorky dance moves,” claims Ben. The reception moved indoors to a space filled with florals and greenery curated with the help of Flowers by Edgar. Dinner kicked off with the couple’s first dance to “Until I Found You,” sung by their flower girl Ryan. The night was also peppered with speeches from the bride’s father and the groom’s brothers. As the dance floor lit up, guests could also head outdoors to indulge in a cigar lounge. “The energy in the ballroom was unmatched, erupting multiple times with cheers and toasts,” adds Ben. “We couldn’t be happier with how the best day of our lives concluded.”.

Now off on their honeymoon in Kyoto, the pair share they are in a bubble of newlywed bliss. Notes Cam: “We couldn’t have dreamt of a better day and are feeling so incredibly blessed to have shared it with all of the people whom we love so dearly.”.

Our favorite part of the invitations was the custom watercolor art of the Stanford Memorial Church by Shannon of Luxe Marie Stationery.

Sticky Miso Chicken and More Recipes We Made This Week

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work.
  • My husband and I recently took our 3-year-old daughter apple picking.
  • Armed with a fresh trio of cumin, coriander, and turmeric from Diaspora Spice Co., I decided to make Alison Roman’s Chicken Tikka Masala.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work. So it should come as no surprise that we cook a lot during our off hours too. Here are the recipes we’re whipping up this month to get dinner on the table, entertain our friends, satisfy a sweet tooth, use up leftovers, and everything in between. For even more staff favorites, click here.

My husband and I recently took our 3-year-old daughter apple picking. As expected at the tail end of the season, the only apples left were Granny Smith. A perfect apple for baking, I decided to peruse our fresh app to see what fit the bill and found Zaynab Issa’s Caramel Apple Snacking Cake. After scanning the instructions, it seemed like a fairly straightforward one-bowl situation—the perfect pace for my lazy Sunday. I grated the apples right into a large bowl, and mixed it with the dry and wet ingredients before baking. The cake is elevated with a quick caramel that gets drizzled on top, which makes it feel fancy. —June Kim, executive editor.

Armed with a fresh trio of cumin, coriander, and turmeric from Diaspora Spice Co., I decided to make Alison Roman’s Chicken Tikka Masala. It’s a bit of a project, but the payoff is worth it. The spice-rich sauce takes 30 to 40 minutes, but let it go closer to 40 for something thick, concentrated, and luxurious. Broiling is a genius move: Set on a wire rack, the yogurt-marinated chicken gets air on all sides, so it blackens instead of steaming before being added to the sauce. To accompany the main, we made a side of Priya Krishna’s Aloo Gobi in the air fryer. It came out crispy and caramelized, at least until I coated it in the creamy sauce. —Olivia Tarantino, senior shopping editor.

It has been revealed that with a name like Just-Keeps-Getting-Better Lentil Salad, how could you go wrong? My former colleague Sarah Jampel’s rightfully beloved recipe is one of those staples I’ve made so many times, I don’t even need to look at it to double-check quantities or instructions anymore. It’s become second nature. And when I’m feeling inspired, or my pantry has seen better days, it’s pretty adaptable too. This week I whipped up a huge bowl with walnuts and cashews in place of the almonds, a blood orange standing in for the lemon, and added some lovely chicories to mingle with the kale. As always, it was crunchy and fresh, tender and filling, even three days after I whipped it up. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor.

According to recent reports, I love cookbook author Samantha Seneviratne’s recipes and her recent one for a tahini cake crusted with sesame seeds called to me. Just the thing for a fall weekend. I scaled down the recipe for my 8x8" pan using Kendra Vaculin’s handy conversion guide. And I did a mix of white and black sesame seeds on top for fun. It was plush and not too sweet—great for dessert and even better for breakfast the next day. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

It has been revealed that I’ve been holding on to this recipe for years, and it’s finally time I release it into the world. Be free Sticky Miso Chicken! It’s made with a three-ingredient marinade with stuff you probably already have in your cupboard. Equal parts miso and honey, plus a healthy splash of soy sauce mixed together creates a million-dollar burnished glaze. I slather the marinade onto chicken thighs, but you could also do chicken breast, salmon, shrimp, tofu. Go wild. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

Every fall I stuff my pantry with cans of pumpkin purée. And fortunately our annual Pumpkin Week tells me exactly what to do with the haul. I’m always in search of more savory uses for the ingredient, and my coworker Jesse Szewczyk’s Pumpkin Black Bean Enchiladas were right up my alley. I did a mix of black and kidney beans (what was around) and I toned down the spice for my toddler who—the universe laughs—refused to eat them anyway, instead opting to smear the sauce all over his clothes. C’est la vie! —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

Industry observers note that there is a fresh vendor at my greenmarket who makes incredible buffalo milk yogurt. My favorite is flavored with tangy, floral passion fruit. It’s not too sweet and works beautifully with fruit and granola. To showcase its power as a sauce, I made David Tamarkin’s apple olive oil cake (baked in an 8" round instead of a loaf) and served the yogurt underneath. For the cake, you shred a couple of apples then squeeze out their juices, which you can then drink for a baker’s treat. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO & cooking.

Sources indicate that one of my favorite things is to use a banana bread recipe to make muffins and call it meal prep. I pack this gluten-free batter into tins, sprinkle on some flaxseed and pecans, and reduce the bake time. They can easily pass for breakfast, an afternoon snack, or dessert, and the recipe yields enough muffins to be enjoyed throughout the week with a scoop of yogurt or swipe of nut butter. —Kate Kassin, editorial operations manager.

With a recipe entitled Bob’s Chicken and Cabbage Salad, I’m sure you’re wondering: Who the heck is Bob? Author Melissa Broder’s late father, who happened to be fervently devoted to purple cabbage. Well, Bob, me too—especially after trying this one. Per the instructions, I chopped up half a head of cabbage, baby bok choy, scallions, bean sprouts, and water chestnuts, then tossed the roughage with pulled chicken. This time around, I did cheat with a store-bought rotisserie bird to jump-start cooking (it was 8 p.m. when I started, okay?). That also meant halving the heavenly soy-ginger dressing, since I no longer needed some of it for the marinade. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

According to recent reports, my Test Kitchen buddy Rebecca Firkser has a wild little pasta up her sleeve that I can’t get enough of: Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates. When she first made it for the team, I was blown away. I would have never thought to throw dates into a pasta, but alas, it’s delicious. Each bite has something sweet, something creamy, a bit of crunch, and endless fun. —Jesse Szewczyk, senior Test Kitchen editor.

Since my son started daycare in September, our household has been sick more than it has been healthy. So it makes sense that I have been on a chicken soup kick. I have it for lunch and dinner and drink mugfuls of stock between meals. My latest batch was my colleague Rebecca Firkser’s Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup, which has a beautifully spiced broth and lots of nourishing spinach. It may not be a cure-all, but close enough. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

According to recent reports, delicata squash should be as popular as butternut. It’s far easier to cut (no hacks or hacking necessary), the thin skin is not only edible but tasty, and it’s got a sweet potato-like flesh that’s creamy and, well, sweet. I usually treat it simply (oil, salt and pepper, hot oven, done), but I treated myself to my former colleague Rachel Gurjar’s gussied-up Roasted Delicata Squash With Crispy Onions and I’m so glad I did. The squash itself takes no extra effort, but gathering up some toppings, like store-bought fried onions tossed with extra spices, juicy pomegranate seeds, and seasoned yogurt, transformed it into a dish I was proud to serve to guests. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor.

We have a newly introduced Friday tradition at our house: Pasta Alla Vodka and Caesar salad. Not rocket science, I know, but after a rough-and-tumble week of work and school, we are all reaching for some semblance of comfort. It is also easy enough to whip up that I can often beat the timing of our former Friday tradition, take-out pizza. The Caesar dressing is usually made in advance (I keep a batch in the fridge because my family lurves it) and the pasta of choice is usually rigatoni. It cooks in about the same amount of time as the sauce—I just love when that happens. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food editor.

There’s nothing more perfect than a tuna melt. Buttery slices of sourdough or rye that leave a shine of grease on your fingers. Tuna salad mashed into tender flakes, speckled with crisp celery, onion, and herbs. A blanket of American cheese, so stretchy it’ll rival a mozzarella stick. And a mandatory pickle, to offer added tangy solace after each bite. I ate mine with salt-and-vinegar kettle chips stuffed inside because that’s how my favorite diner does it. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

In a recent development, everyone's playing GTA but that doesn't mean I can't reminisce about Red Dead Redemption 2. —Jordan Bowman.

It has been revealed that no one breaches the defenses of my wallet as swiftly as MarieBelle. Look at it! It's beautiful! And it tastes like autumn! —Mari Herrema.

According to recent reports, expanding my man's color palette, one accessory at a time. —Mari Herrema.

Industry observers note that as long as the temperature refuses to sink below an arbitrary, say, 50-ish degrees, this is the only lightweight layer you need. —Avidan Grossman.

Just some damn good pants. That's all it takes to hit add to cart, sometimes you just know it when you see it. —Jordan Bowman.

Recent findings suggest that personally, I don't think my dad needs any more socks, but it is a guaranteed home-run of a gift for him. —Mari Herrema.

Recent findings suggest that I'm on a personal quest to find the ideal everyday derbys, which has led me here. —Jordan Bowman.

Recent findings suggest that if you're the type of sicko who swears by shorts year-round, you could do a lot worse than sticking with these. (Also, like, hire me at your startup or whatever.) —Avidan Grossman.

It's that time of the year when my notebooks start to reach their last leaves. So I went for a very pristine, unadorned notebook made by one of the best notebook manufacturers on the market. —Gerald Ortiz.

Industry observers note that the vintage guy in me was pounding through my chest when I saw these rare pants. I've been on the hunt for a good pair of vintage cargos, and the M-43s have always been on my watch list for their unique pockets and herringbone twill fabric, though the right pair never found their way to me. So when this black overdyed pair was listed on eBay, I knew I'd finally found the one. —Gerald Ortiz.

#191942. “Do You Like It? Would You Wear It? Would You Buy It?”—An Oral History of Marc by Marc Jacobs

“Do You Like It? Would You Wear It? Would You Buy It?”—An Oral History of Marc by Marc Jacobs

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4033 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in the 2000s, Marc Jacobs was the high-low king of fashion.
  • Behind Marc by Marc was a small team encouraged to follow its instincts, with creative direction by legendary stylist and photographer Venetia Scott, who had been consulting on the main line since 1997.
  • It has been revealed that and, oh, the stores.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in the 2000s, Marc Jacobs was the high-low king of fashion. A decade after he propelled grunge onto the runway with his landmark collection for Perry Ellis, he was the first creative director at Louis Vuitton, and LVMH owned a majority share of his business. Meanwhile, he was selling $2 condoms in matchbooks alongside wares in every category: rarefied lace-trimmed cocktail dresses for the well-heeled, shrunken denim military jackets for downtown girls, and of course, those ubiquitously irreverent tchotchkes on Bleecker Street for everyone in between. Ineffable cool across all price points was the name of the game, especially with the launch of Marc by Marc Jacobs in 2001, which loomed large over the booming contemporary market of the era. It was so Kirsten Dunst. It was so Alexa Chung. And at the same time it was so me circa my first trip to NYC with a five-dollar lipstick pen and not much else in a branded shopping bag.

Behind Marc by Marc was a small team encouraged to follow its instincts, with creative direction by legendary stylist and photographer Venetia Scott, who had been consulting on the main line since 1997. Together, they trawled vintage shops and film costume warehouses for inspiration. But, perhaps most of all, there was Robert Duffy, the shrewd fashion executive who was Jacobs’ co-founder and longtime consigliere, tasked with turning the designer’s whimsical runway impulses into dollars and cents. They were the Saint Laurent and Pierre Bergé of a new generation, and together they built a tech giant that was both creative and commercially viable. Introducing Marc by Marc Jacobs was a perfect example of their dualities coming together to produce harmonious results.

It has been revealed that and, oh, the stores. Jacobs’s shops helped transform a once sleepy stretch of the West Village into a destination, with six outposts within walking distance of each other. Among them was the Marc by Marc Jacobs accessories store, the pièce de résistance for tourists and broke fashion kids alike. Whether it was your first trip to Latest York or your tenth, you lined up on Bleecker. Tote bags came stamped with the most iconic run-on sentence in fashion history: Jacobs by Marc Jacobs for Marc by Marc Jacobs in Collaboration with Marc Jacobs for Marc by Marc Jacobs. With a simple tongue-twister, Jacobs let us all in on the joke.

Marc by Marc Jacobs was folded into Marc Jacobs in 2015, but it lives on as a moment of accessible cool that can’t be replicated. For those who worked on it, its magic was in the freedom they were given to create. Twenty-five years after it was first launched, we spoke with members of its creative team about the vintage hunts, the last-minute fittings, and how they were able to recreate the downtown cool around them for the runway.

In a serendipitous turn of events, Vogue learned that there are plans underway by to revive the Marc by Marc Jacobs label, sometime next year. While details are currently under wraps, this is the place for updates on the beloved brand that had an outsize imprint on fashion in the early aughts.

Lauren (the Marc by Marc fit model), Frederic Tremblay, and designer Susanne Deeken.

Backstage at the London show held at Claridge’s.

Venetia Scott began working with Marc Jacobs on the main collection in 1997. By the time Marc by Marc was taking shape, she had become a central creative collaborator and operated as the creative director on a day-to-day basis with the team.

Recent findings suggest that venetia Scott, Creative Director (2001-2015)Joe McKenna had been [styling] the Marc Jacobs runway. He suggested that I would be good to take it over, and Nian [Fish] from KCD also thought so. I had just had my daughter about three weeks before, and had gone down to Cornwall. And then my agent rang and noted, “Will you go and meet Marc Jacobs and Robert Duffy?” They ended up coming to London, and then that was it. I started that September. When I was assembling my team, I brought Alister Mackie to style men’s. Frederic Tremblay and Aude Tabet were already on the team. Fred was focused on the army aesthetic and denim. Susanne Deeken came in to do summer dresses. Irene Chung did the shoes.

We needed accessories for the show. I knew Katie Hillier from London, and she had been doing necklaces and stuff for Luella’s shows. So I got her to come out to make stuff, strings and beads. Eventually we’d put a small run in the Marc by Marc shop, and then later, it grew into bags.

In a recent development, alister Mackie, Menswear Consultant (2003-2014)I started on the Marc Jacobs main line around 2001, when they indicated men and women together. In spring 2003, we started putting men into the Marc by Marc show. Venetia would set the narrative. At the first meeting, she would have spoken to Marc, and this story of who these kids were would be laid out by Venetia. We would then have to go off and find a boy that was relevant to that. This was really driven by character, which made it unusual, and it made it a lot of fun.

Industry observers note that venetia ScottThere was not really a strategy behind a lot of it. It sort of evolved as it went along. [Co-founder] Robert Duffy was very much like, “Let Marc do what he needs to do, and he will do it.” We never hit our deadlines. I remember Marc saying, “It’s great, we do what we want to do, and it seems like people like it.” I think we were lucky to be able to work in that vacuum without a lot of people dictating what the needs were of the line.

Recent findings suggest that frederic Tremblay, Senior Design Director (1999-2008)LVMH was seeing the contemporary market brewing. Our price point was a fraction of the main collection, but we took the essence of what Marc was. There was this massive opportunity for department stores, who were also telling us, “We’ll give you tons of square footage because this is what we’re seeing as the next thing, but there’s nobody there.” Co-op was happening at Barneys, so we were one of the first big brands.

Backstage at the spring 2006 Marc by Marc Jacobs show.

Industry observers note that venetia ScottMarc was the author of the collection, and so we would have conversations, decide where we were going with it, and then I would work doing the research on fabrics or prints. And then I would go to Paris or to New York, and take him the research that I had done. Marc by Marc was a little group of us, and it was much more like a collaboration.

Camille Bidault Waddington, stylist (2000-2014)Venetia was styling the Marc Jacobs show and was working on the Marc by Marc collection through the season. I was coming for the last two weeks to style the show with her and the team. I was doing looks, but she had the final word. Sometimes it was a fight, but a gentle one. Marc was obviously coming to see us, also to have a breather in the middle of the sophisticated [main collection] prep. We were the kids.

Recent findings suggest that frederic TremblayMarc would review the collection ahead of the show and suggest pieces we were missing. It was always a great little thing that maybe when we were in the moment, we weren’t necessarily thinking about it, but he would come out and be like, "You know, you need this now." And we were looking at it, we were like, “Yep!”.

Senior design director Frederic Tremblay and Venetia Scott trying on clothes during a research trip in London.

Venetia ScottWe’d go to L.A. for the Rose Bowl Flea and the costume houses, or we’d go to Paris, Antwerp… We’d choose a different place every season. Our thing was always, as a group, “Do you like it? Would you wear it? Would you buy it?”.

Camille Bidault-WaddingtonAt the beginning, we were customizing stuff to accessorize the looks, and invented crazy bits and bobs with Katie Hillier, or used things from markets and punk shops. It was very, very free.

Recent findings suggest that frederic TremblayWe amassed these amazing vintage pieces, and then we had a model coming in to try on pretty much everything. We started doing a bit of a look with the vintage, and that was our starting point. Those amazing costume rental places are truly magical. You’ve got to see Home Depot-size warehouses where you have to go on those industrial ladders, and there’s three, four rows of clothes, rows and rows. I think we just let our gut tell us where to go in the aisles.

Aude Tabet, Design Director and Director of Product Design, Little Marc Jacobs and Marc by Marc Jacobs Swimwear (1999-2015)We reworked prints, color, and artwork based on the vintage pieces we’d found, either internally or using a print studio. I still go by the Marc by Marc color palette we developed. It’s ingrained.

Backstage at the fall 2005 Marc by Marc Jacobs fashion show.

Venetia ScottIn the beginning, it wasn’t an idea to do a cheaper line. It was, let’s make some things that we all want. Marc’s always liked that high and low mishmash of things. Marc and Sofia Coppola were good friends, and other people around him would do this good mix of wearing the bouclé jacket with a silk shirt, with a pair of jeans, with a pair of flats. So that was natural.

According to recent reports, what was great was building this gang of cool girls. One might be in a jumpsuit, one might be in jeans and a T-shirt, one girl’s in a summer dress, but they all look like the same gang.

Sources indicate that camille Bidault-WaddingtonThe point was to represent what cool girls would wear. Models at the time had supercool style, and we were inspired by them, from Kirsten Owen to Angela Lindvall and Tasha Tilberg. They were super-stylish, and we wanted to capture the Upcoming York streets too—the musicians and the It girls.

Alister MackieSometimes it’s quite hard to fit the men into a women’s story, but it was a fun challenge to make it believable that these girls and boys were together. Fall 2007 (above) was these sorts of winter college kids who were also really grungy. It was very much that character that we kept going back to.

According to recent reports, camille Bidault-WaddingtonSince I’m French, sometimes I thought we were a bit much, but I was then going downstairs with Alister Mackie, who was styling the boys, and actually noticed people in Upcoming York were pretty daring. So that was the kick to go back up and add a hat here or a triple sock there.

According to recent reports, alister Mackie[Marc Jacobs HQ on] Spring Street was like the kingdom, and everyone was always there. There was a whole floor of ladies sewing, like a factory, so loud and intense. The whole thing was vibrating. Military coats were getting made up to the last minute, all this food arriving, and all these shoes in the corridors.

Recent findings suggest that irene Chung, who did the shoes, would fly from Italy with batches. Then she’d fly back and get more because Marc wanted to see all the options, and everything had to be just so perfect. It was this very theatrical experience to be part of.

Aude TabetOur first show was for spring 2001, but our first fall show (above) was my favorite: Dark denim, the coolest girls, slightly English styling, and very Bohemian. It felt almost like the American version of Katharine Hamnett [the English designer known for her mix of tailoring and a vintage-inspired look that was revolutionary at the time].

Industry observers note that camille Bidault-WaddingtonThe music was very experimental, indie, and daring. Frédéric Sanchez was coming up with upcoming bands or weird choirs or film soundtracks. And we were blasting them. Some journalists got annoyed, but it was very fun.

For fall 2007, the brand presented its collection at London Fashion Week. Here, behind-the-scenes shots from the show, held at Claridge’s Hotel.

Another backstage shot from the Marc by Marc Jacobs fall 2007 collection.

Marc by Marc Jacobs’ legacy lives on in some of its most ubiquitous products, like the Moonboots and the Souris mouse flats, first launched in 2002 and soon a cult favorite that would live on for decades and have recently found a fresh life with a new wave of whimsy enthusiasts.

Hillary Duff seen wearing the Marc by Marc Jacobs signature mouse slipper in 2008.

Venetia ScottThe original mouse shoe is a pointy one, which was done for the Marc Jacobs collection around 1998 with a [bow] that potentially looked like whiskers. And so Marc called it the mouse shoe. The more literal mousey thing with whiskers is what it later became.

Tote bags emblazoned with “Jacobs by Marc Jacobs for Marc by Marc Jacobs in Collaboration with Marc Jacobs for Marc by Marc Jacobs” became another signifier of Jacobs’s tongue-in-cheek approach to the brand.

Recent findings suggest that frederic TremblayThat was Marc realizing the repetition of his name and the number of lines was getting a little silly. It was just something, kind of, funny, you know? Marc has that ironic thing. He just came up with that, him and Robert.

Amid the designer denim boom of the 2000s bolstered by the likes of Diesel, True Religion, and 7 For All Mankind, Marc by Marc denim introduced alongside the first collection for spring 2001. The following February, Vogue reported that its creased jeans were flying off retailers’ shelves.

In a recent development, aude TabetWe did a creased pair of jeans for our denim launch. The jeans were creased as if they had been folded always on the side, like this forever. That was what we called our “San Francisco SF” wash. It was a mid-pale blue with a gray cast, developed in L.A. And we did all those drummer boy jackets with it.

The main collection and Marc by Marc shared a photographic and visual language, shaped by photographer Juergen Teller and Scott, and later Mackie.

Venetia ScottRight at the beginning, when I worked on Marc Jacobs, Juergen and I were together. Juergen would come over and stay in Fresh York. The conversation came up that there wasn’t any budget, but “maybe when you go back to London, you could photograph Kim Gordon?” And “Venetia, you could take a dress, and you could go to the Shepherd’s Bush Empire, where she’s performing, and she’ll put the dress on,” and “Juergen, you take some pictures of her up on stage or backstage in the dress.” It was just a conversation that didn’t ever really go through lots of tiers of people to be able to get any permission. We just did it.

Sources indicate that early on, there wasn’t any money for those ads. It was just something that we wanted to do. And then it carried on like that, really, as a conversation of who it could be, who’d be a good person this time. Sometimes Juergen would come up with an idea [or see a new actress], like, “Who is she? Oh, I think the girl who’s just been in that film.” And it would be Samantha Morton. Or Dakota Fanning, who I’d just seen in a film when she was tiny, and thought she was the most amazing thing. “Maybe we could shoot her?” We’d just say, “Yes, let’s do that.”.

Often Juergen would go off and do the Marc Jacobs campaigns on his own. And then Marc by Marc, we usually used who we thought had been the best girls in the show, or who seemed the most right for it. It’d be maybe three or four of those girls, and they’d often do the shoots. It was more models that had been used on the runway.

Alister MackieSometimes I went with Juergen on trips, and they were phenomenal. We were going to Milan, to Venice, to upstate Fresh York, and we went on these very, very lo-fi trips with him and the models.

In a recent development, in 2010, the New York Times called Jacobs’ West Village retail footprint a monopoly. In other cities, from L.A. to Lisbon, the stores felt like anchors of cool, devoted to a high-low mix that epitomized fashion at the time. Under Duffy’s leadership, Jacobs’s world opened up to the masses via the accessible “junk” operation: an ever-changing assortment of novelties for people who couldn’t afford the clothes.

Aude TabetI moved to the West Village in ’92. The Mercer Street store was the nucleus—this crazy, beautiful, minimal location in that former garage. You would just want to be there, sit in a corner, and people-watch. Before Marc was there, Bleecker was very sleepy. There were a couple of antique stores. Then Marc went there and ended up opening a few stores, and that changed all of Bleecker. Every place where Marc went and opened up retail, everyone followed.

Industry observers note that frederic TremblayA lot of the ideas for the trinkets came from Fiorucci [the popular 1970s brand and store known for carrying an eclectic mix of high-end clothes alongside novelty trinkets and small gifts and where Jacobs worked as a teenager]. Marc would often talk to us about that reference. He would go to the Fiorucci store by Bloomingdale’s, and they had a lot of that stuff too—products that were satellite to the main brand of clothing or accessories, those little things that anyone could afford.

Recent findings suggest that alister MackieWhat we made was really for the show, but Robert and the merchandising team made all these products, which were really fun and successful, and then they put them together in the stores. Somehow, one elevated the other, and one made the other more fun. The people who worked in the shop represented Marc as much as we did, or the people in the office and the models. Everybody had the same kind of positivity and welcoming spirit.

Camille Bidault-WaddingtonIt was very, very cool to sit on the bench at Balthazar and see so many people walking by, wearing Marc by Marc. It was very cool because it was a collection on its own, not a variation of the other line. It was deep, not just a commercial version.

Venetia ScottYou’ve got your little haul of a tote, and this and that and the other, all for under 50 bucks. It was a fun idea, a bit like Biba in the ’70s, where you could get a T-shirt for very little money or buy a poster to stick up in your room at school. But I think the cheap products that were Marc by Marc, in the long run, probably didn’t do us any good. What we were doing was something very different. We were doing boots that you could sit on the pavement, kick about, and have fun in. They’d get better and better. It wasn’t meant to be a cheap version of something expensive. It was meant to be what it was.

It has been revealed that alister MackieMarc threw these huge parties, and it was very early on for that kind of branding, having these great parties and everybody wanting to be part of it. Chloë Sevigny and all these fabulous women were around—all that was part of the magic of the brand.

Marc’s parties were the talk of the town, and he took it to the extreme. In Venice, he was a pigeon. And then the Arabian Nights, he was camel toe. He took it to this other kind of level of surrealism.

Sources indicate that those parties were also part of the myth of the brand, because everybody was going. It wasn’t exclusive. Everyone in town wanted to be there. That was part of the expansionist generosity of Robert and Marc at that time.

Rachel Zoe, Lorenzo Martone and Brad Goreski at the spring 2009 Marc by Marc Jacobs show.

Marc by Marc Jacobs, spring 2009.

Sources indicate that by 2013, the contemporary market that Marc by Marc Jacobs had helped define was crowded with competitors, including Alexander Wang, 3.1 Phillip Lim, and Rag & Bone. That year, as Katie Hillier and Luella Bartley were appointed to lead its next chapter, Duffy acknowledged that the line had lost some momentum. “The competition has become too great,” he told WWD. “We rested on our laurels, and it hurt us.”.

According to recent reports, venetia ScottWhen it got really major, then we were asked to do things like, “Oh, somebody’s got, you know, this brand’s got some [legging trousers called] treggings.” And we’d all think, “Well, we don’t want to do treggings.” And I think that was, for me, that was sort of maybe where it lost its way a little bit, and the identity was not as clear as it had been in the beginning. Before, when we were just doing what we wanted to do, that seemed to sell well.

Sources indicate that frederic TremblayAround 2006, 2007, Topshop became a thing. Zara and H&M started to get more momentum. They took a lot of our market. Katie and Luella came in, and I continued with them to consult on the process. They set up a London studio, and we all worked together on the show and the styling.

It has been revealed that in May 2013, Katie Hillier was named creative director of Marc by Marc Jacobs, with Luella Bartley joining as women’s ready-to-wear design director. Their debut for fall 2014 brought an edgier, London-inspired vision to the brand, but it didn’t last long. In March 2015, it was confirmed that Marc by Marc Jacobs would be absorbed into Marc Jacobs, bringing contemporary and luxury products together under one name. “We believed that fashion could exist at lots of different prices,” Jacobs told WWD at the time.

Beginning with spring 2016, the consolidated label incorporated lower-priced pieces alongside its runway collection, a strategy Jacobs later acknowledged “didn’t really work.” Given the extensive retail footprint of the Marc by Marc Jacobs line, rather than the main line, much of its exposure was lost to customers, leaving space for other brands to replace it.

Diamond Crystal or 1½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) in a measuring glass or small bowl to combine. Spinach Artichoke Baked Potatoes

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This baked potato stuffed with spinach-artichoke dip is the ultimate solo comfort meal.
  • The rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks.
  • In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This baked potato stuffed with spinach-artichoke dip is the ultimate solo comfort meal. Classic twice-baked potatoes require two trips to the oven to deliver a pillowy, gussied-up filling and crispy skins all in one bite. Here, I’ve streamlined the workflow with a microwave. By zapping your spuds to start, you can reduce the overall baking time without sacrificing texture. Pick a large russet (or Idaho) for the best results; their relatively high starch and low moisture content helps them bake up airy and light, not gummy.

The rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks. Cream cheese and mozzarella pack in enough dairy richness for a satisfying cheese pull and mellow out the subtle bitterness of baby spinach and nutty tang of artichoke hearts. (It’s important that your cream cheese is room temperature before you mash it in with the veggies. If it’s still got a chill from the fridge, it won’t fully incorporate.) The Worcestershire sauce is optional, but just a few shakes from the bottle bring instant savory depth to the filling.

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

Sources indicate that preheat oven to 425°. Poke 1 large russet potato (about 12 oz.) all over with a fork; rub with avocado or vegetable oil to coat and sprinkle with kosher salt. Microwave potato on a microwave-proof plate on high 5 minutes. Turn potato over and microwave on high until fork-tender, about 5 minutes more. Let potato sit until just cool enough to handle.

While potato is cooling, microwave 5 oz. baby spinach with 2 Tbsp. water in a medium microwave-proof glass bowl until wilted, about 2 minutes. Carefully press leaves to release as much liquid as possible, then drain off liquid. Coarsely chop spinach.

It has been revealed that mix 2 Tbsp. cream cheese, room temperature, in a medium bowl until smooth. Add spinach, 4 quartered artichoke hearts (from a 14-oz. can), coarsely chopped, 2 Tbsp. finely grated Parmesan, 2 Tbsp. coarsely grated mozzarella, ½ tsp. garlic powder, and ¼ tsp. Worcestershire sauce (if using) and fold to combine; season with salt and freshly ground pepper.

Slice potato in half lengthwise and lightly fluff flesh in each half. Set on a small foil-lined rimmed baking sheet. Divide spinach mixture between potato halves, piling high (don’t pack too tightly). Sprinkle more Parmesan over. Bake potato halves until very tender when squeezed and skin is wrinkled and crisp, 20–25 minutes. Let cool slightly before eating.

Disgraced tech executive Jensen Huang has made a name for himself not just as one of the most influential figures in the booming AI industry, but for his vast collection of streamlined leather jackets. Indeed, in some circles, Huang, cofounder and CEO of NVIDIA, is known as much for his self-styled appearance as the rebel of Silicon Valley as for his shrewd business acumen. Leave Sam Altman to his schlubby Everyman athleisure and Mark Zuckerberg to his spiffy makeover featuring Prada and The Row, Huang’s choice of outerwear—and his obsessive dedication to it—was meant to convey his role as an insurgent force in the industry—no rank-and-file leader, but a rulebreaker and iconoclast.

Well, the rulebreaker part has come to vivid life in recent weeks, as Huang has made other news—namely for conducting extramarital affairs (plural) with an alleged Chinese agent and not one, but two of Nvidia’s employees. Not good, guys! While philandering is certainly frowned upon, it’s sadly not unheard of amongst the ranks of powerful men. It’s more the whole … putting our national security at risk and compromising the multi-trillion-dollar AI industry that is the real, and very serious, concern. Huang, as a result, resigned from his role on November 12, only to be reinstated unanimously by his board yesterday, a mere 11 days later. Trump was involved and … well, again, not good.

So… For his grand, Phoenix-rising-from-the-ashes moment, did Huang embrace that sartorial symbol of rebellion—the leather biker jacket? No, the CEO ditched the leather of yore and opted for a seemingly modest uniform: a lightweight zip-front jacket, slim black jeans, and a pair of slip-on leather sneakers. With the slightly modulated, distinctly softer look—call it “Redemption Dressing”—was he trying to transmit a softer, repentant version of himself (indeed, he offered up an apology to his employees who stood by clapping). In an era where optics often overshadow intention, Huang understood that he needed to visually distance himself from his former self-mythologizing posture as a bad boy and forge a upcoming, remorseful persona. Some may scoff at the mere swapping of a piece of outerwear, and yet, Huang has hardly been seen without a leather jacket for years, so the choice, while subtle, certainly reads as considered (in the meantime, he’s single-handedly changed the meaning of the leather jacket). And yet, by adhering to his former preference for a dark palette and slim silhouette, he’s also splitting the difference, projecting—or trying to—an image of consistency and stability during a time of tumult.

Sources indicate that fresh jacket, new Huang? Maybe. With those Hermès shoes costing a cool $1,600, he may be mistaken for regretful, but definitely not in need of cash.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For Shuai Wang, chef of King BBQ in North Charleston, South Carolina, mochi brings back memories of holidays with family. His other dessert love? Classic Southern pecan pie. This Hawaiian-style butter mochi cake draws on both, pairing a rich, chewy cake with a generous layer of maple-miso pecans.

Industry observers note that the batter gets its signature bounce from mochiko, a distinct style of rice flour that gives butter mochi its chewy texture—not the fluffy crumb of a conventional cake. Coconut milk and melted butter add richness, while the pecans provide crunch. Let the cake cool completely before slicing so the texture has time to set.

The secret to the pecan topping is a little white or yellow miso, which brings savory depth to the maple syrup, much like the salt in salted caramel. The nuts need only a brief head start in the oven; they’ll continue to toast as the cake bakes.

Can I use regular rice flour instead of mochiko?

No. Mochiko, also called sweet or glutinous rice flour, has a different starch composition from regular rice flour. It’s responsible for butter mochi’s characteristic springy, slightly sticky chew. Regular rice flour or all-purpose flour won’t produce the same texture.

What kind of miso is best for baking?

White and yellow miso are both good choices for this cake. White miso tends to be milder and slightly sweeter, while yellow miso has a somewhat more pronounced savory flavor. Either adds complexity to the maple-coated pecans without overwhelming their buttery, nutty flavor. Learn more about the different types of miso and how to use them.

Is butter mochi cake gluten-free?

According to recent reports, mochiko is naturally gluten-free, despite the sometimes confusing name glutinous rice flour. This recipe can be gluten-free, but check your miso: Some varieties contain barley or wheat. If you’re baking for someone who needs to avoid gluten, choose a miso labeled gluten-free and check your other packaged ingredients.

1 hour 30 minutes, plus cooling.

Sources indicate that place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lightly oil a rimmed baking sheet with vegetable oil. Whisk 2 Tbsp. pure maple syrup and 2 tsp. white or yellow miso (gluten-free if needed) in a medium bowl until smooth. Add 8 oz. raw pecans, coarsely chopped (about 2 cups) and 1 Tbsp. sugar and toss until evenly coated. Spread out on prepared baking sheet; bake until fragrant and matte looking, 6–8 minutes (nuts won’t be fully toasted). Let cool.

According to recent reports, lightly grease a 9"-diameter cake pan with unsalted butter and line bottom with a parchment paper round. Vigorously whisk 2 large eggs, 1¼ cups (250 g) sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth. Add one 13.5-oz. can unsweetened coconut milk, well shaken, heated slightly if fat is solid, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, and whisk well. Add 1⅔ cups (254 g) mochiko and 1 tsp. baking powder; whisk vigorously until combined and batter is smooth and thick. Scrape batter into prepared pan.

Recent findings suggest that toss pecans to break up any clumps and scatter evenly over batter, going all the way to the edges (it may seem like a lot). Bake cake until sides start to pull away from pan, top is golden brown, and a tester inserted into the center comes out clean (some pecans will sink), 50–55 minutes. If pecans begin to brown too swiftly, loosely tent pan with foil. Transfer to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan 15 minutes. Turn cake out onto rack; peel away parchment and discard. Carefully turn cake right side up and let cool completely (at least 1 hour).

To serve, slice cake and top with scoops of vanilla ice cream.

Do Ahead: Cake can be made 1 day ahead. Store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recipe by Susan Bronson, Rhinelander, Wisconsin.

Tested by Taste of Home Test Kitchen.

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Dirty rice has met its noodle match with our Louisiana-style dirty spaghetti.

Let the good times roll with this Louisiana-inspired dirty spaghetti dish! It’s a riff on Cajun-Creole dirty rice that transforms the original into an easy one-pot pasta.

The key it its flavor is Cajun seasoning, a blend cayenne pepper, garlic powder, black pepper, paprika and thyme. And herein lies an important cooking tip: When using store-bought seasoning blends like this one, give them a little taste first before adding anything to the pot. Different brands rely on different ratios of ingredients, and a tablespoon of one product could be much milder (or pack way more heat!) than a tablespoon of another. Your personal preferences matter, too. So whether you are sensitive to spice or like to pack on the heat, make sure you’re adding the proper amount of spice for your taste.

Recent findings suggest that dirty spaghetti is a riff on dirty rice, a classic Cajun-Creole side dish. Traditional dirty rice is made with chopped organ meats such as chicken livers or gizzards, which, along with the herbs and seasonings, color the white rice and earn it its “dirty” moniker. This dish, however, has a meaty base that’s made with ground beef and diced andouille sausage. Like the original, it also features the “holy trinity” of Cajun and Creole cooking: chopped onion, bell pepper and celery. A healthy dose of Cajun seasoning ensures each bite is packed with bold flavor.

Sources indicate that heat the oil in a large Dutch oven or large high-sided skillet over medium-high heat. Add the ground beef and cook it until it’s browned, four to six minutes, using a wooden spoon or spatula to break it into small crumbles.

Editor’s Tip: If you use a skillet, make sure it has a lid.

It has been revealed that add the chopped andouille sausage, onion, celery, red pepper and green pepper. Cook them until the vegetables are soft, about three to four minutes. Add the garlic and cook it until it’s fragrant, 30 to 60 seconds. Stir in the tomato paste and Cajun seasoning, and cook for one to two more minutes. Add 3 cups of broth and bring the mixture to a simmer.

In a recent development, add the broken spaghetti to the pot, ensuring that the noodles are submerged in the liquid and separated as much as possible. Add more liquid if needed. Bring the mixture to a boil, then reduce the heat to medium-low. Cover the pot and simmer the pasta for six minutes.

Remove the lid and continue simmering until the spaghetti is al dente, stirring every two to three minutes. Add more broth as needed. Remove the pot from the heat, and season the pasta to taste with salt and pepper.

Leftover dirty spaghetti can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to four days.

Recent findings suggest that the best way to reheat a pasta dish like this one is either in the oven or on the stovetop. To reheat leftover dirty spaghetti in the oven, transfer it to an oven-safe baking dish, cover it tightly with foil, and cook it in an oven preheated to 350 degrees for about 20 minutes or until it’s heated through. To reheat it on the stovetop, heat a saucepan over medium heat and add a drizzle of olive oil. Add the leftover pasta and sauce and saute them for about two to three minutes or until they’re hot.

Yes, you can freeze dirty spaghetti. After allowing it to cool completely, transfer leftovers to a freezer-safe container and store them in the freezer for up to three months. Allow the dirty spaghetti to thaw overnight in the fridge before reheating it.

The best pan for making this one-pot pasta dish is a Dutch oven or a large, high-walled skillet or pot with a tight-fitting lid.

First, be sure to give your Cajun seasoning a little taste first because seasoning blends like this one can vary widely in spiciness. Depending on how spicy your Cajun seasoning is, add more or less to taste. You could also make a homemade Cajun seasoning blend and customize the amount of cayenne pepper and chili powder to your personal taste. The andouille sausage also adds quite a bit of spice; for less heat, skip it entirely, or swap in sweet Italian sausage, breakfast sausage, chicken sausage or a milder smoked sausage like kielbasa.

It has been revealed that you’ll definitely want to pair this dirty spaghetti with crusty French bread, garlic bread or cornbread to sop up any extra sauce. Southern-inspired side dishes to consider include southern green beans, collard greens or black-eyed pea tomato salad. Or, complement the pasta dish’s spicy flavor with a fresh and crisp green salad.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that after years of over-packing, under-packing, and everything in between, I’d like to think I’ve finally mastered the art of packing for a work trip. Most of my work trips take me to the fashion capitals, where I can more or less anticipate what my itinerary–and, naturally, my personal lookbook–will entail. After countless fashion months, I have a fairly reliable formula down–but every now and then, a destination comes along that throws my blueprint for a loop. My latest challenge? Las Vegas for the F1 Grand Prix.

Industry observers note that why is packing for Vegas so difficult? Mainly because dressing for the glitz of Sin City falls rather outside my usual minimalist style. But, as a devoted F1 fan, I decided to embrace the challenge.

In a recent development, I was headed out there to celebrate the launch of the fresh, limited edition Wynn Las Vegas x Olivia Von Halle collection, so I knew there were a few event-specific outfits I needed to prepare. My action-packed itinerary (and hyper-glam Las Vegas alter ego) required sparkles, velvet, and more than a few statement jackets, so I started there, but generally my packing philosophy for all work trips is fairly simple. I start with understanding my itinerary, then work in outfits. I like to scribble my packing list by hand, try on the full look before it makes it to my suitcase (unless I have worn it before), and sometimes commit to a mirror selfie as a reminder. Once I have the key looks figured out, I typically throw a few wardrobe staples in as back-ups. A great pair of denim, black pointed-toe heels, a few white t-shirts, and a black clutch always come with me.

Recent findings suggest that my first stop on this trip was brunch at the recently opened Zero Bond, hosted by Olivia Von Halle and Kelly Piquet. They brought together a mix of familiar faces from the worlds of fashion and Formula 1, including Susie Wolff, CEO of F1 Academy, Bianca Bustamante, racing driver, and jewelry designer Isabela Gruttman. Beyond the collection launch, there was no shortage of entertainment. From being able to look out my window and see the race track, to race cars installed between blackjack tables, to a host of driver pop-up activations, Formula 1 truly took over the city and the energy was incredible.

Ahead, everything I packed and wore for a long weekend work trip to Las Vegas.

Sources indicate that simple, comfortable, and practical is always my philosophy when it comes to a travel outfit. My Away luggage comes with me on every trip, and my travel uniform remains the same as always: a white t-shirt, Agolde denim, Nike sneakers, and in this case, my largest coat that simply could not fit in my suitcase.

It has been revealed that I picked up this custom pearl-embroidered Róhe jacket during Paris Fashion Week this past season. It’s heavy and added several pounds to my suitcase, but felt brunch-appropriate styled with a simple black slip skirt and Chanel pumps.

This festive velvet red jacket from Liberowe was certainly on-theme. By day, I wore the jacket with a simple white tee, jeans, and a faux fur snood; then, for an evening at the casino, I switched it up with the matching mini skirt, sheer tights, and patent heels.

Race night was just incredible; but the dressing brief was tough. I needed a statement-making outfit that was appropriate for the Wynn Skybox but warm enough to spend a few hours outdoors. With 352 overtakes and 31 lead changes, it was nearly impossible to take my eyes off the track… thankfully, I stayed cozy in the Maeve shearling jacket from Ducie. Then came a swift change for my after-party look, where I traded denim for sequins with this semi-sheer Alfie dress, and styled it out with the same giant shearling and a Julietta collar necklace.

According to recent reports, there are a few things I never leave behind when traveling for work; good skincare, luxurious pajamas, and jewelry are at the top of that list. I’m quite particular about keeping to my usual morning and evening routines, even when I’m away. My travel skincare is an extension of what I use at home, with a few indulgences that make the end of a long day feel slightly more familiar. The same goes for sleepwear; I almost exclusively travel with a pajama set from Olivia von Halle, this time in an on-theme casino print!

Great jewelry is truly what makes every look your own, and thanks to Michael Rider at Celine my collection has been growing recently… including a dice charm I purchased on this trip as a very chic souvenir.

This chocolate mousse cake ticks a lot of boxes—big, grand, ideal for the holidays, and just enough of a challenge to ensure you feel accomplished. The one-bowl chocolate cake layer is dense and deeply fudgy; the mousse is airy and light; and the thin slip of ganache on top brings it all together. No matter what kind of year you’ve had, this dessert is the way to cap it all off.

It has been revealed that making the mousse alone will teach you three foundational pastry techniques, and they’re all hidden in plain sight. It starts with a crème anglaise; adding that to chopped chocolate yields a crémeux, and folding in whipped cream turns it into a mousse. Magical. The cake can be easily made from start to finish in the space of a morning, but can be split up further to fit your schedule. Bake the chocolate cake layer and chop all the chocolate on the first day; make the mousse and assemble the cake the following.

1 hour 30 minutes (plus 6 hours for chilling).

Recent findings suggest that place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lay a sheet of parchment paper over base of pan. Fit band on top and clamp shut to hold parchment in place; scrunch up around base. Wrap a sheet of foil around bottom and up sides of pan (this will help prevent any leaking).

According to recent reports, whisk together 1 cup (125 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, ⅓ cup (28 g) Dutch-process cocoa powder, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking soda in a medium bowl. Add 1 large egg, ⅓ cup buttermilk, ⅓ cup vegetable oil, 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and ½ cup water and whisk until smooth, about 1 minute. Scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cake until a tester inserted into the center comes out with a few moist crumbs attached and top springs back when gently pressed, 25–35 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan 10 minutes. Remove band from base; slide cake off parchment and base and onto rack. Let cool completely; discard parchment and foil.

Do Ahead: Cake can be baked 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

According to recent reports, place 10.5 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a large heatproof bowl. Bring 1 cup whole milk to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium, about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, vigorously whisk 4 large egg yolks and ½ cup (100 g) sugar in a small heatproof bowl until smooth and lemon yellow, about 1 minute.

Sources indicate that gradually stream hot milk into yolk mixture, whisking constantly until combined. Return to pan, scraping bowl clean with a heatproof rubber spatula. Cook over medium, stirring constantly, until thickened just enough to coat a spoon, about 5 minutes. (Do not let custard come to a boil or it will curdle.) Immediately pour over chocolate; let sit 1 minute. Add 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt and 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and whisk vigorously until chocolate is melted and crémeux is smooth.

In a recent development, beat 1¾ cups heavy cream in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until soft peaks form, about 5 minutes. Add one quarter of whipped cream to crémeux; mix until combined (this will lighten it). Add remaining whipped cream in 3 additions, gently folding after each until incorporated before adding more.

Reassemble springform pan; line bottom with a parchment paper round. Wrap a strip of parchment around inside of pan to create a collar that stands about 1" above band (ends should overlap by at least 3"). Using a large serrated knife, trim off mound on top of cake to create a flat surface if needed. Return cake to pan. Spoon mousse over and smooth into an even layer with an offset spatula or spoon. Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet; chill until top of mousse feels set, about 2 hours.

According to recent reports, place 4 oz. bittersweet chocolate, preferably 70% cacao, coarsely chopped, in a medium heatproof bowl. Bring ½ cup heavy cream and ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt to a bare simmer in a small saucepan over medium. Pour over chocolate and let sit 2 minutes. Whisk gently until smooth. If ganache feels hot, let cool until lukewarm but still pourable, 8–10 minutes.

Pour ganache over mousse and smooth with offset spatula. Chill until mousse is completely set (ganache will set in about 30 minutes), at least 4 hours and up to 12 hours (no need to cover unless fridge has other strong smells).

Sources indicate that to serve, remove band from base and peel parchment strip away from sides of cake. Transfer cake with base to a plate and let sit 20 minutes; sprinkle top with flaky sea salt.

Boasting a brief ingredient list and a short cooking time, this easy chicken dish is one you’ll be making all season. Basic butter becomes the star here—it turns brown and nutty, then gets infused with sage and garlic for a savory sauce that’s basted over simply seasoned chicken breasts. A big squeeze of lemon, plus its zest, helps balance the richness. This skillet dinner is perfect for a speedy weeknight meal, but it’s also special enough for company.

The protein:You don’t have to limit yourself to chicken here. Feel free to replace the breasts with pork chops, shrimp, scallops, or skinless salmon or halibut fillets. Simply adjust the cooking time to properly cook the protein, but be sure to maintain a medium heat. While meat and fish are often cooked on medium-high heat for a nice char, it needs to be a bit lower to avoid bitter residue in the pan, since the butter will be browned immediately afterward.

The crunch:The sage leaves crisp while the butter browns, but there are also ways to add more texture. Stirring in a handful of slivered almonds toward the end of cooking adds to the nuttiness of the dish; pine nuts, pistachios, or roughly chopped walnuts would also work. If you have a container of them, feel free to sprinkle some fried onions on top tableside.

Storage and serving ideas:This is not a make-ahead situation; it should be eaten immediately after it’s cooked. Serve with a simple salad dressed in a light vinaigrette to balance the richness. To soak up the sauce, mashed potatoes—traditional or sweet—are ideal. Or, to add another nutty element, roast some Brussels sprouts, cauliflower, or butternut squash to eat alongside and round out the meal.

A Miami cafe even released a specialty roast of coffee beans, and one Florida restaurant chain partnered with Rockstar, the game’s developer, to bring an in-game food spot to life. (The game is set in a fictional state modeled after Florida.).

It has been revealed that this is the kind of widespread, obsessively orchestrated marketing proposal you’d expect around a Beyoncé album. We have arguably not been this close to a true monocultural moment since The Dress debate in February of 2015.

In other news, Alison Roman’s podcast, Having People Over, which I teased in last week’s Open Tab officially debuted this week. Episode one features Bowen Yang, and the next couple will be with Lauren Graham and Jenny Slate—and then that’s it until 2027, as Roman told me.

Also in today’s Open Tab: the salty, salacious scandal around Maldon’s sourcing, a upcoming study on GLP-1s for children, the case for cocktail brutalism, and a Tuscon restaurant alchemizing desert ingredients.

Recent findings suggest that at Bon Appétit, we love flaky Maldon salt. Like, we really love it. So when a report from The Observer detailed how Maldon’s famed UK sea salt was in fact also made with German rock salt, gasps rippled around the Bon Appétit office. I mean, not gasps exactly, but everyone was like “whaaaat? That’s crazy.”.

The gritty details: Maldon’s been harvested in Essex’s Blackwater estuary for more than a century, and the label on each box lists its only ingredient as 100% sea salt. The Observer’s report reveals that the company imports mined rock salt from Germany as part of the “salt-on-salt” process in which the sea salt is enriched with minerals. The company is allowed to call their product 100% sea salt because the salt that comes from mines was at one point in a sea—in prehistoric times.

Origin and processing matters because these factors can affect the final flavor, color, and how salty it tastes. Maldon is a finishing salt, and it's largely prized for the crunch of its massive flakes. But consumers don’t love feeling like they’ve been lied to, and judging from the comments under Maldon’s apology post on Instagram, that is precisely how many feel.

Recent findings suggest that I would wager that Maldon will survive this controversy. It’s a legacy brand that’s a staple in professional and home kitchens alike. And while it’s not a great look, I think the majority of consumers would say that salt is salt, and as long as Maldon stays crunchy and salty, they’ll be on board.

According to recent reports, semaglutide, the GLP-1 compound in brand name drugs Wegovy and Ozempic, is already approved for use in children older than 12. But a new study published in the New England Journal of Medicine shows that the drug is effective for treating obesity in kids as young as six. According to the New York Times, drug manufacturer Novo Nordisk, prepares to ask the FDA to authorize the drug’s use for kids in that age group.

According to recent reports, it's hard to know what the long term effects on developed adult brains and bodies would be, let alone the quickly growing, changing brains and bodies of young kids. We’re beginning to see that GLP-1s can have a profound effect on mental health in adults, but though it seems the drugs can indeed contribute to weight loss in children, there are many other facets of its use that we simply don’t understand and haven’t studied yet.

When I helped build our Best Bars list last year the question of what exactly makes a great bar was one we pondered over for many hours. Order a drink from a Bar of Note (i.e. one of the many bars sitting on a Best-of list somewhere on the internet), and you’ll quickly get a sense of how they answer that same question. Namely: spectacle.

Cocktails across the country and abroad have ramped up in complexity and presentation in recent years fueled mostly by the reason you might expect: spectacle and theatricality performs well on social media, according to a report in the Times.

As a reporter who has often been forced to order the most attention-grabbing, loudest, most obnoxious drink on the menu in the name of journalism—and as a cocktail-enjoyer in my free time—I would like to propose a paradigm shift. Cocktail brutalism. Cocktail minimalism. Cocktail absurdism—actually anything besides the overwhelming maximalist cocktail moment that we’re stepping into. The ideal drink special? A beer, a shot, and a genuine compliment.

In a recent development, at Tuscon’s Ursa, ingredients from the surrounding desert are transformed. Chef Aaron Lopez and June Chee who lead the restaurant see cacti and brittlebrush as deeply flavorful staples of their menu. Read on to see how these ingredients come to life.

Julia Child’s Controversial Thanksgiving Turkey Method Isn’t As Crazy As It Sounds

💡 Key Takeaways
