  • It has been revealed that julia Child had a marvelous way of making even the most intimidating cooking techniques seem entirely within reach.
  • Most of us have spent our lives roasting the bird whole, partly because that’s how it’s always been done and partly because a beautifully browned turkey makes such a magnificent centerpiece on a holiday table.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Julia Child's solution to a common turkey dilemma was equal parts culinary brilliance and holiday theater.

It has been revealed that julia Child had a marvelous way of making even the most intimidating cooking techniques seem entirely within reach. She was a brilliant cook, a gifted teacher, and a woman who understood that a little butter could solve an astonishing number of problems. But perhaps her greatest talent was her willingness to question the rules, even when those rules involved one of America’s most beloved holiday traditions.

Take Thanksgiving turkey. Most of us have spent our lives roasting the bird whole, partly because that’s how it’s always been done and partly because a beautifully browned turkey makes such a magnificent centerpiece on a holiday table. Julia, however, recognized a rather inconvenient flaw in this arrangement: A whole turkey is not well designed for even cooking.

According to recent reports, her solution was ingenious. She took the turkey apart, cooked its individual pieces, and then put the whole thing back together again for presentation. It was a triumph of culinary common sense, with just enough theatrical flair to make the whole thing unmistakably Julia.

Julia called her creation the “re-assembled roast turkey,” a technique she shared in her cookbook, The Way to Cook. Rather than wrestling an entire bird into the oven and hoping for the best, she removed the backbone, separated the leg and thigh portions, and roasted the breast on a bed of stuffing while the dark meat cooked in another pan.

According to recent reports, once everything was properly cooked, she arranged the pieces together on a serving platter, restoring the turkey to something resembling its original form. In her recipe, Julia cheerfully suggested that nobody would ever know the difference.

In a 2012 NPR Thanksgiving segment, Christopher Kimball, who had cooked alongside Julia, demonstrated the method with host Renee Montagne. The two had a wonderful time discussing the reconstructed bird, which they affectionately dubbed “Frankenturkey.” It wasn’t quite traditional, but that was rather the point. Julia had found a way to preserve the spectacle of a whole roasted turkey without actually having to cook one.

It has been revealed that the trouble with roasting a whole turkey is that its various parts have very different needs. The breast is lean and can become dry and stringy when overcooked, while the legs and thighs contain more fat and connective tissue, and generally benefit from cooking to a higher internal temperature. Getting everything just right at the same time is a challenge, even for experienced cooks.

Breaking down the turkey solves much of that problem. With the pieces separated, you can monitor their temperatures individually and remove them as they finish cooking. The dark meat has time to become tender without drying out the breast, and heat circulates more efficiently around the smaller pieces, reducing the overall roasting time.

It has been revealed that it’s a method we’ve championed at Taste of Home. Our guide to cooking a deconstructed turkey outlines the process of breaking down the bird, roasting the individual pieces and getting beautifully crisp skin. You can even ask your butcher to handle the disassembly if you’d rather not begin Thanksgiving morning with a pair of poultry shears.

And there’s another advantage Julia certainly appreciated: With the backbone removed, you’ve already got a head start on making a rich turkey stock for the gravy.

Of course, there’s no requirement that you follow Julia all the way through to the reconstruction. You can simply arrange the carved meat on a serving platter and bring it to the table. But I do love that Julia went to the trouble of putting her turkey back together. She understood that Thanksgiving dinner is as much about tradition and presentation as it is about good cooking, and she found a wonderfully clever way to have both.

The result was better-tasting turkey that still got its moment of glory on the table. And if anyone could make taking a turkey apart and putting it back together seem like the most sensible thing in the world, it was Julia Child.

The Secret to the Creamiest Mac and Cheese Comes in a Can

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (583 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that making a truly excellent bowl of mac and cheese shouldn't take an entire afternoon.
  • In a recent development, I’ve made enough macaroni and cheese over the years to have developed some fairly strong opinions about it.
  • In a recent development, which is why I’m particularly fond of a method that requires just three ingredients: pasta, grated cheese and evaporated milk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

It has been revealed that making a truly excellent bowl of mac and cheese shouldn't take an entire afternoon. Here's the one ingredient I rely on to get the creamiest cheese sauce every time.

In a recent development, I’ve made enough macaroni and cheese over the years to have developed some fairly strong opinions about it. Having two kids has given me plenty of opportunities to experiment, from throwing together the familiar blue box to baking versions that require several kinds of cheese and a considerable amount of attention. I appreciate a proper cheese sauce as much as anyone, but there are evenings when dirtying another saucepan to make a roux and standing over the stove with a whisk feels like an unreasonable amount of ceremony for a bowl of macaroni.

In a recent development, which is why I’m particularly fond of a method that requires just three ingredients: pasta, grated cheese and evaporated milk. It produces an exceptionally creamy mac and cheese without butter, flour or any of the usual fuss, and it’s so simple that even boxed mac begins to look complicated.

In a recent development, evaporated milk is regular milk that’s been heated until about 60% of its water is gone. The result is thicker and more concentrated than ordinary milk, with a richness that makes it especially useful for cheese sauces.

According to recent reports, more importantly, those concentrated milk proteins help the cheese melt into a smooth, cohesive sauce. Ordinarily, adding cheese directly to hot liquid can be a temperamental business. The fat may separate, the proteins can tighten up, and the sauce can become grainy instead of silky. Evaporated milk helps keep everything together, doing much of the work that a traditional flour-and-butter roux would otherwise accomplish.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

One of the things I like most about this method is how little precision it demands. If you’re cooking a pound of macaroni, start with a 12-ounce can of evaporated milk and roughly 12 to 16 ounces of grated cheese. Sharp cheddar provides plenty of flavor, while Monterey Jack or fontina will give you a smooth melt. I generally prefer a combination, but there’s no reason to make a special trip to the store if you already have a perfectly good block of cheese in the refrigerator.

In a recent development, I do recommend grating the cheese yourself, since the anti-caking ingredients in bagged shredded cheese can keep it from melting smoothly. Beyond that, there’s plenty of room for flexibility. There’s no need to measure everything down to the last ounce, which is part of what makes this method so wonderful.

Lindsay Parrill For Taste Of Home.

Boil the pasta in generously salted water as you normally would, then strain it and return it to the pot, reserving about a cup of pasta water. Add the cheese and evaporated milk, warming them gently over low heat. Keep stirring until everything melts into a smooth sauce, adding splashes of pasta water as you go until it reaches your desired consistency.

The same trick works beautifully in more elaborate recipes, whether you’re making a baked southern mac and cheese, a big pan of potluck mac and cheese or a comforting crockpot mac and cheese. All have their merits, but for an ordinary weeknight, I rather like knowing that one pot, three ingredients, and about as much time as it takes to boil pasta are all I need.

For Malin Åkerman, ‘The Hunting Wives’ Is (Still) a Dream Come True

💡 Key Takeaways

  • “She was just a young, stupid girl who fell in love, and it was really wrong.
  • It has been revealed that some of that sympathy also exists in the way Åkerman plays the audacious, gun-toting, bisexual Texas queen Margo Banks in Netflix’s The Hunting Wives, based on May Cobb’s novel, which returns for season two this week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that “Girl, that one’s always a good one,” Malin Åkerman states. I’ve just told her how many times I’ve rewatched her 2008 rom-com 27 Dresses, in which she played the charming, wedding dress-and-crush-stealing Tess, younger sister to Katherine Heigl’s responsible Jane. Tess is, in my view, one of the great 2000s-era villains—though Åkerman doesn’t see her as such.

“She was just a young, stupid girl who fell in love, and it was really wrong. That’s your sister’s crush. Don’t do that, girl. Not cool.” She laughs. “But there was a life lesson in it, and she learned and she grew from it. It’s less villain, more just human.”.

It has been revealed that some of that sympathy also exists in the way Åkerman plays the audacious, gun-toting, bisexual Texas queen Margo Banks in Netflix’s The Hunting Wives, based on May Cobb’s novel, which returns for season two this week. Margo has done some bad things, but she’s certainly looked good doing ’em—and former Democratic campaign strategist Sophie (Brittany Snow) can’t help but be drawn into her orbit. Their Bonnie-and-Clyde love story continues in the new season, and the stakes have never been higher.

Here, Åkerman talks to Vogue about the Margos in her own life, performing with Snow at the Las Culturistas Culture Awards, and why it’s the perfect time to watch a show about lesbians in Texas.

Vogue: It’s a great time to be releasing a show about Texas.

Malin Åkerman: It’s unbelievable. There was a great little picture, Dermot [Mulroney] sent it to us gals, and it was like, “The Hunting Wives Turns Texas Votes,” or something like that. All the lesbians came out [to vote]. I’m going to misquote it, but it’s out there.

Do you think there’s a future where Jed loses the governor race to–.

…I was going to say, to Margo Banks? Maybe she takes over, the Lady Macbeth in the back just pulling all the strings.

That could be really fun if he has someone that he’s up against, a powerful female that maybe Margo has an affair with. Let’s see.

In a recent development, season two shows us a different side of Margo—she’s in a more vulnerable state. I’m curious what you thought of her season two arc. Where do you think her mindset is at the beginning of the show?

Industry observers note that it’s really nice to see the power dynamic shift. Sophie came into her power and Margo’s softening and actually letting someone in, which is huge for a person like Margo, who has been a survivor and keeps everyone at an arm’s length. You see these cracks in her veneer that she’s created for her whole life, really. We start off in a pretty bad place for Margo in season two. She’s in the doghouse, so to speak. She does not like being there.

I loved playing with her vulnerability and really just softening, enveloped in Sophie’s love and protection. That was really nice because I just don’t think that Margo has ever really had that other than [from] her brother, in a weird way, who was the only person that she trusted. I feel like we finally get to see her trusting someone else. Because she doesn’t really trust Jed, that’s just a means to an end. She knows how to play him, she knows how to do her thing to get what she needs.

Recent findings suggest that the Margo–Jed relationship is interesting this season. He acts like a man with power but he is also very vulnerable to her charms. What kind of discussions were you and Dermot having?

All men in power are vulnerable to women if they know how to play their cards right. You know what I mean? There are those women out there who know exactly how to get the guys, they know exactly the buttons to push. Dermot and I, we have a lot of fun conversations. We never like it when we have to play angry at each other because we really love each other. All of us, by the way, on this show, we hate when we have to hate each other. But Dermot and I definitely have much more fun when we get to be in love, so to speak. I don’t think Margo actually loves Jed, but it was fun to have those moments.

Sources indicate that I just love playing Margo and all her agendas behind everything and trying to play it as real as possible, especially with Jed, because she’s really a player. She’s got Sophie on the side [while she’s] telling Jed that he’s everything. Yeah, Dermot and I have a lot of fun. Mostly we just goof around on set, to be really honest with you.

Well, you guys do have a rom-com that’s coming out in a few weeks.

Sources indicate that listen, Dermot asked me when we were on set—it was the last couple weeks of shooting [season one], it was his last day of shooting. He’s like, “I’m about to go do this rom-com on a cruise.” And I was like, “Nope, not doing it, never. I don’t ever want to go on a cruise, it’s not my thing. Too claustrophobic. Don’t want to be on for three weeks. Are you nuts?” And he goes, “Well, the first week it would just be us and you can bring your family and it’ll become this free vacation.” I was like, “Oh, okay. When do we start?” And he goes, “Four days after you wrap this show.” It’s like, Oh my God. But it was my son’s summer break, so I ended up convincing a girlfriend of mine, one of my best girlfriends who’s also a makeup artist, to come along with her kids on the trip. I don’t know how it’s going to turn out, but we had a blast making it.

It has been revealed that we had a little too much fun. We were like, “Is there even a movie in this? I don’t know, but we’re having a great time.”.

Sources indicate that I’m a big Dale Dickey fan, and she plays a fun role in this season. What was it like filming with her?

In a recent development, she’s phenomenal on every level. She’s a phenomenal human being—the nicest, loveliest human you’ll ever meet and a phenomenal actress. I remember seeing her in Winter’s Bone and just going, “Wow, this woman is just great.” And what a face—the realism in the expressions. And she’s just beautiful to watch when she works and she really is invested. She believes in her craft and she’s so collaborative and lovely. All the greatest things you can say about a person, I would say about Dale Dickey.

Dale Dickey as Zelda and Cam Gigandet as Gentle John in Episode 204 of The Hunting Wives.

Thinking about Margo and Sophie this season, they’re both killers, so they can be on a more even playing field. But Sophie does have this secret at the beginning of the season….

Industry observers note that the audience question is, do they really love each other? And listen, that’s an open-ended question. There’s no real answer to that. I think there is love there, for sure. I think on Sophie’s part towards Margo, it’s almost an extension of her addictive personality. Margo’s an addiction. Margo fluctuates between necessity and love because Margo’s just not honest with herself. She’s not open, honest, and vulnerable, so you can’t be that with someone else.

I felt like there were parts of this season where Sophie was scarier than Margo.

In a recent development, totally. You let the beast out and you’re like, Holy shit, she needs something. She’s going to get it. That’s also what attracts these two to each other, is that drive. You get to see why they’re kind of meant for each other in this season. It’s not just Margo. Margo’s not just the crazy one and the wild one. Sophie’s got it in her, she just needs to be unleashed.

Industry observers note that have you had a Margo type in your life, or have you been that type? Someone who draws you into their orbit or brings out something in you that you’re like, Oh, I love being around this person?

It has been revealed that yeah, sure. I mean, I think it’s gone both ways. I think I’ve been in the shoes of a Margo and I’ve been attracted to it. I had a little bit of a fun time in between marriages, so to speak, and there were definitely people who were absolutely wrong for me, but I was very drawn in. Also knowing they were wrong for me, but just couldn’t get enough…it’s such a wild experience. And then I also played the part of drawing people in and just using them for what I needed. I knew it wasn’t going to become a relationship, and just having fun with it almost felt…I don’t know, it was a great time. I understand why Margo is having a great time, but [I haven’t experienced] anywhere near the extent of the deception and the games that she plays. But the draw, I can understand that, where there’s just this sexual energy that pulls you in.

Brittany Snow and Akerman in Episode 205 of The Hunting Wives.

In a recent development, after season one, there was some time where you weren’t totally sure if Hunting Wives was getting picked up again. Now you have a season three renewal already locked in. How does it feel to have that kind of stability?

In a recent development, it’s a fucking dream come true, it really is. I feel so, so lucky. I love this character, it’s a character of a lifetime. I love the people I get to work with. I couldn’t have wished for it…and it’s a steady job. If this goes for 10 years, I’ll be elated. Although maybe we can make Margo just chill a little bit on the working out and looking top-notch all the time, and tanned and everything. Maybe she just lets herself go a little. Let me just enjoy my pizza and my pasta on a daily basis, okay guys? Let’s not judge.

Do you know when you’ll go back for season three?

I’m flying out to Atlanta on November 29. We get started December 2. We’re premiering [season two] and then off we go, Season 3. I’m excited. I miss my Hunting Wives family.

I loved your and Brittany’s performance at the Las Culturistas Culture Awards. How did that come about?

Well, Bowen Yang was sat in front of us at the Emmys, where we ended up surprisingly presenting. We weren’t supposed to present, and so he was with us on that journey. It was so much fun. We were like, “Bowen, we have to present.” He’s like, “What? Right now?” He’s such a lovely person. From that, maybe that seed was planted in his head. We met Matt Rogers as well, and they’re such a great duo. They were the ones who came to us and said, “We have an idea. Hunting Wives and Heated Rivalry have been such a huge hit in the LGBTQ community that it would be really fun to do this, to have you guys open the whole ceremony.” We were super game for that. Like, “Okay, we’ll wear the hockey jerseys, but we need to bring in the Hunting Wives into it all.”.

Sources indicate that do you think there is any kind of connective tissue that links The Hunting Wives and Heated Rivalry’s success beyond the queer relationships? Do you think there’s anything that both highlights have in common?

Sources indicate that I think it’s the forbiddenness of it all. That’s always something that we’re all drawn to because I think we all have our own secret thoughts that we don’t share with everybody. We all have our own fantasies, we all have our own things that we lust [over]. These highlights kind of open them up. Heated Rivalry has a more important message in a way, because this is really something that the author was talking about. Being in such a macho world as hockey is, that’s a really brave thing, to come out publicly and to have a relationship publicly within that. I loved it, I thought it was really beautiful.

It has been revealed that it’s different from Hunting Wives because Hunting Wives is…we’re a little more on the camp side. We’re true just raw entertainment and craziness, but we have that element of exploring sexuality in a town, in a world, where it’s frowned upon.

I’m sure that Margo and Sophie will be some people’s queer awakening in the years to come.

I sure hope so. Bring it on. Come on out, everybody. It’s a great place to be.

In a recent development, when you think back to when you were in maybe your early or mid-20s, were you dreaming of projects like this? What kind of arc did you want your career to have when you were very young?

Oh, gosh. Early 20s, I didn’t know what I wanted more than five minutes ahead of me. I was not one of those people who was planning ahead and goal-oriented. I was along for the ride. I really was letting life take me. I got swept away in this romantic-comedy film era with 27 Dresses and Heartbreak Kid and Couples Retreat. I was just enjoying every moment of it, not thinking about, Oh, this can come to an end.

According to recent reports, after a few of those romantic comedies, I really started craving something that I could sink my teeth into a little more and to try my hand at drama. I started seeking out little independent films, which is something that I love watching: the little indies or foreign films. That’s when I remember The Ticket came along with Dan Stevens, and Billions came along—I feel like that’s a precursor to Margo Banks, Lara Axelrod.

Hunting Wives came at the perfect time because I had had that moment during COVID and after, where there were a lot of projects that were, I call them “yes projects.” I was saying yes because I needed to work, but I wasn’t feeling passionate about them anymore and it was really making me sad. I felt like projects that I really wanted to do, I couldn’t get in the room, and I started to have a lot of, I call them “head gremlins” talking to me, dark voices in my head. The voices telling me, Yeah, this is it. You’re expired. I mean, you had a good run. Say thank you, feel grateful. I just went, No.

It has been revealed that for the past five years I’ve been working on my true passion project. Won’t say anything yet, but hopefully it’ll come to fruition. It’s something that I’ve built from the ground up and it’s written, I’ve got a director attached. We just need to get out there and get it made. But other than that, when Hunting Wives came along, it just felt like, oh, this was the hit that I really needed as far as getting passionate again about the work that I’m doing, because I just love this character and this job. It was incredible to not only be passionate about a character, but to feel relevant in my business again.

Do you think your definition of success has changed over the years?

I do think so. Becoming a parent changed all of that. Success for me, really, the most important success is the success of my family. And in business, I feel like I look back and I go, I’ve had a great career and how lucky am I if it continues? This is wonderful. So I’m happy for this show to have its success because all the people who are in it are so deserving. But success is a really…for me, it’s not linked to my work anymore. It really is linked to, am I successful as a person? Am I succeeding in my day-to-day life? Am I handling life well? In your 20s we talk a lot about being successful and a lot of it is linked to work. And then as we grow older and we realize what’s really important, then it shifts.

I’ve been asking myself those questions a lot lately, like, how do you define yourself outside of work?

Sources indicate that exactly. And that success is, how do people see you and how are you presenting to the world? Have you succeeded in becoming the person that you want to be, the best version of you? And where’s the work still need to be done? I have a 13-year-old boy who still wants to cuddle me at night and tells me he loves me [when I] drop him off at school. He is like, “Bye, Mom. Love you. See you later.” Thirteen. I’m like, “I have succeeded. This is a huge success.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, cook fillets and oil from two 2-oz.
  • long pasta (such as linguine or spaghetti) in a large pot of boiling salted water until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that even those who swear they don’t like anchovies should be willing to take a “no thank-you” portion of this pasta. Sizzled with garlic, the tiny fish melt into a briny sauce that’s similar to bagna cauda, the warm Northern Italian dip whose savory quality comes from remarked anchovies. Instead of serving alongside crudités, toss this sauce with hot long pasta like linguine or spaghetti. No extra vegetables or protein needed, but I wouldn’t kick a salad with beans and bitter-slanting greens (kale, radicchio) off the table.

More weeknight-friendly pasta dinners this way.

In a recent development, cook fillets and oil from two 2-oz. tins oil-packed anchovy fillets, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven over medium-low heat, breaking up fillets with a wooden spoon or heatproof rubber spatula, until anchovies are melted and mixture is bubbling, about 2 minutes. Add 6 garlic cloves, finely grated, and cook, stirring often, until fragrant, about 30 seconds. Remove pan from heat.

Cook 12 oz. long pasta (such as linguine or spaghetti) in a large pot of boiling salted water until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions. Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Gradually pour 1 cup pasta cooking liquid into anchovy mixture in pan, whisking constantly to incorporate. Place pan over high heat and bring sauce to a simmer. Add pasta and cook, tossing vigorously with tongs, until pasta is al dente and sauce is slightly thickened, about 2 minutes.

Remove pasta from heat and add 3 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces. Toss until butter is melted and pasta is coated and glossy, about 45 seconds. Add 1 cup coarsely chopped parsley, 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice and toss to combine, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep pasta saucy. Divide among shallow bowls to serve.

I Tested Peloton's Upcoming, More Affordable Folding Treadmill

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1683 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in my mind and, I think the minds of many others, Peloton has always been a stationary bike brand.
  • Industry observers note that nevertheless, Peloton actually has been making treadmills since 2018.
  • The fresh Tread Flex, however, heads in a slightly different direction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in my mind and, I think the minds of many others, Peloton has always been a stationary bike brand. The Bike, after all, was its first product, turning the Peloton name into a catch-all term for at-home cycling that we now hear everywhere, from broadcasts of the Tour de France and Giro d'Italia to television sitcoms. (A running gag online is that Peloton's upscale, soothing video workout content is worlds away from The Office's Dwight Schrute leading a group of stationary riders off an imaginary cliff.).

Industry observers note that nevertheless, Peloton actually has been making treadmills since 2018. The first Tread delivered the same proposition as the Bike: premium hardware that looks good enough to bring out of the basement, as well as access to interactive, instructor-led runs and HIIT classes on a big, immersive screen. Over the years, Peloton has brought improvements to that first Tread: larger screens, voice controls, AI-informed movement tracking for form analysis and coaching.

The fresh Tread Flex, however, heads in a slightly different direction. It has a simpler belt, simpler speakers, a smaller screen. It's $1,300 cheaper than the next step up, and $4,500 cheaper (!) than Peloton's slat belt-equipped Tread+ Vision. Its affordability isn't even its main selling point, however, because the Tread Flex has a nifty final trick: it folds up to save space.

Industry observers note that could these space and money-saving tactics make the Tread as popular as the Bike? Well, I run nearly every day, and ever since a tester Tread Flex showed up at my door, I've been doing it indoors much more frequently. In my experience, here's what makes Peloton's latest worth considering.

Treadmills tend to have a problem that stationary bikes don't: the nicer they get, the bigger they get. Premium models have larger motors and roomier running platforms. In short, they're heavy. (The Tread+ Vision is a hefty 460 pounds.) The Tread Flex is 170 pounds less, and that's crucial to its ability to fold up, because that feature wouldn't be much of a selling point if it felt like adding a power clean to the end of every run.

In reality, stowing the Tread Flex is quite easy. You just lift up the running deck from the end and push it forward until a hydraulic cylinder locks into place. There's a pin clip to lock it. To drop it down, you push forward on the deck and then on the hydraulic support, then walk it back. At about 45 degrees, the hydraulics take over completely; you can go put on your running shoes while a gentle thump lets you know the deck is back on the ground.

Folding up the Tread Flex drops its area from about 16.5 square feet to half that. (The Tread+ Vision is around 19.25.) Just as importantly, I've discovered, is that lifting the deck brings the machine up onto a set of locking wheels. I've kept mine in a designated corner, but it's so easy to move that it wouldn't be much hassle to wheel it out and lower it for every workout, if your space required it. Get your cardio out of the way, then get your cardio out of the way.

In a recent development, okay, so folding and moving a treadmill might be a pain if you're using it every day. But I suspect if you're running that often, you're doing some of it outside. I live less than an hour away from the Canadian border, and run on roads and trails five or six times a week all year round. Good layers get you pretty far, and there's a reason why run clubs continue to boom while SoulCycle-adjacent Mile High Run Club closed all its studios this year.

Sources indicate that treadmills are for something else. They're for a warm-up prior to lifting, or for bootcamp-style HIIT workouts that combine sprinting intervals with weight intervals. The prioritization value of time spent doing these doesn't seem to align with the space investment a treadmill requires if you don't have a pool house or significant garage. (I have a sun porch-slash-mudroom where I keep firewood and ski boots in the winter and a napping couch in the summer.).

Recent findings suggest that this is how, I think, the Tread Flex makes the ultimate proposition as the ideal home treadmill. A treadmill doesn't replace a usual running routine; it adds to it. On Monday I do my usual seven miles down the road and back on the river trails; on Tuesday I let Andy Speer kick my ass with sprints and kickstand deadlifts. (And, sure, when it's -10° and blowing in late January, I might run inside, now that I have the option.).

Sources indicate that none of the above would matter as much if it came at the cost of quality. I've run on hotel treadmills that sound like your grandma's washing machine and feel similar to how they look, i.e., stomping around on hollow plastic. The Tread Flex may not have the cushioned slat belt the Tread+ Vision has, but it's definitely not that.

Recent findings suggest that what it does have is a spec that's right in line with top-notch treadmills. Its max speed is 12.5 miles per hour (a 4:48 mile, in runner's units), a 12.5% max incline grade (but no decline), and a 20-inch by 59-inch running surface that, though not cushioned, feels good to run on. The swiveling screen is nice and massive at 21.5 inches, with HD resolution and a touchscreen interface. I particularly like how adjusting speed and incline is done with rolling knobs, which feel much better—and more natural—to engage with than buttons when you're gasping at threshold pace.

Industry observers note that on top of that is Peloton's interactive experience: You can take live classes where you can pit yourself against others and get kudos from the instructor. The pre-recorded catalogue includes thousands of classes for yoga, Pilates, and meditation, in addition to strength and the running, cycling, and rowing the company makes machines for.

Recent findings suggest that the Tread Flex also provides personalized training plans, smart pacing guidance based on where you're at, automatically adjusting incline for classes, and of course leaderboards and an entire ecosystem of badges and achievements to earn, if you're into all that. For $50 per year, that is.

It has been revealed that oh, and did I mention it's a good-looking machine? It's sleek; an attractive, soft-edged Z with a minimal screen instead of a board of colorful buttons. Nobody's throwing around the word "console" to describe this thing. That's good; home gym setups deserve different consideration than gym rigs. If images of Crunch Fitness flash through your head every time you glance into the corner, something has missed the mark.

Where Peloton's Tread Vision treadmills are clearly high-end, the Tread Flex toes the line against mainstream consumer models. Its features match up with some of the most popular machines, and its price, while at the higher end of the spectrum, does too. But the Tread Flex gets there with more style, and with Peloton's huge ecosystem of live and archived class content.

So, if we're looking at other treadmills out there, my quick answer is yes. The Tread Flex is the utilitarian Peloton Treadmill, but it's still a Peloton treadmill.

Industry observers note that how you answer this question really requires asking yourself a series of other questions first. What do you want a treadmill for? How much do you want to invest? Do you want access to fitness classes—especially ones other than running—and are you okay with the $50/month subscription fee?

Form factor and access to classes and content are non-negotiables. The Tread Flex might be Peloton's new entry-level treadmill, but it's far from a simple running machine. Flex refers to that nifty fold-up feature, but also to this treadmill's ability to integrate into an exercise program that also includes strength training, HIIT workouts, yoga, and on and on.

As a runner who prefers to log miles outside whenever possible, I was encouraged by how much I enjoyed running on the Tread Flex. The classes are fun, and Peloton's instructors are real pros, but even in Just Run mode, the Tread Flex proved responsive and comfy. It's getting dark around 4:30 PM these days, and my daylight windows for running on the well-used roads around me have narrowed like a Death Star trash compactor. It's nice to know I can snag seven miles after sundown if need be.

Sources indicate that well, if you aren't limited by space or cash, the Tread Vision and Tread+ Vision get you bigger screens, AI-enabled running form feedback and coaching, and a more cushioned, broader running area. If you just prefer running or walking on a treadmill to doing it outside, investing more heavily in a treadmill is worth considering (though the Tread Flex will still be great).

The Tread Flex's real competition is the NordicTrack Commercial 1750, which you'll find recommended on just about every treadmill buying guide on the internet. The machines are similar in function and specs, but there are some differences. The NordicTrack's running surface is two inches wider and one inch longer; it has a slightly more powerful motor; it can decline to -3% grade; its belt is slightly cushioned; it has a built-in fan; and NordicTrack's class and entertainment platform, iFit, is cheaper at $39 a month.

In comparison, the Tread Flex takes up slightly less space, has a higher max speed (12.5 mph over 12 mph), a steeper incline (12.5% over 12%), and a larger screen (21.5 inches over 16 inches). The rolling knobs to adjust speed and incline are nicer to use. My partner, who designs commercial and residential interior spaces, agrees with me that the Tread Flex is a better-looking machine.

List price for the Tread Flex is $300 cheaper, but the NordicTrack seems to be perpetually on sale. So it might come down to looks, that 3% decline, or what class platform you'd like to buy into.

This Egg Wash Secret Makes the Prettiest Pie Crusts Every Time

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that thanksgiving pies have a way of bringing out the perfectionist in even the most relaxed bakers.
  • An egg wash is supposed to give pastry a lovely golden color and delicate sheen, but getting it to cooperate isn’t always as simple as beating an egg and picking up a pastry brush.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

The secret to a beautifully golden Thanksgiving pie might be the simplest ingredient in your kitchen.

Sources indicate that thanksgiving pies have a way of bringing out the perfectionist in even the most relaxed bakers. Yet you might spend half an hour creating the perfect pie dough design, carefully crimping the edges or cutting little leaves from scraps of pastry, only to pull the finished pie from the oven and discover that your beautiful handiwork has browned unevenly. It’s a small disappointment in the grand scheme of things, but after all that effort, a little indignation is understandable.

An egg wash is supposed to give pastry a lovely golden color and delicate sheen, but getting it to cooperate isn’t always as simple as beating an egg and picking up a pastry brush. Fortunately, there’s an easy trick that makes a noticeable difference, and it comes courtesy of a familiar face in the baking world: Great British Baking Show judge Paul Hollywood.

Paul’s secret is simply to add a pinch of salt to the beaten egg. He lets it sit for about five minutes before brushing it onto pastry dough. In a BBC Food demonstration, Paul uses the technique to glaze scones, but it works just as well for giving pie crusts a beautiful, even finish.

Industry observers note that beat an egg with a small pinch of salt until they’re well combined, then set the mixture aside for a few minutes. Give it another quick stir before brushing a thin, even layer over the pastry. The amount of salt won’t affect the flavor, and there’s no reason to make any other adjustments to your favorite pie recipe.

It has been revealed that the difference is subtle but useful. Instead of clinging stubbornly to your pastry brush or collecting in the little crevices of a crimped edge, the egg wash spreads more easily.

Emiko Franzen For Taste Of Home.

According to recent reports, if you’ve ever tried brushing a plain beaten egg onto pastry, you’ve probably noticed that it can be surprisingly thick and stringy. That’s because the proteins in the egg give it structure—a nuisance if you need to spread it evenly. Adding salt loosens those proteins, making the egg wash thinner and more fluid after a few minutes. It glides over the pastry more smoothly, leaving a light, even coating rather than stringy puddles.

It has been revealed that the egg itself is what gives pastry its golden color and glossy sheen. Salt doesn’t make the crust magically browner; it simply helps the egg wash do its job better. The result is a more consistent finish, particularly around the edges and decorative details where egg wash tends to collect.

A pinch of salt won’t turn a lopsided pie into a masterpiece, but it can help a well-made crust look its best. And after we’ve spent an unreasonable amount of time weaving strips of pastry into a lattice for a Thanksgiving pie, I think we’re entitled to a little help with the finishing touches.

Sides are the true stars of Thanksgiving dinner. With so many delicious options to choose from, it's nearly impossible to pick just a few favorites. Interiors, and interiority, are recurring subjects of Charlotte Eskildsen’s collections for The Garment. For pre-fall, the designer imagined a woman living in a townhouse in central Copenhagen near the Marble Church, a very chic area, who wears clothes in “her own really private way... Nothing in this collection is too tied up,” the designer noted. “Even if it’s suiting, it will stretch, and it’s comfortable to wear.”.

In a recent development, some of the garments have a feeling of intimacy that comes from their origin in the boudoir. Lingerie dressing is a trend that Eskildsen isn’t ready to give up as she sees it as an expression of femininity that counters the outward strength often expected of women. So next to a lace-trimmed skirt with an asymmetrically inserted godet and a collarless jacket, the many slip dresses in the collection looked somewhat saccharine and less street-ready than the more structured looks. She’s “dressed, but she doesn’t know if she wants to go out or not,” the designer mentioned of her muse. (This cozy, hazy should-I-or-shouldn’t-I feeling assumes win-win options.).

In betweenness is at the heart of all pre-fall collections which need to adapt to snow and sun. For cooler temps there is a smart cropped black leather jacket shown with tailored white pants. An injection of romance comes in the form of a flowy Daisy Buchanan-ish dress the color of a snowflake with bias cut lines which combines silk chiffon, jacquard, and silk wool. There are “a lot of cut lines to be able to mix all the fabrics so it’s like a blanket of different fabrics,” as Eskildsen put it. Hygge, in other words, but make it haute.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Whole wheat flour provides structure plus fiber, while brown rice flour helps the biscuits bake up crisp.
  • It has been revealed that I like Gouda for its aroma—it drives my dog into a frenzy—but sharp cheddar or Swiss will work too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These homemade dog treats are crunchy, cheesy, and enthusiastically approved by my little curmudgeon. The recipe began with a dog biscuit from the December 2005 matter of Gourmet. While the generous quantities of butter, brown sugar, and salt in the original gave me pause, I used it as inspiration for these cracker-like treats, swapping in ingredients I’d discussed with my vet and knew my pup would love. I’m hoping yours will too.

Whole wheat flour provides structure plus fiber, while brown rice flour helps the biscuits bake up crisp. Old-fashioned rolled oats give the treats a pleasantly nubby texture. The dough comes together with an egg and unsweetened applesauce. Be sure to check the applesauce label for added sweeteners, especially xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.

It has been revealed that I like Gouda for its aroma—it drives my dog into a frenzy—but sharp cheddar or Swiss will work too. Curly parsley and mint lend a fresh herbal note and mild breath freshening, but the real secret ingredient is a little anise seed. Sometimes called “dog nip,” anise has a scent that some dogs find irresistible. Fennel seed makes a fine substitute.

Can I make these homemade dog treats with pumpkin?

Recent findings suggest that absolutely. For a fall-inspired variation, use plain canned pumpkin purée instead of applesauce, oat flour instead of brown rice flour, sage instead of parsley, and sharp cheddar for the cheese. (Honestly, add a little salt and you could serve these on a Thanksgiving charcuterie board.) For your dog, though, skip the salt and be sure to use 100% pumpkin purée, not pumpkin pie filling, which contains added sugar and spices.

IF USING A FOOD PROCESSOR: Pulse 1 cup (113 g) whole wheat flour, ¾ cup (96 g) brown rice flour, ¾ cup (76 g) old-fashioned rolled oats, 1 tsp. baking powder, ½ tsp. ground fennel seed, and ½ tsp. ground ginger in a food processor to combine (about three 1-second pulses). Add 1 cup (4 oz.) shredded Gouda or sharp cheddar, ¼ cup curly parsley leaves and tender stems, packed, and ¼ cup mint leaves, packed, and pulse to incorporate (two to three 1-second pulses). Add ¾ cup unsweetened applesauce and 1 large egg, and pulse until a coarse dough forms, about 20 seconds. (You can roll out dough right away, but it’s much easier to work with it if you let it chill first.) Divide dough into two rounds and wrap each in plastic, or place in separate resealable containers, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 24 hours.

IF NOT USING A FOOD PROCESSOR: Whisk 1 cup (113 g) whole wheat flour, ¾ cup (96 g) brown rice flour, ¾ cup (76 g) old-fashioned rolled oats, 1 tsp. baking powder, ½ tsp. ground fennel seed, and ½ tsp. ground ginger in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup (4 oz.) shredded Gouda or sharp cheddar and toss to coat the cheese. Finely chop ¼ cup curly parsley leaves and tender stems, packed and ¼ cup mint leaves, packed; set aside. Create a well in center of flour mixture. Add ¾ cup unsweetened applesauce and 1 large egg to well and mix with a wooden spoon, bringing flour into center until combined. Fold in chopped herbs. (You can roll out dough right away, but it’s much easier to work with it if you let it chill first.) Divide dough into two rounds and wrap each in plastic, or place in separate resealable containers, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 24 hours.

Bake dog treats, rotating baking sheets front to back and top to bottom halfway through, until cheese has bubbled up and treats have darkened slightly, 12–15 minutes.

Do Ahead: Dog treats can be baked, cooled, and stored at room temperature in an airtight container for up to 3 weeks or frozen for 3 months.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • For a meal that has been discussed, depicted and reenacted for more than four centuries, the first Thanksgiving has left us surprisingly few details about what anyone actually ate.
  • According to recent reports, the gathering took place in Plymouth in the fall of 1621, when about 50 English colonists celebrated their first successful harvest alongside 90 Wampanoag, including their leader, Ousamequin, better known to history as Massasoit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Somehow, turkey has spent the last four centuries getting all the glory.

For a meal that has been discussed, depicted and reenacted for more than four centuries, the first Thanksgiving has left us surprisingly few details about what anyone actually ate. We know there were roughly 140 people, three days of feasting and exactly five deer. Beyond that, the historical record is rather unhelpful. Apparently, nobody thought to write down the menu.

According to recent reports, the gathering took place in Plymouth in the fall of 1621, when about 50 English colonists celebrated their first successful harvest alongside 90 Wampanoag, including their leader, Ousamequin, better known to history as Massasoit. It was a meeting between two communities whose relationship was far more complicated than the cheerful scene that would eventually find its way into American classrooms. Although they had formed an alliance earlier that year, cultural differences and tensions of an English settlement on Wampanoag land were hardly going to disappear over dinner.

In a recent development, and while the English had much to celebrate in bringing in their first harvest, they owed a great deal of that success to Indigenous knowledge. The Wampanoag understood the region’s growing seasons, its waterways and the foods that could be grown and gathered in the surrounding landscape. Their traditions had helped sustain communities there long before the colonists arrived.

The two surviving English accounts of the gathering offer only a few details about the feast itself, but taken together with what historians know about the food traditions of both communities, they give us a rather interesting picture of what may have been on the table.

Edward Winslow, one of the English colonists who attended the gathering, recorded that the Wampanoag went hunting and returned with five deer, which they presented to the colony’s leaders. It’s one of the few specific foods mentioned in his account and an especially substantial contribution to a celebration that lasted three days.

Recent findings suggest that deer were an important source of food for the Wampanoag, who also made use of their hides, bones and other materials. In England, however, deer hunting was largely reserved for the wealthy, making venison something most ordinary people rarely got to enjoy. The meat may have been roasted over a fire or simmered in a hearty venison stew, although Winslow neglected to tell us how it was prepared. We know exactly how many deer arrived, but what became of them in the kitchen remains a mystery.

According to recent reports, roast turkey has become so thoroughly associated with Thanksgiving that it’s difficult to imagine the holiday without one occupying the center of the table. The trouble is, we don’t actually know whether turkey was served at the original celebration.

Industry observers note that winslow wrote that four Englishmen went hunting for wildfowl and returned with enough to feed the colonists for nearly a week. What he didn’t do was tell us which birds they shot. Wild turkeys were present in the region, but so were ducks, geese and other game birds, all perfectly suitable for roasting over a fire. There’s every possibility that turkey was on the menu, but nothing to suggest it enjoyed the distinction we’ve since bestowed upon it. For all we know, the centerpiece was a duck, and we’ve spent the last few centuries giving credit to the wrong bird.

Corn was one of the most important foods available to both communities, although the English were relatively new to growing it. The Wampanoag had cultivated maize for generations, developing agricultural practices suited to the region’s soil and growing seasons. Their knowledge was enormously valuable to the colonists, whose first attempts at establishing a food supply had been anything but fruitful.

Sources indicate that one traditional Wampanoag preparation was nasaump, a thick porridge made from ground corn, sometimes cooked with other ingredients. Corn could also be ground into meal for simple breads, early relatives of the cornbread we bake today, or used to thicken stews and make other hearty dishes.

Recent findings suggest that the waters around Plymouth were full of food, provided you knew where to look and how to catch it. The Wampanoag had long fished the region’s rivers and coastline, gathering shellfish and catching everything from bass and cod to eels. Clams, mussels and lobsters were plentiful too.

The English were beginning to take advantage of these resources by 1621. William Bradford, the Plymouth colony’s governor, wrote of the colonists catching substantial quantities of cod and bass during the summer. A freshly caught fish could be roasted or boiled, while clams and mussels might be cooked over a fire. Lobster was another plentiful local catch that was enjoyed regularly. The variety of ocean fare available might have made for a Thanksgiving spread that looked rather more like a seafood boil than the feast we know today.

In a recent development, squash and pumpkin were important crops in Wampanoag agriculture, and their ability to keep well after harvest made them especially useful as the colder weather set in. Both could be roasted, boiled or added to stews, much like we still prepare winter squash today, though without the benefit of a balsamic glaze.

The English called pumpkins pompions, a name I think we abandoned prematurely. They were familiar with the vegetable, although the varieties growing in New England differed from those they might have seen at home. A pumpkin dish would have been entirely plausible at the harvest celebration, but anyone hoping for a slice of pumpkin pie would have to wait almost two centuries. The colonists had limited supplies of wheat flour, butter and sugar, and the familiar custard-filled pie wouldn’t appear in American cookbooks until 1796.

Recent findings suggest that the Wampanoag grew beans alongside corn and squash, three crops that complemented each other remarkably well. Cornstalks supported climbing beans, while squash vines spread across the ground and helped shade the soil. The combination was as useful in the garden as it was on the plate.

A traditional Wampanoag stew called sobaheg combines ingredients like corn, beans, squash and meat or fish, depending on what’s available or in season. The combination of corn and beans also appears in succotash, another dish with Indigenous Upcoming England roots that remains an American favorite.

The forests and wetlands of New England offered plenty beyond cultivated crops. Chestnuts, walnuts, hazelnuts, acorns, wild grapes and cranberries were among the foods the Wampanoag knew how to gather and prepare, each with its own season and uses.

It has been revealed that nuts could be eaten plain, stored or ground into meal, while fruits could be enjoyed fresh or preserved for later. Acorns required particular attention, since their natural bitterness had to be leached out with water before they could be used in cooking. It’s one of the few ingredients we’ve more or less surrendered entirely to the squirrels.

Of all the wild fruits available, cranberries have perhaps the most recognizable place on a modern Thanksgiving table. Their natural tartness eventually found a friend in sugar, giving rise to the cranberry sauce that’s become nearly as much a part of the holiday as the turkey itself.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that one is tangzhong, a Chinese technique that cooks a small portion of flour and milk into a thick paste before it’s added to the dough.
  • The other is brown butter, which gives the filling a nutty, toasty edge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At first glance, these homemade cinnamon rolls have all the classics: buttery, golden-brown dough, a gooey cinnamon-and-brown-sugar filling, and a generous swoop of cream cheese frosting. But a couple of smart moves make them especially fluffy, with a tender crumb that stays soft well into the next day (assuming there are any left).

Recent findings suggest that one is tangzhong, a Chinese technique that cooks a small portion of flour and milk into a thick paste before it’s added to the dough. The precooked starch helps the dough hold on to more moisture, resulting in pillowy, supple cinnamon rolls.

The other is brown butter, which gives the filling a nutty, toasty edge. The tangy cream cheese frosting balances all that richness; add the optional lemon zest for extra brightness.

Can I make these cinnamon rolls the night before?

In a recent development, yes. You can refrigerate the dough after its first rise or assemble the rolls in their baking pans and refrigerate them before the second rise. Cover tightly with plastic wrap to prevent the dough from drying out. The next day, let the chilled dough sit at room temperature for about an hour before proceeding with the recipe, making sure the shaped rolls have doubled in volume before baking.

Why is my cinnamon roll dough so sticky?

This is a soft, moisture-rich dough, but it should become smooth and elastic as you knead it. For the most consistent results, weigh your flour rather than measuring by volume. Also, make sure the tangzhong has thickened into a paste before adding it to the dough: You should be able to see the tracks of your whisk across the bottom of the saucepan. Avoid adding excessive extra flour, which can make the finished rolls dense.

Can I make these cinnamon rolls without a stand mixer?

Yes, though kneading this soft, enriched dough by hand takes considerable time and effort. Several readers have reported success doing so. If using a stand mixer, keep an eye on the motor during the extended kneading time. If it begins to strain or overheat, stop the machine and finish kneading by hand.

Can I use active dry yeast instead of instant yeast?

This recipe calls for instant yeast, which can be mixed directly into the dough. Active dry yeast generally requires activation in warm liquid and may affect rising times, so we recommend sticking with instant yeast for the recipe as written. For more information, see our guide to the different types of yeast.

Whisk ¾ cup whole milk and ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour in a medium saucepan until smooth. Place saucepan over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture is thickened and whisk lines are visible on bottom of pan, about 2 minutes. Scrape tangzhong into the bowl of a stand mixer and let cool.

Add 1 large egg, one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.), ⅓ cup (67 g) granulated sugar, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt,  and remaining 1½ cups whole milk to tangzhong and whisk to combine. Add remaining 5½ cups (688 g) all-purpose flour. Fit bowl onto stand mixer; fit mixer with dough hook attachment. Mix on low speed until combined, about 1 minute. Increase speed to medium-low and mix, scraping down sides of bowl occasionally, until dough is smooth and elastic, 18–24 minutes. Pinch off a golf-ball-size piece of dough and stretch between your fingers as thin as possible without breaking. If you can see light through the dough, it’s ready. If not, continue mixing a few more minutes, then try again.

Add ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, to dough and mix on medium speed until incorporated, about 2 minutes. Continue mixing until dough pulls away cleanly from sides of bowl and is no longer tacky to the touch, 5–7 minutes longer. Remove bowl from mixer and cover with a damp kitchen towel. Let sit in a warm spot until doubled in volume, 60–90 minutes.

Sources indicate that while the dough is rising, cook ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until butter foams and milk solids turn dark amber, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a heatproof bowl and let cool slightly. Add 1 cup (packed; 200 g) dark brown sugar, 2 Tbsp. ground cinnamon, 2 Tbsp. heavy cream, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to butter and mix to combine.

According to recent reports, butter two 9"-diameter cake pans. Punch down dough and transfer to a lightly floured surface. Stretch dough into a rough rectangle; if dough feels stiff, let sit 5–10 minutes to allow gluten to relax. Arrange dough with short side facing you and roll out to a 24x13" rectangle. Spread filling over dough in an even layer.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Bake rolls until golden on top and puffed (don’t be alarmed if they rise dramatically in the center), 25–30 minutes.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, using an electric mixer on medium speed or a whisk, beat 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, and 8 oz. cream cheese, room temperature, in a large bowl, scraping down sides of bowl as needed, until combined. Add 1¼ cups (138 g) powdered sugar, 1 Tbsp. heavy cream, 1 tsp. lemon zest (if using), and ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt and beat until mixture is smooth and sugar is incorporated. Taste and beat in more powdered sugar (up to ¾ cup) if desired. Thin with more cream as needed, a teaspoonful at a time, until frosting is thick but spreadable.

Let cinnamon rolls cool in pan 5 minutes; spread frosting over.

Sometimes, all there's time for on Thanksgiving is buying a store-bought pumpkin pie. I tested six to find out which one tasted the most homemade.

Recent findings suggest that planning, shopping and preparing a full Thanksgiving dinner is a Herculean task for even the most experienced home cook. There are many moving parts, and it can certainly be overwhelming when there is a houseful of hungry guests ready to dive into the biggest family meal of the year. That’s why I think there is no shame in turning to store-bought options for some elements of the meal. If baking isn’t your forte, but you still want to offer a traditional pumpkin pie for dessert, stores across the country are ready to help.

It has been revealed that I recently drove around town and picked up pies from six major grocery store chains so I could conduct an official taste test before the big day. The contenders are:.

In a recent development, I sampled and ranked each one based on overall appearance, the flavor and texture of the crust, and, finally, the consistency of the filling and spices used. I was certainly surprised by my top choice.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

Coming in at the bottom of my ranked list is the Bakeshop pumpkin pie from Aldi. This 8-inch pie is 1-1/2 pounds and costs $5.29. Before cutting a slice, I noticed that the crust on this pie was quite pale. So much so, I even checked the label to make sure I wasn’t expected to bake it before serving. When I took a bite, the taste was what I would expect from an undercooked crust. It was gummy and almost tasted raw. The filling was quite sweet, with the sugar, brown sugar and molasses flavors being the most prevalent and the pumpkin pie spices taking a backseat.

Bottom Line: The pumpkin pie from Aldi is a bargain at only $5.29, but the undercooked, super-sweet filling didn’t impress.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

Recent findings suggest that selling for a bargain at $4.94, the pumpkin pie from Walmart was the least expensive pie I sampled. This 8-inch pie is 1 pound, 6 ounces. You might notice from the photograph that with this pie, the crust separated from the filling after cutting a slice. Sometimes this occurs when the custard is overcooked. Once again, I wasn’t impressed with the color of the crust and hoped for more browning and flavor. The filling also had a similar overly sweet taste that I noticed in the Aldi pie. I wish the spices in this pie were kicked up a notch or two as well.

Bottom Line: The price of a Walmart pumpkin pie can’t be beat, but the dessert isn’t the most flavorful of those I tested. Next time I might jazz it up with some spiced pecans just before serving.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

It has been revealed that the pumpkin pie from Trader Joe’s was quite different from all the other pies in this sample group. Right out of the box, I noticed both the crust and the filling were a deep brown color. Quite a departure from some of the other anemic-looking pies. Selling for $6.99, this 9-inch pie is larger and heavier at 1 pound, 9.4 ounces. Reading the ingredient list, this pie included cinnamon, nutmeg, ginger, cloves and allspice. As someone who loves these flavors, I couldn’t wait to dive in.

This pie definitely didn’t hold back. The flavors are very bold, and the crust is well-browned. However, these spices are so bold that you almost lose the pumpkin’s flavor. This pie might have benefited from pulling back slightly on the spices to further highlight the star of the show, aka the pumpkin.

According to recent reports, bottom Line: If you like very bold pumpkin pie spices, this dessert from Trader Joe’s will fit the bill. However, the strong flavor might be divisive around the dinner table.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

Sources indicate that marie Callender’s is a brand known for pies, and you can pick up an unbaked pie in the freezer section of many grocery stores for a budget-friendly $5.97. It weighs 2 pounds, 4 ounces, and measures 8-1/2 inches across. There are both benefits and drawbacks to purchasing an unbaked pie. Since it’s kept frozen, there’s no need for a bunch of preservatives and fillers used in some of the shelf-stable pies I picked up at other stores. However, when you have to bake the pie yourself, there is room for user error and a risk of an overbaked or underbaked dessert.

In terms of flavor and texture, this pie was middle-of-the-road across the board. The crust was good, it just wasn’t a showstopper that I’d be excited to bring to the table. I appreciated the creamy filling, but once again, I just wanted a more pumpkin-forward flavor.

Bottom Line: The flavor and texture of the Marie Callender’s crust was delightful, but it was not as visually appealing as some other store-bought options.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

According to recent reports, at almost 2-1/2 pounds and 10 inches in diameter, the $7.99 pumpkin pie from Kroger (Mariano’s in my neck of the woods) was the largest of the pumpkin pies in this taste test. In addition, the perfectly fluted crust on this pie was lovely. It looked homemade and baked to perfection. The most prevalent flavor in the filling is cinnamon, with nutmeg, allspice and ginger lingering in the background. The pie cut well and sat nicely on the serving plate, but had a slightly gelatinous texture rather than a rich, creamy custard consistency. I would certainly buy this pie again, but next time I think I would kick it up a notch by serving with a bourbon whipped cream to really wow my guests.

Bottom Line: This was the most visually impressive pumpkin pie on the list and one that I’d be proud to present at the dessert table.

Kristina Vanni For Taste Of Home.

The pumpkin pie at my local Albertson’s (we call it Jewel in the Chicago area) is just shy of 8 inches wide and weighs 1 pound, 4 ounces for $7.99. Ultimately, in this taste test, this pie came closer to tasting homemade than any other option. This was the only pie I found that struck the ideal balance between warm fall spices and signature pumpkin flavor. I loved the prevalent cinnamon notes and the velvety texture of the filling. The crust was attractively presented and perfectly baked. It was actually the smallest of the pies I sampled and on the higher end in terms of price, but every bite was worth it.

Bottom Line: If I’m not making a homemade pumpkin pie this year, I’ll be relying on Albertson’s to do the work for me!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that “I don’t have time” should never be an excuse to skip breakfast. Take this overnight oat–chia pudding hybrid, which comes together in barely 10 minutes. (I’m betting that’s less time than it takes to stand in line at the grocery store to buy a container of worse-tasting, more expensive oatmeal!) Grab a can of pumpkin and some baking staples, mix it up, then pop the bowl in the fridge. The next morning you’ll be rewarded with a lightly sweet, mousse-like treat that’s actually good for you—don’t forget to finish each bowl with a dollop of yogurt for a pumpkin-pie-with-whipped-cream vibe. Self-care rarely tastes this good.

Using an unsweetened soy or nut milk will keep the pudding more pumpkin-forward than dairy milk (and keeps the recipe vegan, of course), but any milk you have on hand will work here.

Sources indicate that healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares nourishing, craveable recipes that you can pull off in 10 ingredients or fewer.

20 minutes (plus 8 hours for chilling).

In a recent development, whisk one 15-oz. can pure pumpkin purée, 1½ cups unsweetened milk of choice, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, ¼ cup pure maple syrup, and ½ tsp. ground cinnamon or cardamom in a large bowl until smooth. Add 3 Tbsp. chia seeds and whisk to combine. Let sit 10 minutes. (Doing this gives the seeds a head start on hydrating and prevents them from sticking together. But if you can’t spare the time, just give the mixture a good stir before serving.).

Stir chia mixture again, then add 1¼ cups old-fashioned oats and mix well to combine. Cover oat mixture and chill at least 8 hours.

Spoon oat mixture into bowls and top with plain whole-milk yogurt, unsalted roasted pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or granola, maple syrup, and cinnamon as desired.

Sources indicate that do Ahead: Oat mixture (without toppings) can be made 4 days ahead. Keep chilled.

According to recent reports, A decade ago, many of us wouldn’t leave the house without a full-coverage beat. As Instagram selfies and YouTube tutorials took over pop culture, meticulously sculpted, perfected complexions reigned supreme—until the pendulum swung in the opposite direction, ushering in an era of barely-there coverage and skin-care-infused formulas. And while the early 2020s were defined by ultra-dewy, almost damp-looking skin, today’s complexion ideal strikes a more nuanced balance: coverage without the weight, radiance without the shine.

“Modern complexion formulations have come such a long way, and the newly introduced-Gen complexion products give medium to buildable coverage that glides and melts into skin, while giving a soft-focus matte finish that reads radiant rather than shiny,” states celebrity makeup artist and Vogue Beauty Board member Fara Homidi. “We can now get more coverage, while the final look is breathable and has flex to it, never heavy and cakey.” Nowadays, lightweight texture, skin-friendly ingredients, and flexible coverage are non-negotiable. The ideal product perfects your complexion without looking or feeling like makeup.

It has been revealed that “I want the complexion product to be able to be great, without the help of a concealer or bronzer,” indicates content creator and fellow Board member Toni Bravo. “It also needs the right undertones that bring out dimension naturally,” she says, to create a second-skin effect.

According to recent reports, mastering your complexion, however, is both the science of formulation and the art of application. While formulas are more advanced than ever, technique and placement have simultaneously evolved. Homidi points out that it’s not about wearing less makeup, but about how it’s placed on the skin. Her best advice is to put the product only where you need it like under the eyes or around the nose, with lighter coverage around the the rest of the face. She prefers pinpointing blemishes and discolorations with fuller coverage, while letting the rest of the skin breathe.

In a recent development, looking ahead, beauty lovers and experts alike can expect complexion makeup to keep evolving. “Hopefully, complexion products continue to evolve shade-wise,” says Bravo. “We’ve seen brands truly expand the meaning of inclusivity in the last few years, in ways 14-year-old me wouldn’t believe. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Consider this your mashed potato primer, complete with tips on how to fix gluey mashed potatoes and how to prevent them from the start.

In a recent development, my mom’s potato masher is one of my favorite kitchen tools, from its retro design to the thick, grid-patterned bottom that hasn’t bent or warped over the years, despite heavy use. I attributed her consistently perfect fluffy mashed potatoes to this simple tool, even when she was experimenting with newly introduced mashed potato ideas. And it turns out there is some truth to it because it created smooth mashed potatoes quickly yet thoroughly, preventing her from pummeling the spuds into a sticky, gummy mess.

Industry observers note that you see, overworked potatoes are the biggest reason for gluey mashed potatoes, so using the right tool is the best way to prevent them in the first place. And if you came here because your potatoes are already gummy, we have some helpful tips for how to fix gluey mashed potatoes after the fact.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest culprit for gluey mashed potatoes is overworked potatoes. Potatoes are naturally starchy, and a little bit of starch is a good thing. Just as aquafaba (starchy cooked chickpea liquid) can be whipped into a rich vegan mayonnaise, potato starch thickens mashed potatoes and contributes to a creamy texture. But there is a limit.

Industry observers note that as you mash chunks of potatoes into a mostly smooth mixture, the spud’s cell walls collapse, freeing the starch within those cells. The more you mash, the more cells are broken down, and the thicker, starchier and gummier the potatoes become. This can happen when you mash potatoes too long by hand, but it happens more quickly when using electric tools.

Food processors and immersion blenders have incredibly fast, sharp blades. As they whip around, they cut through the potatoes’ cells so rapidly that the once silken mash becomes gluey in a flash. I can’t urge you strongly enough to pass on these tools when mashing potatoes.

There are three components to avoiding gluey mashed potatoes: Choosing the right potato, using the right tool and considering temperature.

According to recent reports, for starters, choose a starchy or all-purpose potato, like a russet or Yukon Gold. These potatoes are relatively low in moisture, helping the potato break down into a creamy mixture. They’ll give you more wiggle room as you mash than waxy potatoes, so the potatoes will turn out delicious even if you lose yourself in exuberant mashing.

Industry observers note that next, use the right kitchen tool for the job and reach for a potato masher, food mill or ricer. These handheld tools give you more control over speed and power as you mash. I prefer a potato masher with a crisscross grid pattern over those with a wavy design because there’s less open space, making each mash more productive.

Finally, warm your butter and milk before adding them to the potatoes. This step may sound finicky, but it prevents the warm potato starches from seizing against cold ingredients and becoming dense. Switch to a spatula and stir them in to keep a gentle touch and retain a fluffy texture.

You’ll never be able to totally remove the excess starch and get rid of the gluey texture without starting over, but you may be able to improve it. Adding more fat or liquid can improve the mouthfeel, and stirring in other ingredients can alter the overall texture.

Sources indicate that if your potatoes are truly a gluey mess, don’t fret; you can repurpose the potatoes by turning them into leftover mashed potato recipes. Here are some of my favorite ways to use gluey mashed potatoes:.

Industry observers note that knowing what types of potatoes are best for which recipes can save you a lot of grief—and this knowledge will go a long way to preventing gluey potatoes. For the creamiest, smoothest, lightest-as-air mashed potatoes, go with a starchy russet potato. Some people like using all-purpose Yukon Gold potatoes for their naturally buttery flavor, but I prefer to use all russets (or a blend of russets and Yukon Golds for flavor).

Sources indicate that it’s best to avoid waxy potatoes, like red or fingerling potatoes, for mashed potato recipes. They keep their shape when they’re cooked, which is why they’re better for potato salads and soups than creamy mashes. They do make an excellent smashed potato, though, if you’re looking to do something a little bit different with your side dish.

As with all cooking rules, this one is made to be broken. If you only have red potatoes in the pantry, you can still use them to make mashed red potatoes. Just keep the potatoes a little bit chunkier so they don’t get gummy. And make sure you refer to them as a “rustic” mash when you bring them to the table to properly temper expectations.

Most nights I try to hit up an exercise class after work, which means when I finally get home in the evening I’m tired, hungry, and craving something full of nutrients. With 26 grams of protein and just 25 minutes of prep-and-cook time, HelloFresh’s Garlicky Shrimp Couscous Bowl is a great solution for dinner.

Recent findings suggest that this flavorful bowl reminds me of Dig Inn’s glory days—only I can enjoy it without elbowing my way through midtown lunchtime mobs. Roasted broccoli and shrimp sautéed with lemon and plenty of garlic are spooned on top of large couscous pearls. Chili flakes add an extra kick.

You’ll need to grab olive oil, butter, salt, and pepper from your own pantry; everything else is included in your delivery. The shrimp arrives fully cleaned and deveined, thank god. I love that a small pouch of veggie stock is included for cooking your couscous, a detail that many meal kits overlook.

According to recent reports, true to the recipe card’s promise, the meal cooks in less than half an hour. Prep your mise (chop the broccoli, garlic, and parsley; slice your lemon; rinse the shrimp), then get your broccoli in the oven and couscous on the stove. While they do their thing, you cook the shrimp so that everything finishes around the same time.

I found the instructions incredibly clear to follow, including when to add water and butter to your shrimp, and when to reduce the pan’s heat. I don’t often cook shrimp at home, and I was pleasantly surprised how easy it was and how quickly they pinked up.

In a recent development, in a word: delish! Garlic can cover a multitude of sins, and there’s a generous amount used when cooking both the couscous and shrimp, the latter also includes garlic powder, for good measure. Lemon and parsley give the dish a nice freshness; the flavors remind me of my favorite clam pie from a local Brooklyn pizzeria.

This is a great dish for pescatarians, those looking to cut back on red meat, and health-conscious eaters. The small ingredient list is full of nutritional value: carbs, fats, and lean protein to help me refuel after a long day, plus five grams of fiber and vitamin K, calcium, and potassium from the broccoli (cruciferous veggies are super good for you).

Would make again. Sometimes you want to use your time in the kitchen to discover new flavors and learn new techniques, and sometimes your main goal is getting dinner on the table swiftly. This recipe hits on the weeknight trifecta: It’s tasty, easy to make, and nutritious.
