Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Sources indicate that this holiday season, skip the mimosa and pour a poinsettia cocktail instead. It’s tart, sparkly and guaranteed to make any brunch feel like a holiday party.

Cranberries are a fast way to really make it feel like December has arrived. And this ruby-colored poinsettia cocktail, which gets its name from the brilliant red flowers in season at the same time, is our fresh go-to cranberry drink.

Recent findings suggest that this festive holiday cocktail doesn’t get any flavor from the poinsettia (definitely don’t eat those), but it matches the color of the flowers with a mix of tart cranberry juice and a splash of triple sec (for orange-y sweetness). It’s topped off with chilled champagne for festive effervescence. No shaker, no muddler, no syrup simmering on the stove. Just a sparkler you can pour for a crowd faster than my uncle can bring up politics.

Industry observers note that that’s exactly why this is my go-to pour for Christmas parties, New Year’s Eve countdowns or any cozy fall or winter get-together. You can pour a round for a crowd in the time it takes to find the bottle opener and a few fresh cranberries. A rosemary sprig makes every glass look like it belongs on a holiday card.

Pour the cranberry juice into a champagne flute or wine glass.

Editor’s Tip: Chill your glasses in the fridge or freezer for 10 to 15 minutes before pouring the cocktails. A cold glass keeps the drink crisp and helps hold onto the bubbles longer.

If you’re using it, add the triple sec to the glass with the cranberry juice.

Slowly top the glass with the chilled champagne.

Editor’s Tip: Tilt the glass slightly as you pour, just like you would with a beer, so the bubbles don’t foam up and spill over the rim.

In a recent development, if desired, drop a few fresh cranberries into the glass and tuck in a sprig of rosemary. Serve the cocktails right away while the bubbles are at their liveliest.

According to recent reports, poinsettias are best poured and enjoyed right away, since champagne goes flat rapidly once it’s opened and mixed. If you have extra cranberry juice and triple sec mixed up, cover it and refrigerate it for up to three days. Recork any leftover sparkling wine with a champagne stopper, and keep it in the fridge for a day or two.

Recent findings suggest that yes, partially. You can turn this into a batched cocktail by stirring together the cranberry juice and triple sec in a pitcher and chilling the mixture until party time. When guests arrive, pour about 1-1/2 ounces of the base into each glass and top it with champagne. Adding the bubbles at the last minute keeps every glass as sparkly as the first.

Recent findings suggest that it comes down to how sweet you like your drinks. Pure cranberry juice is tart and tangy, and the triple sec adds just enough sweetness to balance it without dulling that pucker. Cranberry juice cocktail, on the other hand, is usually sweetened and/or blended with other juices, so it makes a softer, sweeter poinsettia. If you’re serving a mixed crowd, I like to stick with the pure stuff and set out a little extra triple sec for anyone who wants it sweeter (and doubly, a bit boozier).

They’re very close relatives. A classic mimosa is roughly equal parts orange juice and champagne, while a poinsettia gets a smaller pour of cranberry juice, so it tastes more like champagne with a cranberry accent. The triple sec also sneaks in a little orange flavor, giving a nod to the mimosa. Plus, cranberry-orange recipes are always a hit!

Sources indicate that chilling everything ahead of time sets the stage for the best poinsettia. Since this drink is built in the glass and served without ice, it’s the cold juice and cold champagne that keep it refreshing. Warm champagne also foams up more when you pour it and loses its bubbles faster. Pop the juice and triple sec in the fridge a few hours before serving, and give your bubbly at least three hours in the fridge or 20 to 30 minutes in an ice bucket.

Latest Update: Where’d You Go, Crêpes Suzette?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1154 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s something simultaneously comforting and dazzling about setting a dessert on fire: Candles atop a birthday cake; the meringue encrusting a baked Alaska; the caramelized fruit in a classic bananas Foster.
  • It has been revealed that crêpes Suzette is a surprisingly simple dish considering its decadent, theatrical reputation.
  • In a recent development, for such a famous dish, though, its appearance on restaurant menus is increasingly rare.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s something simultaneously comforting and dazzling about setting a dessert on fire: Candles atop a birthday cake; the meringue encrusting a baked Alaska; the caramelized fruit in a classic bananas Foster. But chief among them is one whose very name promises something different, something with French sophistication and an air of mystery that demands a moniker all its own: crêpes Suzette.

It has been revealed that crêpes Suzette is a surprisingly simple dish considering its decadent, theatrical reputation. The drama comes from the flames—thin, traditional French crêpes are drenched in a sauce made of orange liqueur, which is then set ablaze (typically tableside in many restaurants), causing the spirits to simmer and the sugars to caramelize. French chef Andrea Calstier, of Michelin-starred La Bastide in North Salem, Latest York, grew up eating them with his family, and in the brasseries of his home country.

In a recent development, for such a famous dish, though, its appearance on restaurant menus is increasingly rare. And for such an iconic French dessert, well, it may not technically be French at all. So where did these flaming pancakes come from? Where did they go? And isn’t it about time we bring them back?

While there are conflicting reports about the original creator of crêpes Suzette, the top candidate is Henri Charpentier, chef at the Café de Paris in Monte Carlo, Monaco, in the late 1800s. But while multiple roads lead back to Charpentier, the path gets murky, contradicted by both general plausibility and Charpentier himself.

Originally, Charpentier claimed credit for the iconic dish in his autobiography, Life à la Henri: Being the Memoirs of Henri Charpentier. In this 1934 volume, he suggested that the dish was a happy accident, tinged with drama. He alleged that as a young man working at the Café de Paris, he had been carrying a platter of crêpes to the Prince of Wales (the future King Edward VII) and stepped too near a chafing dish, setting the crêpes on fire, to the shock and delight of the prince, who proposed naming the newly created dish after his dining companion, a young woman named Suzette. (Frustratingly little information is available on who this Suzette may have been, if she was a real person at all.).

The story has the right theatrical touches for the dish, but it is almost certainly apocryphal, not least because Charpentier himself, in an interview with American writer Elsie Lee for the 1950s “Compleat Imbiber” series, said that he had developed the dish by taking a beloved childhood fruit crêpe and adding the then-fashionable touches of a liquor-based sauce and, presumably, a flame.

Wherever it came from, though, and whatever Charpentier had to say about it, Suzette’s unwitting legacy has endured for more than a century—her crêpes have remained a household name, even if they have fallen somewhat out of style. While chef Calstier notes that they’re still “served in many restaurants” in his native Marseille and that “French customers…are accustomed to seeing crêpes Suzette in any brasserie,” he admitted that “here in the U.S., they are more difficult to find.”.

Part of the reason may be that, as with many dishes that predate the Edwardian era, it simply went out of fashion. But according to Lucile Plaza, executive chef at Benoit Fresh York, it’s a result of the dish’s inherent service requirements: “True tableside service requires high staffing levels and precise choreography that a busy modern kitchen can’t always support daily,” she states. In London’s West End, fine-dining heavyweights Savoy Grill and The Ritz take this showmanship to the extreme, with portable burners and bottles of Grand Marnier on wooden trolleys.

But while there are complications to adding an edible spectacle to a restaurant menu, there are benefits, too. Chef Plaza notes that for the kitchen, “Suzette is brilliant because it is the ultimate way to use leftover crêpes. The intense bathing in the hot, rich citrus sauce revives the starch perfectly.” But not every restaurant that serves crêpes Suzette does so with a tableside flourish: In London’s St. John’s Wood, Oslo Court Restaurant, which is famous for its retro menu of classics like steak Diane and sole Veronique (two more of Edward VII's girlfriends, perhaps?), crêpes Suzette are brûléed with a torch in the kitchen rather than set aflame at the table. Adding crêpes Suzette to a menu may only be as hard as a restaurant wants it to be.

A burst of blue-tinged flame may not be necessary for the dish to achieve its signature caramelization, but it is key to the show—and a major point in favor of the dish’s present-day revival. As the old saying goes, “we eat with our eyes first,” and it’s truer than ever today. In fact, for many diners in the age of social media, it’s the phone that eats first, and that’s where crêpes Suzette has real potential for a modern renaissance. Nearly 400,000 viewers have watched a YouTube video of the tableside crêpes Suzette service at the London Ritz, and more than a million have viewed a TikTok of crêpes Suzette being prepared tableside at Switzerland’s five-star Suvretta House in Saint Moritz.

According to recent reports, spectacle is cool again, and whether dining out or cooking at home, we want to feel astonished and excited by the foods we eat. While a tableside flambé may prove logistically complicated at a restaurant scale, the feat is significantly easier to pull off at home—all it takes is a lighter or a match and a little confidence. Chef Calstier, for one, states that crêpes Suzette are a favorite of his wife, Elena, adding, “You can prepare everything in advance and do the flambé in front of your guests to wow them.” Plus, he says, “they don’t require many ingredients, beyond that bottle of Grand Marnier that we all have stashed away somewhere. They’re quite simple to make.”.

It has been revealed that moreover, as delectable as classic crêpes Suzette are, they lend themselves well to newly introduced takes and customizations. Chef Plaza’s version at Benoit has a cherry twist: “Replacing Grand Marnier with kirsch is a natural match,” she indicates. “The dry cherry distillate brings an incredible aroma to the tableside without adding cloying sugar.” Meanwhile, at La Bastide, chef Calstier dishes up a twist that uses French toast instead of crêpes while sticking to the classic flavors and flambé. We asked one of our favorite pastry chefs, Caroline Schiff, author of Daily Desserts: Treats on Repeat, to develop a savory version for us, which she describes as “a cheeky little twist” on the classic. In her take, inspired by French onion soup, crêpes layered with caramelized onions and nutty gruyère are set ablaze with a splash of sherry. “They are at once a novelty and a nod to the classic,” she says.

Charpentier, one imagines, would approve.

Tech Report: In Alison Roman's World, Curation is King

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (683 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, with only weeks before opening, Alison Roman’s Brooklyn brick-and-mortar is still unfinished.
  • Sources indicate that the chaos doesn’t seem to be getting to the cookbook author, chef, and aspiring empire-builder.
  • Recent findings suggest that what Roman has built has grown beyond recipes and bean propaganda.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, with only weeks before opening, Alison Roman’s Brooklyn brick-and-mortar is still unfinished. “Today they’re doing up the walls and putting in the floors,” Roman says. In short, it does not yet look like a dreamy European-inspired grocer. There are still a mountain of calls to be made, meetings to be had, speed bumps to overcome.

Sources indicate that the chaos doesn’t seem to be getting to the cookbook author, chef, and aspiring empire-builder. “It’s been so fun,” Roman, a Bon Appétit alum, indicates of the process. Perhaps that shouldn’t be a surprise; this breezy effortlessness is at the bedrock of the Alison Roman universe. You know the kind of nonchalant magic I’m talking about: chilling wine bottles in a bathtub of ice, buckets of take-out fried chicken at dinner parties—I mean, this woman was one of the foremost proponents of brothy beans.

Recent findings suggest that what Roman has built has grown beyond recipes and bean propaganda. The ever-creeping edges of her lifestyle brand now encompass a jarred tomato sauce brand, once cheekily titled A Very Good Sauce, now renamed Roman’s. There’s also the new podcast, Having People Over, where she hosts guests for a meal and a yap, plus the speaking tour she’s calling “Food, Life and Other Strong Opinions.” There are the shoes (sleek mules and chunky clogs) she made in collaboration with New York–based footwear brand Margaux. And now First Bloom, the grocery store–slash–wine bar–slash–café that—as of mid-November—is on track to open in December.

The Brooklyn shop is an extension of the original Catskill’s location of the same name. Roman says this newly introduced outpost is “a totally different proposition of what we are offering people.” There’s more budget to work with, there’s more staff, there’s more space, and there’s more food.

Whereas the upstate location’s function is closer to utility—meat and produce from local farms are a major feature—in Brooklyn (where specialty grocers abound) Roman is focusing on something more akin to world-building. But do not call First Bloom a shoppy shop, those whimsically designed boutiques that seem to pop up everywhere selling the same $45 squiggly candlesticks and squeeze-bottle olive oils everyone seems to have. “I think ‘shoppy shop’ is derogatory,” Roman notes. “In a world where you can buy anything from anywhere, sometimes it’s nice to be told what to do.”.

In a recent development, at Brooklyn’s First Bloom, the shelves will be stocked with products that Roman herself deems “hyper-defensible.” There’s a reason they’re stocked, and a reason for how they’re priced. They’re best in class or a personal favorite of Roman’s. “Perspective and curation is a really special thing to be able to convey,” she says.

Industry observers note that the vision for First Bloom is set, but with the opening just a month out, Roman doesn’t have all the details nailed down. “We are going to have a rotisserie chicken,” she states. “I don’t know how much it’s going to cost yet,” she follows up rapidly, before I can ask. There will also be a couple salads and a couple sandwiches on offer—plus another secret off-menu sandwich for the neighborhood regulars and the real Roman-heads who know to ask for it. “I’m very if-you-know-you know,’” she says. But Brooklyn’s First Bloom isn’t just for popping into—you’ll be able to lounge with a glass of wine or relax with a snack and a coffee.

It has been revealed that alison Roman’s world is organic, craft-centered, and easy but considered. To step into it is an enticing foil to the AI-fueled tasteslop tilt-a-whirl on which we find ourselves. It’s a vision of a slow, steady, wabi-sabi life that many of us only aspire to. A life where one can even somehow enjoy, say, a monthslong commercial renovation project in one of America’s most competitive real estate markets. That’s the draw of First Bloom. The hard-to-find tinned fish, yes, but also the ease of living in Alison’s world if only for an hour.

And if not, well, it seems like there’ll be a pretty good rotisserie chicken, at least.
